papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Efficient and Robust Deep Models: Evidence, Techniques, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student transfer recipe into a broad set of methods that enable model compression, robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving training, and architectural search. Across modalities and tasks—NLP, speech, vision, graphs, ranking and recommender systems—KD-based approaches consistently trade minimal performance loss for large gains in speed, memory, interpretability or deployability. The diversity of KD formulations (feature-based, layer-mapping, data-free, online/mutual, multi-teacher, meta-learned teachers, and task-adaptive compression) provides practitioners with targeted tools to address constraints such as limited data, non-iid federated shards, low-frequency tokens in translation, and privacy requirements. Based on empirical results across the literature, KD should be considered a first-order technique in any pipeline that must deliver high-quality models under resource, privacy, or latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and often indispensable method for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance when its objectives, data strategies, and student architectures are chosen with task and deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability, and explicit handling of transferred errors, biases, and rare-case failures. For robust, production-ready compression, KD should be applied as a configurable, task-aware element of an integrated compression pipeline that also leverages representation-aware objectives, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary architecture-aware transformations.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied compression techniques provide a practical toolkit for shrinking large deep models into smaller, deployable ones while retaining much of their task performance. Over the last decade researchers have developed a range of distillation targets (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention and relational maps, contrastive signals), teacher-student schedules (offline, online, multi-teacher, lifelong), and complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search, block-structured pruning). Empirical work shows KD often acts both as information transfer and regularization, enabling deployment across vision, language, multimodal, graph, generative, and medical-imaging tasks; however, success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of propagated errors or biases. Best practice is task- and capacity-aware design that combines appropriate distilled signals, alignment of inputs/representations, and complementary compression methods to meet target constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while enabling adaptation across tasks, domains, and modalities. When combined with representation-level objectives, careful teacher engineering, pre-training of compact architectures, and input-side interventions (e.g., augmentation or data synthesis), KD routinely yields large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss and can enable deployment under tight compute, latency, or privacy constraints. At the same time, KD is not a single recipe: success depends on optimization choices, teacher–student alignment, and dataset properties, which motivates tailored distillation objectives, data strategies, and evaluation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Gross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Path for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical tool that enables deployment of compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teachers to smaller students. KD supports many transfer targets and protocols and can materially reduce model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal cure: success depends on task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. The most reliable deployments treat KD as the central element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than the sole method.

papers_seen.author: Horton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context-Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applied family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. KD routinely achieves strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across modalities and tasks when its objectives, teacher–student design, data strategies, and complementary compression methods are chosen with deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and distribution, and explicit safeguards against bias, robustness, and privacy failures. Best practice treats KD as a configurable building block embedded in an integrated compression pipeline tailored to the task and environment.

papers_seen.author: Robertson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. The literature shows that appropriately chosen distillation signals, teacher–student design, and data strategies allow compact models to recover much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and deployment cost. Practical pipelines commonly combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and adapt to constraints such as privacy, heterogeneous devices, and limited or unlabeled data. Despite widespread empirical success, important limitations persist—teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, degraded rare-output behavior, and theoretical gaps linking distillation signals to student generalization—motivating ongoing work in adaptive teacher selection, data-free distillation, and task-aware compression design.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a configurable toolkit—selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or task-adaptive architecture search)—practitioners routinely obtain compact models that retain much of teacher performance. Success requires explicit attention to teacher quality, data availability or synthesis, optimization schedules, and safeguards against transferred biases or degraded rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Orr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Theory, and Practical Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques for transferring information from high-capacity teacher models to smaller or otherwise constrained student models so they retain functionality while reducing latency, memory, and computational cost. Over the past decade KD has evolved from logits-based soft-label supervision to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-feature matching, layer-wise and task-aware mappings, adversarial and contrastive objectives, ensemble and self-distillation, data-free synthesis, and federated or heterogeneous-device protocols. Empirical and theoretical work indicates KD often acts both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, task alignment, and careful design of objectives and model interfaces. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data scarcity or domain shift, preserving rare-token behavior in sequence tasks, principled layer-to-layer alignment across heterogeneous architectures, and mitigating teacher-induced biases.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while retaining much of teacher performance. A diverse set of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals; offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free variants). Empirical work across vision, language, speech and multimodal tasks shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and when training/data procedures are adapted to task and deployment constraints. Remaining gaps include principled layer alignment across heterogeneous architectures, robust distillation under limited or private data, preservation of long‑tail/low‑frequency behaviors, and theoretical understanding of when particular teacher signals are necessary.

papers_seen.author: Manning
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient — A Position and Recommended Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. Empirical evidence across vision and language shows that KD can reduce inference cost, latency, and memory requirements and enable deployment under privacy, communication, and resource constraints. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, unbiased, or optimal compressed models: failures arise from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, transfer of teacher errors and biases, poor handling of low-frequency phenomena, and vulnerability under distribution shift or adversarial attack. Practical compression therefore treats KD as a core component within an integrated pipeline—combining representation-aware objectives, curriculum and sample-selection strategies, adversarial or synthetic-data generation for data-scarce regimes, and complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to realize reliable, resource-aware students.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods include soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online and data-free protocols, and teacher/student co-design; in practice KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware engineering. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation under limited or mismatched data, mitigation of transferred biases and degraded rare-token behavior, principled selection of distillation targets, and automated hardware-aware co-design.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Evidence, Methods, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practically validated set of techniques for transferring information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. A broad toolkit—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or privacy-aware synthesis, and curriculum or adversarial sample selection—enables students to retain much of teacher performance across vision, language, multimodal, retrieval, and federated settings. Despite strong empirical successes, important engineering and scientific challenges remain around teacher–student alignment, data availability and synthesis, preservation of low-frequency behaviors, robustness and fairness, and principled automated design for heterogeneous deployment environments.

papers_seen.author: Ramsey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly effective and widely adopted framework for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD is best understood as a configurable core technique: it provides many transferable signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, contrastive objectives, and synthesized data), and—when combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search and coupled with task‑aware data strategies—can enable large reductions in size and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. However, KD is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data regime, and explicit measures for robustness, privacy, and fairness strongly shape outcomes. Practitioners should therefore treat KD as an essential but non‑turnkey component of integrated compression pipelines, selecting targets, mapping strategies, and safeguards to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Francis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques constitute a practical toolkit for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. The field has expanded beyond simple logits-matching to include intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free generation, curriculum and online protocols, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when student capacity, data availability, and teacher–student alignment are appropriately managed, but important challenges remain including handling low-frequency phenomena, teacher bias propagation, distributional mismatch, and reliable transfer under data scarcity or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Reed
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated framework for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. KD encompasses multiple transfer signals and training protocols and is most effective when designed with task- and deployment-awareness. While KD frequently yields large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss, reliable deployment requires combining KD with complementary compression primitives and explicit measures to mitigate teacher imperfection, data scarcity, distribution shift, and bias propagation.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practically effective family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to compact students. KD methods differ in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, online, or self-distillation), and how distillation interacts with data constraints, privacy, and complementary compression primitives. Empirically, KD is widely applied across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, federated settings, and reinforcement learning; its success depends on teacher quality, data and augmentation choices, and architecture alignment, and common failure modes include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, and difficulty with low-frequency phenomena. Practical deployment treats KD as a task-aware component within an integrated compression pipeline combining pruning, quantization, architecture search, and careful data or objective design.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression — Powerful but Not Sufficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods (soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational objectives, and data- or generator-based synthesis) repeatedly enable large reductions in model size and inference cost when combined with task-aware design and complementary compression primitives. However, KD's success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, distribution shift, and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Treating KD as a configurable component of integrated compression pipelines, rather than a one-shot cure, leads to more reliable and deployable compact models.

papers_seen.author: Galloway
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Versatile Framework for Model Compression: Evidence, Limits, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable framework for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities, deployment constraints, and learning paradigms. Empirical work shows KD can produce compact models that approach teacher performance while enabling domain adaptation, federated and privacy-aware training, multimodal-to-mono-modal transfer, and efficient generative models. However, KD is not a panacea: optimization difficulties, propagation of teacher errors, sensitivity to teacher strength and data regime, and task-specific issues (e.g., generation vs. classification) require targeted algorithmic refinements. Advances such as feature-based distillation, adversarial and curriculum-based schemes, data augmentation during distillation, meta-learned teachers, and teacher-free formulations mitigate many failure modes and extend KD to low-data, heterogeneous-device, and few-shot settings. The combination of these innovations positions KD as a central tool for practical model compression and adaptation when used with methods that explicitly address its known limitations.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Barker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad and practical toolkit—ranging from soft-label/logit matching to intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free protocols, and multi-teacher or self-distillation schemes—has been developed and applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks. KD frequently produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its success depends on careful design choices for distillation targets, teacher–student compatibility, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Thompson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful and empirically validated approach for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment, privacy-aware releases, and domain adaptation when designed with task- and data-awareness. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and match of data, and careful handling of transferred biases and low-frequency phenomena. The strongest practical systems treat KD as a central component within an integrated compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture search, and targeted data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated as the practical, flexible core of an integrated model-compression pipeline: it often yields the largest efficiency gains for deployment while requiring careful, task-aware design and combination with complementary techniques. KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost, latency, and memory across modalities, but reliable deployment demands attention to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data strategy, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and long-tail behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Curry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses information from large teacher models into smaller student models to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Research and practice have developed a diverse toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, using contrastive/relational objectives, generating or selecting distillation data, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combining KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work across vision, language, recommendation, speech, and multimodal tasks shows distilled students frequently recover much of teacher performance, though effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and alignment of objectives and representations. Key open problems include reliable transfer of rare or structured behaviors, robust distillation under data heterogeneity and privacy constraints, principled teacher selection and co-design, and automated, task-aware distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Terry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, empirically grounded toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners choose among soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or federated protocols; these methods are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Success depends on principled choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and targeted mitigations for transferred biases and distribution-shift failures.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Context‑Sensitive, and Best Used in Hybrid Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically proven technique for converting large teacher models into smaller, efficient students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD reliably reduces latency, memory, and energy costs and can transfer robustness or domain knowledge, but it is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher and student design, data regime, and deployment constraints. For robust, deployable compression, KD is best treated as a configurable core component within integrated pipelines that combine representation-aware objectives, data strategies, and complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical, widely used toolbox to transfer behavior and representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, resource-efficient students. The approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel statistics, or generated samples), whether original training data are available, and whether the objective emphasizes efficiency, privacy, robustness, or interpretability. Across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks, carefully designed distillation objectives and training pipelines—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search—produce compact models that approach teacher performance under deployment constraints. Key practical challenges are capacity and optimization mismatch between teacher and student, data- and privacy-limited settings, distribution shift and low-frequency phenomena, and the risk of transferring undesirable teacher traits; promising responses include task-aware filtering of teacher signals, multi-layer mapping strategies, data-free sample synthesis, and privacy-preserving noise mechanisms.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational, Versatile, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to meet deployment, privacy, and latency constraints. KD spans logits-based supervision, representation and feature matching, adversarial and generator-based data synthesis, multi-teacher or online schemes, and task- and domain-aware adaptations. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful training practices (projectors, curriculum, selective sampling), KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable new capabilities (cross-domain transfer, federated heterogeneity, and multi-modal compression). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), distribution shift, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Practitioners should treat KD as a flexible framework that must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Wolf
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression: Central, Practical, but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely used family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD methods have expanded from simple logits-matching to include feature- and layer-level imitation, self-distillation, data-free and federated protocols, and many-to-many teacher–student mappings. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD regularly yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and data availability or synthesis. KD is best treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, augmentation, or synthetic-data strategies—rather than as a standalone panacea.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. Across modalities and tasks, a diverse toolkit — including logits/soft-target matching, feature- and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online and data-free protocols, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design — has been shown to deliver large efficiency gains with modest performance loss when applied with task-aware engineering. Important remaining challenges include theoretical understanding of what is transferred, robust and private distillation under data scarcity or distribution shift, and reliably preserving fine-grained or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Chandler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal domains, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving much of teacher performance; it is most effective when combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation, and hardware-aware design). The literature also highlights several persistent challenges — teacher and capacity mismatch, optimization and data limitations, privacy and distribution shift — and converges on practical strategies such as careful choice of distillation signals, layer alignment, multi-teacher or online protocols, and synthetic-data or data-free approaches to operate under constrained access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, pragmatic set of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models into smaller student models so that compact models can preserve much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD is effective across modalities and tasks when its objectives, training protocols, and data strategies are chosen to match the task, teacher–student capacities, and deployment constraints; however, KD has clear failure modes and limits that require integrated mitigation. I argue that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of end-to-end compression pipelines rather than a standalone, one-size-fits-all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Hines
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Conditional, and Best Used in Hybrid Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a substantial fraction of teacher performance and is essential for latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployments. However, KD’s reliability is conditional: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, choice of distillation signals, and data strategy strongly affect outcomes. Best practice treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines distillation with pretraining, data selection or synthesis, pruning/quantization, and architecture-aware design to mitigate failure modes such as teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency degradation, bias transfer, and distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Ashley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Patterns, and Practical Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD variants include matching teacher logits, imitating intermediate representations, aligning attention or relational structures, ensembling multiple teachers, adversarial and data-free distillation, and student- or task-aware curricula. KD is commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adapted for settings with limited or private data, federated training, and non‑standard outputs (e.g., generative or structured prediction). Empirically, thoughtfully designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and in many cases enable practical deployment trade-offs, but they are not universally effective: success depends on student capacity, data and distribution match, choice of teacher signals, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and rare‑phenomena degradation. Ongoing research focuses on principled objectives, robust and private distillation, and task‑aware architectures for structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, practical toolbox for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. The field encompasses a diverse set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational maps, contrastive signals), multiple training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, multi-teacher and ensemble schemes), and data strategies that include data-driven, synthetic, and data-free approaches. KD is routinely integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and applied across modalities (NLP, vision, speech, generative models, recommender and graph systems). Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the distillation signal and its alignment, and the availability and curation of data; remaining challenges include preserving low-frequency behaviors, avoiding transfer of teacher biases, and maintaining robustness under distribution shift and limited-data regimes. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an overall compression pipeline with task-aware signal selection, careful teacher–student co-design, and targeted mitigations for privacy, fairness, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Mcintyre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models so they run under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structures, adversarial or data-free synthesis) and are routinely combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multilingual tasks shows that properly designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful choice of objectives and layer mappings. Important open problems include robust data-free distillation, principled transfer choices for heterogeneous architectures, and controls for fairness and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies have become central to deploying large neural networks in resource-constrained settings. Across vision, multimodal, and language domains, researchers have developed approaches that transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller students via logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or adversarial objectives. Work spans supervised and unsupervised settings, data-free or black-box scenarios, continual and federated use-cases, and concerns such as privacy and adversarial robustness. Practical recipes combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, progressive module replacement, and many-to-many layer mapping to balance accuracy, latency, and memory. Open challenges remain in data- and domain-limited regimes, robust and private compression, and principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer for a given downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Solis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD methods span output-level supervision, intermediate-representation matching, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and many-to-many layer mappings, and are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. When applied with task-awareness — i.e., selecting appropriate distilled signals, matching teacher and student capacity, and adapting data and optimization — KD reliably delivers favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision, language, speech, detection, and federated settings. Nevertheless, KD has well-documented failure modes (capacity and optimization gaps, bias transfer, degradation on rare phenomena, and privacy concerns), and future progress depends on principled theory, automation of teacher–student matching, and responsible, privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Bryant
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential and practical family of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory while often preserving much of a teacher’s performance, but it is not a standalone cure: success depends on careful choices of transfer targets, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. For reliable deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable, task‑aware core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware objectives, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design).

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Mcguire
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Dependent Component of Compression Portfolios
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces the deployment cost of large deep models while preserving much of their predictive and representational power. Rather than being a single recipe, KD is best treated as a flexible, task- and capacity-aware instrument that should be combined with complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with careful choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate teacher-induced failure modes for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Bates
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically oriented set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory use, latency, and communication while often retaining much of task performance. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple logit/soft-target matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, data‑ and privacy‑aware protocols, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success is highly context dependent: it depends on teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and choice of distillation data (or synthetic alternatives), and explicit handling of transferred biases, low‑frequency phenomena, and distribution shift. Practical deployments treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines, applying task‑aware objective design, layer mapping, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a narrow training trick into a broad, practical paradigm for compressing and adapting large deep models to resource- and data-constrained deployment settings. A rich family of KD formulations — from logit matching and feature imitation to adversarial, data-free, and online schemes — together with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and teacher ensembles) enables substantial reductions in memory and latency while largely preserving model quality. However, KD is not universally effective out-of-the-box: its benefits and risks depend on task characteristics, data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and deliberate choices of what and how to transfer. When practitioners treat KD as a toolkit of targeted strategies and validate choices against task constraints, it yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity to the original model.

papers_seen.author: Wallace
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically proven family of methods for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD spans outputs-only approaches (soft targets) to rich objectives that match intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure, or contrastive signals. It operates across many data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free, synthetic-data), and is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to achieve deployment constraints on latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity. The effectiveness of KD is strongly context dependent: success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and layer mappings, and data strategies (including augmentation, curriculum, and synthetic generation). Common failure modes include propagation of teacher errors or biases, difficulty preserving low-frequency or long-tail behaviors, and optimization barriers that prevent perfect mimicry, motivating targeted remedies such as multi-signal objectives, multi-teacher ensembles, teacher scheduling, meta-learned teachers, and joint optimization with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Durham
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of methods for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants—from soft-logit supervision to intermediate-feature and relational/contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols—enable reduced memory, latency, and communication costs while often preserving most teacher performance. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and task- or data-aware procedures; its reliable application requires explicit attention to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, optimization schedules, and safeguards for bias, rare-case behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically effective family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals) and across training protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation and data-free synthesis). Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in inference cost and memory footprint, but outcomes are highly context-sensitive: they depend on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and distribution of data, and the choice of distillation objectives and layer mappings. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component within hybrid compression pipelines that combine pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and privacy- or domain-aware interventions.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically validated framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational and contrastive signals), can operate in multi-teacher and data-free settings, and integrates with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data strategy (including synthetic or public data when originals are unavailable), and task-aware objective design. KD has documented failure modes — e.g., propagation of teacher errors or biases, difficulty preserving low-frequency phenomena, and distributional mismatch — which motivate targeted remedies such as multi-signal objectives, teacher scheduling, meta-learned teachers, and joint optimization with other compression tools. Treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a single recipe, KD is an essential practical tool for model deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Collier
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, broadly applicable family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Empirically KD often recovers much of teacher performance and enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and inference cost, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and nature of distillation data, and the choice of distilled signals. For robust, production-ready compression KD should be treated as a configurable core that is integrated with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data and curriculum strategies, and explicit safeguards for bias, robustness, and low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Gallegos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and versatile approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical evidence across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows KD routinely recovers much of the teacher’s performance and enables practical deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a drop‑in solution: its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and nature of distillation data, and explicit measures to mitigate failure modes such as bias transfer, optimization gaps, and degraded handling of low‑frequency phenomena. Treating KD as a configurable, task‑aware core within an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, and robustness/fairness safeguards—yields the most reliable path to deployable, efficient models.

papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile family of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial or data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher protocols—have been shown to recover much of a teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and computational cost. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful selection of what and how to transfer; open challenges remain in robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and enabling private or data-free distillation at scale.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware Core of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely yields substantial latency and memory reductions while retaining much teacher performance when it is applied as part of an integrated, task- and data-aware compression pipeline. However, KD is context-sensitive: its reliability depends on choices of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies (including synthetic or teacher-generated data), and explicit measures to avoid propagating teacher artifacts or biases.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal information from large teacher models into smaller student models so that students retain much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and deployment constraints. KD has been adapted across logits-, feature-, and relation-level objectives, combined with complementary compression primitives, and applied in specialized settings (federated, data-free, recommender, and generative). Its practical value is substantial, but realizing that value requires careful design choices around what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate failure modes such as teacher bias, low-frequency degradation, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Vasquez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise deployment‑suitable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners use logits/soft targets, intermediate feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, and data‑side strategies (including data‑free synthesis and augmentation). KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when its design is adapted to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints. Important limitations include capacity mismatch, teacher error or bias transfer, distribution shift, and challenges in preserving low‑frequency or long‑tail behavior; addressing these requires task‑aware objective design, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and hardware constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate features, attention/relational signals) and in diverse protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free). Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of a teacher's performance and can even improve generalization in some settings, but it also has well-known failure modes—teacher bias propagation, difficulty preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and sensitivity to data availability and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, as well as careful data and objective design.
