papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically effective approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students. While KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and supports deployment under compute, latency, and privacy constraints, its reliability depends on task-aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data regimes, and complementary compression methods. papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted set of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. The field encompasses many distillation targets and training protocols, and KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies. Empirical work shows KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but practical success depends on teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and deliberate mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, degraded rare-token behavior, and distribution shift. Ongoing challenges include principled theory of what transfers, reliable distillation in low-data or heterogeneous regimes, preserving long‑tail behaviors, and automated, hardware‑aware co‑design.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. KD methods encompass soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and data‑free protocols, and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. While KD frequently recovers a large portion of teacher performance and enables deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints, its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity, choice of distilled signals, and data regime. For robust, high-fidelity compression, KD is best treated as a configurable component of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline that includes safeguards and complementary techniques to address known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Hardy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and representations from larger (teacher) models into smaller (student) models, enabling deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain mismatch. Across vision, language, multimodal and generative settings, distillation has expanded from logits matching to a diverse toolbox that includes feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, online and self-distillation, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization and architecture search. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and stabilizes student training, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, availability and selection of data, and defenses against transferred biases and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Practical deployments therefore treat distillation as a configurable component within compression pipelines, pairing distilled signals with task- and deployment-aware engineering.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential, empirically validated approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. KD methods—ranging from soft‑logit matching to intermediate‑feature and attention transfers, adversarial or contrastive objectives, and multi‑teacher schemes—regularly enable large reductions in inference cost and parameter footprint while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD’s effectiveness is strongly dependent on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data availability and quality, and optimization dynamics; therefore, reliable compression in practice requires combining KD with task‑aware design choices and complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis) and explicit mitigation strategies for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide flexible, broadly applicable ways to transfer performance from large teacher models to compact student models so they can run under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. A diverse set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel maps, relational signals) and procedures (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, meta-learned teachers, data-free synthesis) have been developed and integrated with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, ensembling). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, graphs, and recommendation systems shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve deployability, though success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases. Remaining directions include automated, task-adaptive transfer choices, robust data-free distillation, and principled controls for fairness and distribution shift.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfers information from larger or composite teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource or privacy constraints, and sometimes improve generalization. KD methods include matching teacher logits, imitating intermediate representations, aligning attention or relational structure, adversarial and data-free approaches, and online or multi‑teacher schemes. Empirical practice shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when integrated into task-aware compression pipelines, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the data used for transfer, and complementary compression choices such as pruning or quantization. Open challenges remain in reliably transferring robustness, handling distribution shift and long-tail behaviors, and formalizing automated teacher–student design for varied deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential but Insufficient — Toward Integrated, Task‑Aware Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile way to compress large models into smaller students that retain much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under constraints of latency, memory, and privacy. KD variants span logits matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, multi- and self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. However, KD is not a turnkey cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and distribution match, and complementary compression techniques. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, curriculum/data strategies, and explicit mitigation of bias and rare-case failures—to reliably produce compact, high‑quality models for NLP and other modalities.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware, and Complementary Tool for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for producing smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teachers into compact students. KD routinely enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, and supports a spectrum of signals and training protocols. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and distribution shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of compression pipelines—powerful when combined with complementary methods and careful engineering, but requiring task‑aware safeguards to be reliable in production.

papers_seen.author: Lamb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Conditional Core of Model-Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically proven approach for producing smaller, faster, or deployment-specialized models in deep learning and NLP. When treated as a configurable core technique—choosing what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods and data strategies—KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes (bias propagation, low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift). Robust deployment requires task-aware design, multi-signal objectives, and integration with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or data synthesis strategies.

papers_seen.author: Bradshaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted family of techniques for transferring behavior and representations from larger or composite teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD spans soft-target/logit matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, relational or contrastive objectives, self- and multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or generator-based approaches; it is routinely combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and pretraining to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work across vision, speech, graphs, and natural language processing shows KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance, but its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and careful choice of transfer targets and training protocols.

papers_seen.author: Fox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers, but it is not a standalone cure-all. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and representations across modalities when chosen and tuned with regard to teacher quality, student capacity, data regimes, and deployment constraints. Best practice treats KD as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies—while adopting safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Duarte
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller students to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (logits, features, relations) and in varied data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free), and they are most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task-aware choices about what to transfer. While KD often preserves much of teacher performance, its success is context-dependent: it relies on teacher quality, student capacity, suitable data or synthetic-data protocols, and explicit strategies to protect rare outputs and fairness under distribution shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution, and I provide actionable guidance and open problems to prioritize in research and practice.

papers_seen.author: Hayes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Versatile, and Context-Sensitive
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core technique for compressing and adapting large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD offers a flexible set of targets and workflows—soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational and contrastive signals, online and self-distillation, and data-free protocols—that enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and alignment between teacher and student; it also risks transferring undesirable behaviors. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware objectives, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet production constraints and preserve downstream performance.

papers_seen.author: Larson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated paradigm that compresses large models into smaller, deployable students while also enabling robustness, domain and modality transfer, privacy-aware training, and architectural adaptation. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data-free synthesis, and task-aware training), carefully designed distillation pipelines provide favorable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and resource consumption for practical deployments across vision, language, multimodal, and sequential tasks. Despite strong practical gains, reliable distillation depends on principled choices about what to transfer, teacher–student pairing, and data availability, and outstanding theoretical and empirical challenges remain in heterogenous, privacy-sensitive, and distribution-shifted settings.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more deployable students across modalities and tasks. KD techniques extend beyond matching logits: they include internal-representation distillation, adversarial and relational approaches, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware methods, and architecture-aware replacements. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can preserve or even improve generalization, enable domain adaptation, and permit deployment under resource, privacy, or latency constraints—provided practitioners attend to known failure modes such as teacher bias, low-frequency lexical errors, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate across multiple signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure) and training paradigms (offline, online/multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, data‑free/adversarial synthesis). Empirical work shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and compute constraints, but its success is context‑dependent and typically benefits from integration with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data strategies (augmentation, synthetic data, data‑free approaches), and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Lester
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically important family of techniques for producing compact student models from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, multimodal, and constrained-deployment settings, KD uses diverse transfer targets and training protocols to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals, student capacity, and data strategies to task and deployment constraints and on integrating KD with complementary compression methods and privacy-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Park
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target supervision to a configurable toolkit including intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher protocols, data‑free synthesis, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD often recovers much of a teacher’s performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success is context-dependent and requires careful choices about teacher design, student capacity, data strategies, and mitigation of bias or distributional issues.

papers_seen.author: Nunez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has matured from a technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster ones into a broad set of methods that address efficiency, domain adaptation, privacy, robustness, fairness, and cross-modal transfer. By moving beyond simple logits matching to layer- and feature-level alignment, multi-teacher schemes, data-free and few-shot settings, and meta-learned teachers, distillation can both preserve performance and add functional guarantees (e.g., robustness, fairness) that are crucial for real-world deployment. This paper argues that knowledge distillation should be considered a foundational component of model compression pipelines and of strategies for adapting large pre-trained models to constrained, specialized, or sensitive applications.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance—and occasionally improve upon it—when practitioners choose appropriate distillation targets, align teacher and student capacity, and combine KD with complementary compression methods and data strategies. However, KD is context-dependent: its success depends on data availability, teacher quality, optimization schedules, and mitigation of propagated errors or biases. Treating KD as a task-aware toolbox rather than a single recipe yields the most reliable outcomes for deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Solis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. KD methods encompass soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and data‑free protocols, and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. While KD frequently recovers a large portion of teacher performance and enables deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints, its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity, choice of distilled signals, and data regime. For robust, high-fidelity compression, KD is best treated as a configurable component of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline that includes safeguards and complementary techniques to address known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: A Central, Context‑Aware Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD can transfer predictive behavior and internal representations through many targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and protocols (offline teacher, multi‑teacher, online, adversarial, and data‑free variants). Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability and nature of distillation data, and protections against transferred biases or privacy leakage. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—chosen and tuned with task, data regime, and deployment constraints in mind—rather than a standalone cure‑all.

papers_seen.author: Hayes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Findings from the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical set of techniques to transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large or composite teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. Over a decade of work has produced a diverse toolbox (soft-label matching, feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online protocols, and data- or privacy-aware variants) and established KD as a core component of many compression pipelines. KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when carefully matched to student capacity, data regime, and deployment constraints, but it is not a universal solution: successful application depends on teacher quality, student architecture and capacity, the choice of distilled signals, data strategy, and mitigation of bias, distribution shift, and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Acosta
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible family of techniques that transfer information from large teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller student models to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, compute, and privacy. Methods operate at multiple levels — from soft-label/logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational, and contrastive objectives — and include online, offline, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, data‑free, and adversarial synthesis protocols. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful data and training strategies; its limitations arise from teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity or distribution shift, and risks of propagating teacher errors or biases. Practical usage therefore treats KD as a configurable, task‑aware component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a single turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Leonard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Beyond in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a compression trick into a broad set of techniques that enable efficient deployment, cross-modal transfer, federated and privacy-preserving learning, and improved generalization across domains. Empirical results across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs) show that KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while retaining most of the teacher performance. However, the success of KD depends on careful choices — teacher quality, what to distill (outputs, features, internal representations), data availability and augmentation, and the loss or alignment mechanism — and recent work proposes multiple refinements (multi-teacher schemes, adversarial critics, projector modules, teacher-free variants) that mitigate known failure modes. The balance of empirical evidence and theoretical analyses indicates that KD is both practically indispensable for many compression tasks and a fertile area for research on how knowledge should be measured, transferred, and regularized.

papers_seen.author: Cordova
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely reduces inference cost and memory while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its reliability is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, architecture alignment, and complementary compression primitives critically shape outcomes. A pragmatic recommendation is to treat KD as the central component of compression pipelines while explicitly adapting objectives, data protocols, and auxiliary methods to the deployment constraints and known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD transfers information from teacher to student via soft logits, intermediate representations, attentional or channel signals, and relational objectives; it is often combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain-adaptation constraints. While KD frequently preserves much of a teacher’s performance and can improve robustness or generalization in some settings, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and responsible handling of bias, privacy, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Pope
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring capabilities of large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while retaining much of their task performance. Approaches span matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate representations, many-to-many layer mappings, attention- and projector-based transfers, data-free and zero-shot schemes, multi-teacher and online protocols, and integrations with quantization, pruning, and architecture search. Empirical work across language, vision, 3D perception, retrieval, and federated settings shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is combined with suitable data strategies, teacher design, and complementary compression methods. Important open challenges remain in data-scarce or privacy-sensitive regimes, robust transfer across heterogeneous architectures, and principled selection of what and how to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Cole
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient, Task‑Aware Core for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely applicable technique for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. Empirical and methodological work across modalities shows KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and supports many deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy). However, KD's success is conditional on choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data regimes, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, distribution shift, and degraded handling of low‑frequency phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable, task‑aware component within an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation‑aware objectives, data strategies, and complementary primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet real deployment requirements.

papers_seen.author: Levy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context‑Dependent Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or specialized models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teachers. When integrated with complementary compression methods and task-aware engineering, KD routinely enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and objective design, and it raises open challenges in robustness, privacy, and automatic student design.

papers_seen.author: Galvan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Necessity, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are essential engineering primitives for making large deep models practical in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings. Empirical results across vision, language, and multimodal tasks show that carefully chosen distillation targets, training schedules, and data strategies enable small students to recover much of teacher performance. At the same time, important challenges remain—data heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, low-frequency behavior preservation, and principled teacher selection—motivating focused research and deployment practices.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Evidence, Methods, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practically validated set of techniques for transferring information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. A broad toolkit—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or privacy-aware synthesis, and curriculum or adversarial sample selection—enables students to retain much of teacher performance across vision, language, multimodal, retrieval, and federated settings. Despite strong empirical successes, important engineering and scientific challenges remain around teacher–student alignment, data availability and synthesis, preservation of low-frequency behaviors, robustness and fairness, and principled automated design for heterogeneous deployment environments.

papers_seen.author: Gilbert
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger or more complex teacher models into smaller, faster student models to meet constraints of latency, memory, privacy, or deployment. The field presents a diverse toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational structure), protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free), and architecture-aware adaptations that are frequently combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and control shows distilled students can recover much teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and data strategies are addressed; however, KD faces limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, propagation of teacher artifacts, and challenges in reliably transferring robustness, low-frequency behaviors, and fairness. Best practice treats KD as a toolbox within an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline, selecting distilled signals and data strategies according to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware toolkit and combined with complementary compression methods, distillation enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. However, its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data strategy; it must be applied conditionally with safeguards against error and bias propagation.

papers_seen.author: Thomas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Contextual Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. Empirical and methodological work shows KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and inference cost. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architectural alignment, data availability and design, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors, biases, and rare-case degradation. For robust, production-ready compression pipelines, KD should be treated as the central mechanism embedded within task-aware practices that include complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful teacher–student engineering, and data- and fairness-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware toolbox for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into compact student models. KD methods include output-level (soft logits) supervision, intermediate representation and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and online or multi‑teacher training. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which data to use or synthesize, KD routinely yields large reductions in parameter count and latency while preserving most of teacher performance. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it is limited by teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution shift, and risks such as propagated teacher biases and degraded rare-token or out‑of‑distribution behavior. Addressing these limits requires task-specific protocols, privacy‑ and robustness‑aware designs, and more principled, automated approaches to objective selection and layer alignment.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer knowledge from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient models while preserving performance. Across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings, researchers have applied KD for inference speedup, deployment on resource-constrained devices, privacy-preserving model release, and enhanced robustness or interpretability. Methods vary from standard teacher–student soft-label supervision to data-free distillation, adversarially chosen boundary samples, many-to-many layer mappings, generative replay, and architecture-aware compression. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss when combined with task-aware design, careful sample selection, and appropriate optimization; challenges remain around distributional mismatch, low-frequency token handling, heterogeneous architectures, and privacy/validation in data-free scenarios. Emerging directions include task-adaptive compressed models, joint optimization of pruning and KD, federated/distilled learning across heterogeneous devices, and cross-modal distillation for generative capabilities.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD methods operate across multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free), and are commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical evidence shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under constraints on latency, memory, compute, and privacy. However, success is context-dependent: it hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis strategy, and careful selection of transfer signals and training procedures. Persistent challenges include principled theoretical accounts of what transfers, reliable distillation under data scarcity or heterogeneous/federated data, mitigation of bias and rare/low-frequency behavior degradation, and scalable privacy-preserving or data-free approaches.

papers_seen.author: Vaughn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Demand-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically powerful and practically versatile approach for compressing large models and transferring behavior to smaller students. KD succeeds across modalities by matching logits, intermediate features, attention, or relational structure and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Recent work extends KD to settings with no original data, privacy constraints, heterogeneous architectures, and specialized tasks (graphs, non‑autoregressive generation, lifelong learning). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher–student design, data strategies, and task-aware objectives, and important open problems remain (capacity mismatch, teacher bias transfer, preserving low-frequency behaviors, principled layer mapping, and rigorous theoretical understanding).

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression, Robustness, and Privacy in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models. Beyond mere size reduction, contemporary KD techniques transfer internal representations, enable deployment under data- and privacy-constrained conditions, mitigate architectural and modality mismatches, and interact non-trivially with regularization practices. I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational toolchain in applied deep learning and NLP systems—one that must be combined with tailored alignment, privacy-preserving, and teacher-selection strategies to fully realize its benefits in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Hardy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and representations from larger (teacher) models into smaller (student) models, enabling deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain mismatch. Across vision, language, multimodal and generative settings, distillation has expanded from logits matching to a diverse toolbox that includes feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, online and self-distillation, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization and architecture search. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and stabilizes student training, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, availability and selection of data, and defenses against transferred biases and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Practical deployments therefore treat distillation as a configurable component within compression pipelines, pairing distilled signals with task- and deployment-aware engineering.

papers_seen.author: Poole
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied compression techniques provide a practical toolkit for shrinking large deep models into smaller, deployable ones while retaining much of their task performance. Over the last decade researchers have developed a range of distillation targets (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention and relational maps, contrastive signals), teacher-student schedules (offline, online, multi-teacher, lifelong), and complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search, block-structured pruning). Empirical work shows KD often acts both as information transfer and regularization, enabling deployment across vision, language, multimodal, graph, generative, and medical-imaging tasks; however, success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of propagated errors or biases. Best practice is task- and capacity-aware design that combines appropriate distilled signals, alignment of inputs/representations, and complementary compression methods to meet target constraints.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student logits-matching recipe into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing models and enabling deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous hardware. Modern KD variants transfer not only soft labels but also internal and feature representations, employ multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, and integrate with federated and data-constrained workflows. When matched to the task (e.g., feature-level distillation for representation-heavy NLP, projector adapters for mismatched architectures, or privacy-aware ensembles for federated settings), KD enables small models to approximate or sometimes match larger teachers while offering routes to improved robustness and inclusivity. However, realizing these gains requires attention to teacher quality, capacity gaps, the form of distilled information, and sample-wise effects of soft targets. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-order, configurable component of model-compression pipelines and present evidence-based practical recommendations for when and how to apply its variants.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick; it is a versatile, practically proven framework that enables resource-efficient deployment, privacy-preserving learning, cross-modal and cross-domain transfers, and even improvements in robustness. When combined with complementary techniques — feature mimicking, projector modules, teacher annealing, label-smoothing–style regularization, and data-free or federated protocols — distillation can address the main bottlenecks of modern deep and multilingual models: size, latency, heterogeneity of devices, limited or private data, and domain shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component in any strategy for compressing or adapting deep models for real-world NLP and vision deployments.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Small-footprint Highway Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning has significantly advanced state-of-the-art of speech recognition in the past few years. However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. Previously, we investigated a compact highway deep neural network (HDNN) for acoustic modelling, which is a type of depth-gated feedforward neural network. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. In this paper, we push the boundary further by leveraging on the knowledge distillation technique that is also known as {\it teacher-student} training, i.e., we train the compact HDNN model with the supervision of a high accuracy cumbersome model. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing compact, deployable neural models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational or contrastive signals) and across diverse protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data-free/privacy-aware schemes). When combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables large reductions in latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of teacher performance. Its empirical success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability and synthesis strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, distribution shift, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Component of Task‑Aware Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable technique for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller student models, producing compact systems suitable for resource‑constrained deployment. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or hardware‑optimal compression. Reliable production compression pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable core element that must be combined with teacher–student co‑design, data strategies (including data‑free synthesis), and complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation to meet practical constraints and mitigate failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Ortiz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful and versatile family of techniques for producing compact student models from larger teachers, but its effectiveness is strongly context dependent. For reliable, high‑fidelity compression in deep learning and NLP, distillation should be treated as a core element of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline that combines careful teacher–student design, appropriate distilled signals, data strategies (including data‑free or privacy‑sensitive variants), and complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Terry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Sensitive Path for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven and versatile technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When designed around appropriate transfer targets, teacher–student alignment, and data regimes, KD frequently enables substantial reductions in size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. However, its effectiveness depends on task and deployment constraints, and KD must often be combined with complementary methods and task-aware design to avoid failure modes and to meet real-world requirements.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller, faster students to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and compute. A diverse set of distillation targets and training paradigms—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate feature and attention-map imitation, layer-wise mapping, adversarial and data-free generation of surrogate examples, online and multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, and integration with architecture search or pruning—have been developed and adapted to vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most of the teacher's accuracy (and in some settings improves generalization or robustness) when combined with task-aware choices of signals to transfer, data augmentation, and teacher-student design; remaining gaps and failure modes are linked to teacher quality, data availability and distribution shift, heterogeneous architectures, and fairness or robustness concerns.

papers_seen.author: Austin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. KD methods have been adapted into many variants and protocols and show strong empirical gains across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, but their success is highly context-dependent: it hinges on teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis strategy, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and distribution-shift failures. Treating KD as a configurable core component within integrated compression pipelines that combine representation-aware objectives, data strategies, and complementary primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design) produces the most reliable practical deployments.

papers_seen.author: Hayden
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded framework for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary teacher models into compact students. KD methods include soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online protocols, data-free or zero-shot schemes, and self-distillation. Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of teacher performance when combined with suitable data strategies, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD’s effectiveness is context dependent: success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and safeguards against transferred artifacts, distributional mismatch, and social harms. The practical consensus treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a plug-and-play solution.

papers_seen.author: Webster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, or specialized models. When designed around task constraints, student capacity, and available data, KD preserves much of a teacher's capabilities while enabling deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy limits. Its greatest value comes from treating distillation as a configurable toolkit—combining soft-targets, representation matching, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, and multi-teacher or self-distillation—with complementary compression techniques to meet real-world constraints. Success requires careful handling of teacher–student alignment, data scarcity, distribution shift, and bias transfer, but a task-aware, hybrid pipeline makes KD one of the most practical routes to effective model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD transfers information at multiple levels—soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/relational structure, or synthesized examples—and can be organized in diverse protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation, and data‑free regimes). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design, KD routinely produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. However, KD’s success is strongly context dependent: it depends on teacher quality and calibration, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and match of distillation data (or quality of synthetic surrogates), and careful objective and pipeline design to avoid propagating teacher errors or degrading long‑tail behaviour. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline, not a universal panacea.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, versatile approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical and methodological work shows KD routinely yields large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance, but its reliability depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student design, data regimes, and complementary compression techniques. I argue KD should be treated as the central, configurable element of integrated compression pipelines—essential for many deployments but insufficient by itself for robust, fair, and hardware‑aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes methods, extensions, and applications of knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques in deep learning and NLP. It covers teacher-student paradigms (offline and online), multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, layer- and feature-based distillation, data-free and privacy-aware distillation, task-aware and architecture-aware adaptations, theoretical perspectives, and applications beyond classification (e.g., generation, detection, graph learning, and machine reading). The review highlights recurrent practical challenges—capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, redundant teacher information, data and privacy constraints—and points to promising directions such as task-aware filtering, many-to-many layer mappings, and adversarial/data-free sample generation to enable distillation under limited resources or access.

papers_seen.author: Ballard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile framework for compressing large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD encompasses a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data‑free), and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and data strategies. Practical deployment treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component of broader compression pipelines and adopts safeguards for robustness, privacy, and low-frequency or long-tail behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Hays
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, practically oriented family of methods for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models. Over the past decade KD has diversified beyond simple soft-target (logit) matching into a toolbox that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher training, self-distillation, data-free or zero-shot schemes, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD routinely improves student efficiency–accuracy trade-offs and supports deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success is highly context dependent: it depends on teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and selection (or synthesis) of data, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, optimization mismatch, and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a single plug-and-play algorithm.

papers_seen.author: Simpson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression: Promise, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD methods vary in their transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), training paradigms (offline, online, multi‑teacher, meta‑learned teachers, data‑free synthesis), and integration with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across retrieval, vision, speech, and NLP shows distilled students frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware design choices, careful teacher–student alignment, suitable data strategies (including synthesis or privacy‑aware protocols), and explicit safeguards against propagated teacher artifacts and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Pena
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Context‑Sensitive Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD methods range from soft-logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational and adversarial objectives, and operate in offline, online, data‑free and federated regimes. While KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, its success is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data strategy, and complementary compression primitives strongly determine outcomes. For reliable deployment, KD should be treated as the core of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware toolbox for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into compact student models. KD methods include output-level (soft logits) supervision, intermediate representation and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and online or multi‑teacher training. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which data to use or synthesize, KD routinely yields large reductions in parameter count and latency while preserving most of teacher performance. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it is limited by teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution shift, and risks such as propagated teacher biases and degraded rare-token or out‑of‑distribution behavior. Addressing these limits requires task-specific protocols, privacy‑ and robustness‑aware designs, and more principled, automated approaches to objective selection and layer alignment.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable collection of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary models (“teachers”) into smaller, more deployable models (“students”). Over the last decade KD has diversified beyond simple soft-label matching to include feature- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free protocols, and online or self-distillation schemes. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of a teacher’s performance while enabling reductions in parameters, latency, and memory, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware design, careful handling of data and teacher imperfections, and integration with complementary compression methods.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Potency, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile toolkit for compressing and adapting large neural models for deployment, cross-task transfer, federated settings, and multi-modal scenarios. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or module replacement), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and compute with modest accuracy loss. However, gains are not automatic: careful choice of what to distill (outputs, intermediate representations, or selected samples), how to mix hard/soft signals, and how to adapt KD to distributed or data-free regimes strongly affects outcomes. I argue that KD is most effective when it is task-aware, representation-aware, and integrated with other compression methods, and that future work should prioritize principled selection of distilled knowledge, robustness to teacher imperfections, and practical protocols for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Wright

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking model size and latency while preserving performance across computer vision, natural language processing, recommendation, and federated settings. Research has expanded beyond the original logits-matching paradigm into feature mimicking, many-to-many layer mapping, teacher engineering, multi-teacher schemes, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and task-adaptive compression. Empirical and theoretical work highlights important interactions between data complexity, teacher strength, inductive bias, and augmentation strategies, and identifies practical challenges including model-heterogeneity, data heterogeneity, and the need for robust data-free methods. The field increasingly emphasizes not only how to distill but also what to distill (logits, features, inter-class relations, view- or task-specific knowledge) and how to adapt distillation to application constraints (privacy, federated settings, domain shifts, resource budgets).

However, compared to conventional Gaussian mixture acoustic models, neural network models are usually much larger, and are therefore not very deployable in embedded devices. We have shown that HDNN-based acoustic models can achieve comparable recognition accuracy with much smaller number of model parameters compared to plain deep neural network (DNN) acoustic models. Furthermore, we also investigate sequence training and adaptation in the context of teacher-student training. Our experiments were performed on the AMI meeting speech recognition corpus. With this technique, we significantly improved the recognition accuracy of the HDNN acoustic model with less than 0.8 million parameters, and narrowed the gap between this model and the plain DNN with 30 million parameters.
