papers_seen.abstract: Vision transformers (ViTs) have gained popularity recently. Even without customized image operators such as convolutions, ViTs can yield competitive performance when properly trained on massive data. However, the computational overhead of ViTs remains prohibitive, due to stacking multi-head self-attention modules and else. Compared to the vast literature and prevailing success in compressing convolutional neural networks, the study of Vision Transformer compression has also just emerged, and existing works focused on one or two aspects of compression. This paper proposes a unified ViT compression framework that seamlessly assembles three effective techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. We formulate a budget-constrained, end-to-end optimization framework, targeting jointly learning model weights, layer-wise pruning ratios/masks, and skip configurations, under a distillation loss. The optimization problem is then solved using the primal-dual algorithm. Experiments are conducted with several ViT variants, e.g. DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on the ImageNet dataset, and our approach consistently outperforms recent competitors. For example, DeiT-Tiny can be trimmed down to 50\% of the original FLOPs almost without losing accuracy. Codes are available online:~\url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Versatile, but Context‑Dependent Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely applicable family of techniques for producing compact student models from larger teachers. When designed as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline, KD routinely yields strong tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity; however, reliable deployment requires task‑aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and explicit mitigations for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, flexible set of techniques for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. The literature frames KD as a configurable core of practical compression pipelines: methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free synthesis, and multi-/self-distillation workflows. KD is effective across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks when combined with task- and capacity-aware design choices and complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability or synthesis of suitable data, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation under data scarcity or distribution shift, preventing propagation of teacher biases and low-frequency degradation, and automating teacher–student co‑design for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable paradigm for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when its objectives, data strategies, and student architectures are chosen with task and deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful mitigation of transferred biases and robustness gaps. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data- or privacy-aware synthesis.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically proven family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD offers a rich set of signals and protocols—soft logits, intermediate features, attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi‑teacher and self‑distillation, and data‑free or privacy‑aware variants—that can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD’s effectiveness is conditional: success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability or synthesis of suitable data, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and distributional failures. Treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, KD reliably improves efficiency while preserving much teacher performance; treated as a turnkey solution, it risks suboptimal or unsafe outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Travis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central but Insufficient — Advocating Integrated Compression Pipelines for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, empirically validated approach for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models, enabling deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. While KD reliably recovers much of teacher performance across modalities when carefully designed, it is context-sensitive: its success depends on choices of distillation targets, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred errors or biases. Consequently, KD should be treated as the core component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware distillation signals, architecture-aware adaptations, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Mckinney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Task‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded approach for producing compact models from larger teachers to meet latency, memory, energy, and privacy constraints. KD methods span outputs-level supervision, intermediate-representation matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free synthesis, and multi- or self-distillation protocols. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when combined with careful design about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives. Nevertheless, KD is not a universal cure: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis ability, and explicit mitigations for robustness, fairness, and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within integrated compression pipelines rather than a one-shot solution.

papers_seen.author: Bradley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applied approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to compact students. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD enables substantial efficiency gains while often retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. Its effectiveness depends on choices about what signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression primitives; accordingly, KD is best treated as a configurable core of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a one-size-fits-all remedy.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central, practical toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. A diverse set of distillation signals and training protocols—ranging from logits/soft labels to feature- and attention-level matching, contrastive and relational objectives, ensemble and online schemes, and data‑free or privacy-preserving techniques—are routinely combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and neural architecture search. Empirical evidence shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while producing substantial efficiency gains, but practical success is context dependent and requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability, and mitigation of transferred failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Logan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Configurable Component for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a highly effective and broadly applicable approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and useful properties of larger teachers. Empirical and methodological work shows KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision, language, and generative settings, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data regimes, and objective design. Therefore KD should be treated as a first-order, configurable component within integrated compression pipelines—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—and deployed with explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and rare-phenomenon preservation.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Configurable First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile, and empirically supported family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. It reliably reduces inference cost and often preserves much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, but its success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, the data regime, and deployment constraints. Therefore KD should be adopted as a first‑line, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines, combined with complementary methods and targeted safeguards to address known failure modes and domain-specific challenges.

papers_seen.author: Wyatt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a mature and practical set of techniques for converting large, high‑performing models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical evidence across vision, language, and multimodal tasks shows that distillation—when applied with task awareness, appropriate choice of distilled signals, and complementary compression techniques—can recover much of teacher performance while meeting constraints of latency, memory, and privacy. However, its success is conditional on teacher quality, data regimes, teacher–student alignment, and explicit mitigation of biases and low‑frequency failures; therefore, distillation should be integrated into end‑to‑end compression pipelines and not treated as a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, often ensemble or pre-trained, teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD includes matching teacher outputs (soft logits), imitating intermediate representations, transferring attention or relational structures, and using multi-teacher, online, self-, or data-free protocols. In practice KD is combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. While KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve student generalization, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and match, and careful choice of distillation signals; persistent challenges include optimization gaps, distribution shift, low-frequency/rare-case degradation, bias transfer, and federated or heterogeneous-device constraints. Ongoing work focuses on principled objectives, layer-mapping strategies, privacy- and data-aware distillation, and robust, task-aware pipelines for production deployment.

papers_seen.author: Sanchez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Practicalities, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller students to reduce inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving much of task performance. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple logit matching into a broad set of targets and protocols—soft targets, intermediate-feature alignment, attention/relational objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and multi- or self-distillation—frequently combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is effective across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and alignment of data (or synthetic alternatives), and careful design of objectives and pipelines. Remaining practical limits include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, degradation on low-frequency phenomena, and reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints; current remedies emphasize task-aware objective design, multi-signal supervision, teacher adaptation, and integration with other compression primitives.

papers_seen.author: Dominguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of methods for transferring information from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, and other modalities KD variants (logits/soft-targets, intermediate features, attention or relational transfers, and data‑synthesis/data‑free approaches) enable substantial reductions in inference cost and memory while often preserving most of a teacher’s performance. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and careful data or privacy strategies—and when practitioners attend to teacher–student compatibility, data regime, and task constraints. Known limitations include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, sensitivity to distribution shift and rare/low-frequency phenomena, and optimization or alignment challenges that require method selection and safeguards tailored to deployment goals.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: The Promise and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central method for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains, KD variants enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, promote interpretable surrogates, and support ensemble compression. However, KD also transfers teacher biases, faces optimization and data-distribution challenges, and requires careful choices of objectives, data augmentation, and teacher-student protocols to be effective in practice.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or specialized teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed many variants—logit transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble- and teacher-aware algorithms, data-free and few-shot protocols, and meta-learned teachers—to address practical deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, device heterogeneity) while also pursuing robustness, fairness, and task adaptation. This synthesis summarizes dominant methods, representative applications, empirical patterns, and common failure modes that guide practical use and future research.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance—and occasionally improve upon it—when practitioners choose appropriate distillation targets, align teacher and student capacity, and combine KD with complementary compression methods and data strategies. However, KD is context-dependent: its success depends on data availability, teacher quality, optimization schedules, and mitigation of propagated errors or biases. Treating KD as a task-aware toolbox rather than a single recipe yields the most reliable outcomes for deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and often indispensable method for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance when its objectives, data strategies, and student architectures are chosen with task and deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability, and explicit handling of transferred errors, biases, and rare-case failures. For robust, production-ready compression, KD should be applied as a configurable, task-aware element of an integrated compression pipeline that also leverages representation-aware objectives, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary architecture-aware transformations.

papers_seen.author: Gomez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision and NLP, KD spans logits/soft-label matching, feature- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and online-teacher schemes, data‑free and privacy-aware protocols, and self- or teacher-free variants. When combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and designed with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and task constraints, KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss. Practical deployment requires task-aware choices, careful alignment of teacher and student, and explicit mitigations for distributional mismatch, rare-token behavior, and transferred biases; important open problems remain in principled theory, robust/private data-free distillation, and heterogeneous architecture transfer.

papers_seen.author: Matthews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A wide variety of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational maps), protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, data-free), and integrations with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) have been developed. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Clay
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, broadly applicable mechanism for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller student models and is essential for practical model compression in deep learning and NLP. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or hardware‑optimal deployment: it must be designed in a task‑aware way, combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and paired with data and curriculum strategies to mitigate failure modes such as teacher bias, poor low‑frequency behavior, capacity mismatch, and distribution shift. Treating KD as a configurable core inside an integrated compression pipeline yields the most reliable production outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically effective family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals) and across training protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation and data-free synthesis). Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in inference cost and memory footprint, but outcomes are highly context-sensitive: they depend on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability and distribution of data, and the choice of distillation objectives and layer mappings. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component within hybrid compression pipelines that combine pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and privacy- or domain-aware interventions.

papers_seen.author: Peck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Dependent Engine for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and flexible family of methods for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, speech, and recommendation tasks show KD can recover most of a teacher’s performance while delivering substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication cost. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime and selection, the choice of transfer signals, and how KD is combined with complementary compression methods. For reliable deployment, practitioners should treat KD as a task‑aware toolbox—selecting what to transfer, aligning teacher and student carefully, addressing data or privacy constraints, and integrating pruning/quantization or architecture-aware design—while explicitly mitigating limitations such as teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted approach for producing compact models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. The approach spans simple soft-label transfer to richer objectives that match intermediate representations, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and supports many protocols (offline, online/co-distillation, multi-teacher, self-distillation and data-free variants). KD is most effective when integrated into a broader compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum learning, and data strategies—and when choices about transfer targets, layer alignment, and data are tailored to task and deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often preserves most of teacher performance and can improve student generalization, but it has concrete failure modes (teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, degradation on rare phenomena, privacy and fairness risks) that require targeted mitigations and evaluation.

papers_seen.author: Burton

Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multimodal domains shows KD frequently restores a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success depends critically on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data strategy, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as teacher-error propagation, bias transfer, and degraded low‑frequency behaviour. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and careful data/objective choices—to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hancock
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses and transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models. A wide family of distillation objectives and workflows—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation, relational, contrastive, adversarial, online, and meta-learned schemes—has been developed and applied across domains including vision, speech, graph learning, machine translation, and NLP. Empirical results show distillation often preserves most teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on careful design choices around teacher quality, student capacity, data, and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful mitigation of transferred biases and robustness gaps. papers_seen.author: Reid

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to compact student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels of supervision, support varied training protocols, and are commonly integrated with complementary compression primitives to satisfy latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Practical success depends on careful choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness and fairness; remaining challenges include reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, preserving low-frequency or structured behaviors, and principled guidance for heterogeneous architectures and federated settings.

I argue KD should be treated as the central element of a task‑aware, validated compression pipeline rather than as a stand‑alone cure.

papers_seen.author: Barker

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Conditional Component of Integrated Model-Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practically powerful family of techniques for producing compact, fast models from larger teachers. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance across tasks and modalities and can be adapted to settings with limited or private data. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its benefits depend critically on choices about which teacher signals to transfer, student capacity and architecture, data strategy, and mitigation for transferred errors, biases, and low-frequency behavior. For reliable deployment, KD should be used as the configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data and curriculum strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Donovan
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques reduce model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students). Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed logit- and feature-level distillation, layer-wise and many-to-many layer matching, task-aware filtering, projector-based adapters, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, and data- or privacy-constrained workflows. Empirical work demonstrates that carefully designed distillation protocols can retain much of teacher performance (and sometimes improve generalization) while enabling deployment constraints such as latency, memory, and privacy; theoretical analyses offer insight into when soft labels help and when hard labels are necessary. Remaining challenges include bridging capacity gaps, dealing with mismatched architectures and modalities, operating without original data, and guaranteeing privacy under compression.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become primary approaches for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings. The literature spans methods that transfer soft-labels, internal feature representations, and ensemble knowledge; extensions address teacher imperfections, data scarcity or privacy, task-specific adaptations for NLP and vision, and hardware-aware compression. Empirical work demonstrates that careful design choices—such as which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student layers, whether to incorporate self-distillation or multi-teacher training, and how to combine pruning or low-precision numerics—substantially affect final accuracy and efficiency. The field also benefits from theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Remaining challenges include distilling robust semantics for low-frequency phenomena, distillation without access to original data, and co-design for hardware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Serrano

Realizing KD’s benefits in practice requires careful attention to teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, what signals are transferred and how layers are mapped, data availability or synthesis strategies, and interventions to mitigate bias, rare‑token degradation, and distribution shift.

However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, data and augmentation choices, objective design, and handling of distributional or architectural mismatch. Careful engineering and complementary compression techniques are necessary to realize KD's benefits in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Leblanc

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically essential component of modern model-compression pipelines: it enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not a universal remedy. Real-world success requires task‑ and capacity‑aware choices, data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or privacy-aware data), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as teacher bias transfer, teacher–student mismatch, and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Treated as a configurable, task‑conditional component within an integrated compression pipeline, KD is the practical backbone of deployable deep and NLP models.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez

Combining representation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and task-aware layer mapping yields practical recipes for real-world compression and adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Garrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Practical, but Not Sufficiently Complete Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. KD techniques extend beyond logit matching to feature- and layer-level alignment, attention and projection-based mappings, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and data-constrained regimes (few-shot, data-free). KD reliably improves deployment trade-offs (latency, memory, and sometimes robustness or privacy), but it has concrete limits—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data heterogeneity, and task-specific design needs—that make KD most effective when integrated with complementary compression and training practices.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core set of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Methods range from matching teacher logits to aligning internal features, attention maps, and layer correspondences; they are frequently combined with pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, and architecture search. KD supports many practical settings — including data-limited, data-free, few-shot, federated, and cross-modal scenarios — but its effectiveness depends on choices such as which teacher signals to transfer, student capacity, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases. Ongoing directions include principled theory for transfer objectives, robust and private distillation, and task-aware designs for structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Fuller

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students to achieve deployable tradeoffs between accuracy, latency, memory, and privacy. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when its transfer objectives, teacher–student compatibility, and data strategy are chosen to match task constraints, but it also has well-documented failure modes (teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and poor transfer of low-frequency or structured behaviors). For reliable production use, KD should be treated as the configurable core of a broader compression pipeline that integrates representation-aware transfers, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, together with monitoring and mitigation for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Fuentes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When integrated with complementary compression techniques and adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints, distillation routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs. papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, practical framework for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient students for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A diverse toolkit of distillation objectives and protocols—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-/self-distillation, and data-free protocols—has been developed and applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and multimodal tasks. papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. Combining KD with complementary techniques (quantization, architecture transformations, pruning, and task-aware layer mapping) yields the best tradeoffs between compression and downstream accuracy.

While KD frequently retains much of a teacher's performance and can improve student generalization, its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability, and careful mitigation of transferred errors, biases, and distributional mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Burgess
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods include output-level supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, online and multi-teacher protocols, and progressive or task-aware procedures. Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, generative and multimodal tasks shows that when KD is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task- and data-aware engineering, it often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing resource cost. Practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Important open challenges remain in principled selection of distillation targets, reliable transfer under data scarcity and distribution shift, avoiding propagation of teacher biases and rare-token degradation, and automated, hardware-aware co-design.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically powerful approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models from large teachers. KD reliably improves accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when its objectives and protocols are matched to task constraints and student capacity. However, KD is not a one‑size‑fits‑all solution: teacher quality, data availability (or synthetic/data‑free methods), teacher–student architectural mismatch, and the risk of transferring biases or low‑frequency behaviors all shape outcomes. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core component of an integrated compression pipeline that couples distillation with pruning, quantization, architecture design, data strategies, and monitoring for robustness and fairness.

However, KD is not a turnkey solution: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional mismatch create failure modes that require deliberate mitigation and integrated design.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Necessary Core and a Configurable Toolkit for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when it is treated as a configurable toolkit—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to generate or select data, and which complementary compression techniques to combine. However, KD is conditional: its reliability depends on teacher quality, data design and availability, teacher–student alignment, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors or biases. For robust, production-ready compression one should therefore treat KD as the core of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline that includes pre-training, multi-teacher or meta-teaching protocols, and deployment-aware primitives such as pruning or quantization.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Adaptation: Teaching to Adapt
papers_seen.abstract: Domain adaptation is crucial in many real-world applications where the distribution of the training data differs from the distribution of the test data. Previous Deep Learning-based approaches to domain adaptation need to be trained jointly on source and target domain data and are therefore unappealing in scenarios where models need to be adapted to a large number of domains or where a domain is evolving, e.g. spam detection where attackers continuously change their tactics.   To fill this gap, we propose Knowledge Adaptation, an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation scenario. We show how a student model achieves state-of-the-art results on unsupervised domain adaptation from multiple sources on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark by taking into account the domain-specific expertise of multiple teachers and the similarities between their domains.   When learning from a single teacher, using domain similarity to gauge trustworthiness is inadequate. To this end, we propose a simple metric that correlates well with the teacher's accuracy in the target domain. We demonstrate that incorporating high-confidence examples selected by this metric enables the student model to achieve state-of-the-art performance in the single-source scenario.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically supported approach for reducing model size and latency across vision, language, multimodal, and graph domains. KD techniques range from logit matching to feature- and relation-based objectives, adversarial and data-free schemes, and are effective when chosen and tuned for the deployment context. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and mitigation of propagated errors or bias. Best practice treats KD as a central but context‑sensitive element of integrated compression pipelines that include pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, and task-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Lynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Component for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal settings when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student design are selected for the deployment context. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all cure: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as propagated bias, poor low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware distillation, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: The Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression (but Not a Standalone Cure)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable technique for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training regimes (offline, online, multi-teacher, and data-free variants), and combinations with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, detection, and healthcare shows KD routinely enables substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and careful objective and architecture design. Best practice treats KD as the central, configurable element of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that explicitly addresses data scarcity, distribution shift, privacy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, efficient student models to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Over the past decade, KD methods have evolved from simple soft-target (logit) matching to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi‑teacher and online regimes, and data‑free or adversarial synthesis. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can preserve much of a teacher’s performance and in many cases improve generalization, but practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of signals to transfer, and the availability and match of distillation data; reliable deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware objectives, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Cochran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Pragmatic, Multifaceted Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster models while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a multifaceted framework—covering logits, intermediate representations, feature maps, sample selection, and data-side interventions—KD enables deployments under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. Effectiveness depends on matching the distillation signals to student capacity and task structure, and on addressing failure modes such as teacher bias and data scarcity. Combining KD with complementary techniques (quantization, architecture transformations, pruning, and task-aware layer mapping) yields the best tradeoffs between compression and downstream accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Walton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical technique for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller students. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals, synthetic data) and in protocol (offline, online, self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, data-free variants). Empirical results across vision, language, generation, and graph domains demonstrate that distilled students can approach teacher performance when distillation is carefully designed and combined with complementary compression techniques; however, success depends on factors such as teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes including bias transfer and degraded performance on rare phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that also uses pretraining, architecture-aware design, and safeguards for privacy and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Collier
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, broadly applicable family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Empirically KD often recovers much of teacher performance and enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and inference cost, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and nature of distillation data, and the choice of distilled signals. For robust, production-ready compression KD should be treated as a configurable core that is integrated with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data and curriculum strategies, and explicit safeguards for bias, robustness, and low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Lucas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. The literature converges on a toolbox of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and layer-mapping, relational and contrastive objectives), a variety of training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free/zero-shot), and common integrations with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance, but outcomes are strongly context-dependent: they depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, choice of transfer signals and data regime, and explicit measures to avoid transferring teacher errors, biases, or fragile behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Configurable Core of Practical Model-Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically supported approach for converting large teacher models into compact, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Treated as a configurable toolbox rather than a single recipe, KD produces favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when combined with complementary compression primitives and with intentional choices about what and how to transfer. At the same time, KD is not automatic: reliable deployment requires addressing teacher–student mismatch, data limitations, and the risk of propagating undesirable behaviors. I argue that KD should be adopted as a central, context‑sensitive component of hybrid compression pipelines whose design is driven by task constraints and by explicit mitigation strategies for known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to representation and feature matching—and has been adapted for online, multi-teacher, self-supervised, data-free, cross-modal, and federated scenarios. Across vision, language, speech, and graph domains, careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate teacher imperfections determines the success of compression. Best results arise when distillation is combined with complementary techniques (architecture adaptation, quantization, pruning, or curriculum strategies) and when practitioners attend to data-availability, distribution shift, and task-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Franklin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Practical Findings, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically validated toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. When distillation is designed with attention to which signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data regimes (including data-free or privacy-aware workflows), and when it is integrated with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture search), students can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Despite empirical successes, KD’s effectiveness is context-sensitive: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, degradation on low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Leonard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Beyond in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a compression trick into a broad set of techniques that enable efficient deployment, cross-modal transfer, federated and privacy-preserving learning, and improved generalization across domains. Empirical results across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs) show that KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while retaining most of the teacher performance. However, the success of KD depends on careful choices — teacher quality, what to distill (outputs, features, internal representations), data availability and augmentation, and the loss or alignment mechanism — and recent work proposes multiple refinements (multi-teacher schemes, adversarial critics, projector modules, teacher-free variants) that mitigate known failure modes. The balance of empirical evidence and theoretical analyses indicates that KD is both practically indispensable for many compression tasks and a fertile area for research on how knowledge should be measured, transferred, and regularized.

papers_seen.author: Welch
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation in Practical Model Compression and Generalization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche compression trick into a broadly applicable paradigm that enables deployment of large models across modalities, supports privacy- and resource-constrained federated scenarios, and improves generalization when combined with task- and architecture-specific techniques. Empirical evidence shows that KD alone yields large gains for small students, while hybrid approaches that distill internal representations, use curriculum or meta-learning, augment data, or jointly optimize architecture and distillation produce state-of-the-art trade-offs between size, speed, and task performance. KD is therefore a foundational tool for modern model compression strategies and should be used in concert with complementary methods (e.g., pretraining, low-precision numerics, structural compression, and privacy-aware distillation) to meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Robust Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large models and transferring useful knowledge to smaller or specialized models. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and sometimes improved generalization when combined with complementary strategies (e.g., architecture search, pruning, or data management). However, distillation outcomes depend on data, teacher-student alignment, and training design; success requires adapting KD objectives and pipelines to the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Barrett
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, and Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. Across tasks and modalities, KD variants transfer outputs or internal signals to reduce model size and latency while often preserving most task performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures and capacities, how to handle data (real, augmented, or synthetic), and how to combine distillation with complementary compression techniques. When treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, KD enables deployable models under latency, memory, and privacy constraints—but it is not a standalone panacea and requires task‑aware engineering to mitigate failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, distribution shift, and degraded long‑tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Fischer
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, widely applied family of methods that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller, more deployable student models. KD spans output-level supervision (soft logits), intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data-aware or data-free variants. When combined with careful teacher–student design, data and curriculum strategies, projector or layer‑mapping choices, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD routinely yields favorable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, memory, and energy. Its effectiveness is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distributional alignment, and the choice of distillation signals crucially determine outcomes. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: The Centrality and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Beyond reducing parameter counts and inference latency, distillation enables transferring inductive biases, protecting privacy in federated settings, enabling few- and zero-shot compression, and supporting task-adaptive and automated compression workflows. However, distillation is not a panacea: dataset heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, and redundant teacher representations can limit gains. Best practice combines representation-level and layer-aware techniques, multi-teacher or teacher-free strategies where appropriate, and task-aware selection of distilled information to maximize compressed-model utility.

papers_seen.author: Holt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central Utility, Practical Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for transferring capabilities from large teacher models into compact student models so that high-performing systems can run under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, features, attention, relations) and training regimes (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free) and is routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to produce deployable models. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on task-aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and explicit handling of bias, low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Morton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, flexible paradigm for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models so they can be deployed under compute, memory, latency, or privacy constraints. When designed with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search), distillation routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance. However, distillation is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and the distillation signals chosen; it can propagate teacher artifacts and struggles with optimization gaps, capacity mismatch, and low-frequency behavior. Addressing these limits requires joint teacher–student design, confidence- or curriculum-aware sample selection, data-free or privacy-aware synthesis when data are unavailable, and incorporation into broader compression pipelines tailored to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and often more socially or operationally suitable models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks KD has been shown to preserve much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and in privacy-sensitive or distributed settings. KD is most effective when combined with complementary practices such as pre-training, data augmentation, careful layer-matching, ensemble guidance, and hardware-aware pruning.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer behavior and/or internal structure from larger, often ensemble or multi-modal teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to intermediate-feature, attention, and relational matching—and are widely used to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under memory or latency constraints, and support domain or modality adaptation. The effectiveness of KD depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and careful design of what and how knowledge is transferred; combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and targeted training protocols improves reliability in practice.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. When designed around task objectives, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints—and when combined with complementary compression primitives—KD routinely reduces inference cost, memory footprint, and communication overhead while preserving much of teacher performance. Yet KD is not automatic: it requires careful choices about distillation signals, architecture alignment, data strategies (including data‑free or synthetic data when originals are unavailable), and safeguards to avoid propagating teacher errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Nuanced Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger or ensemble teachers. It supports a wide range of objectives—logit-level transfer, feature- and representation-level matching, relational and adversarial objectives, and many-to-many layer mappings—and is applicable across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models) and settings (offline, online, data-free, federated, multi-teacher). When combined with careful teacher-student co-design, targeted data strategies, and complementary compression techniques, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while also serving secondary goals such as interpretability or robustness. KD is powerful but not automatic: success depends on matching objectives to tasks, mitigating teacher-induced errors or biases, and addressing optimization and data-distribution challenges.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used toolkit for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students in vision, language, multimodal, and other settings. KD encompasses a family of transfer signals and training protocols that, when chosen and tuned for task constraints and student capacity, frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute. Practical deployments treat KD as a configurable component within integrated compression pipelines that also include pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies; success depends on teacher quality, the student’s capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of appropriate data, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, capacity mismatch, and distribution shift.
