papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for producing compact student models from larger teachers. When designed with attention to which signals to transfer, student capacity and architecture, and distillation-data strategies, and when combined with complementary compression primitives, KD routinely yields favorable tradeoffs between efficiency and performance across modalities. However, KD is not a universal cure: its reliability depends on mitigating failure modes such as transferred biases, degraded rare‑token behavior, teacher–student mismatch, and distributional shift. Treating KD as a configurable, task‑aware element of integrated compression pipelines — rather than a turnkey replacement for other techniques — produces the most reproducible deployments and points to principled research directions for robust, privacy‑aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Moon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable component of a compression pipeline and adapted to teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and deployment constraints, KD reliably reduces inference cost while preserving much of a teacher's performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. However, KD is not a turnkey cure: it must be combined with projector or layer-mapping techniques, ensemble and adversarial strategies where appropriate, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) while explicitly mitigating failure modes such as bias transfer, low-frequency degradation, and data scarcity. Continued theoretical and empirical work is needed to standardize best practices, automate signal selection, and robustly distill structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive and representational information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to meet deployment constraints such as latency, memory, and privacy. KD has been adapted to diverse transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational maps), multi-teacher schemes, data-free or few-shot regimes, and domain- or task-adaptive pipelines. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful teacher–student design, KD routinely yields large reductions in model size and runtime while preserving most of the teacher's performance. However, distillation is not automatic: practitioner attention is needed to address teacher selection, data availability and distribution shift, capacity mismatch, low-frequency behavior, and risk of transferring biases or teacher artifacts.

papers_seen.author: Rocha
papers_seen.title: Few Shot Network Compression via Cross Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Model compression has been widely adopted to obtain light-weighted deep neural networks. Most prevalent methods, however, require fine-tuning with sufficient training data to ensure accuracy, which could be challenged by privacy and security issues. As a compromise between privacy and performance, in this paper we investigate few shot network compression: given few samples per class, how can we effectively compress the network with negligible performance drop? The core challenge of few shot network compression lies in high estimation errors from the original network during inference, since the compressed network can easily over-fits on the few training instances. The estimation errors could propagate and accumulate layer-wisely and finally deteriorate the network output. To address the problem, we propose cross distillation, a novel layer-wise knowledge distillation approach. By interweaving hidden layers of teacher and student network, layer-wisely accumulated estimation errors can be effectively reduced.The proposed method offers a general framework compatible with prevalent network compression techniques such as pruning. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that cross distillation can significantly improve the student network's accuracy when only a few training instances are available.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Modalities, and Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques are now essential for deploying high-performing deep learning models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. A broad set of distillation strategies—ranging from soft-label supervision and feature mimicking to data-free (zero-shot) distillation, adversarially guided feature transfer, self-distillation, and automated architecture search guided by teacher models—enable substantial reductions in model size and computational cost while preserving or even improving performance across vision, language, multimodal, and sequence tasks. Best practice combines input-side methods (data augmentation and mixup), representation-level transfer, and careful teacher-student design choices to match the deployment objectives (efficiency, fairness, interpretability, or privacy).

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. It supports multiple information-transfer mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and can be adapted to constrained settings (limited data, privacy, heterogeneous devices). KD is most effective when used as part of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or pretraining—and when practitioners mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer, rare-token degradation, or teacher–student mismatch. With careful design choices (what to transfer, how to align layers, which data to use), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving task performance across modalities.

papers_seen.author: Ballard
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to produce deployable systems under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of KD objectives and training regimes—ranging from soft-logit matching to intermediate feature and relation-level imitation, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols—combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) enables substantial efficiency gains while often preserving much of teacher performance. KD�s practical success is conditional on task-aware choices about what to transfer, teacher�student alignment, data availability and augmentation, and explicit handling of bias, low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from logit matching into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, multimodal, and generative settings. The methods include soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online/self-distillation, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture- or hardware-aware design. Empirical work shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication when combined with complementary compression techniques. However, success is context dependent: it requires careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, data strategies (including data-free options), and mitigations for transferred biases or degraded rare-token behavior. Ongoing directions emphasize automated signal selection, joint optimization with pruning/quantization, federated and privacy-aware distillation, and robust cross-modal or generative-model compression.

papers_seen.author: Schwartz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a diverse set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller, more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and specialized domains, KD methods routinely enable substantial reductions in inference cost and parameter footprint while often retaining much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful selection of distillation targets, alignment of teacher and student architectures, and appropriate data strategies; KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression primitives and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context‑Sensitive Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a powerful and broadly applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. It routinely yields large efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance, but its effectiveness is strongly context-dependent: success requires task‑aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle data and deployment constraints, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression primitives. Treating distillation as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline produces the most reliable outcomes in practice.

papers_seen.author: Sanders
papers_seen.title: What is known about Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, KD routinely improves accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when matched to student capacity, distillation signals, and data regimes; however, its success is conditional on teacher quality, student architecture and capacity, data availability, and protections for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task-aware data strategies—rather than as a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Quinn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential but Not Sufficient — A Case for Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated toolkit that transfers information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. KD methods span soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention and relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-aware or data-free schemes. While KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher capability and enables deployment under resource and privacy constraints, its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the distillation signals chosen, and the data regime. Consequently, KD is best treated as a central, configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and careful data and evaluation strategies.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. Empirical results across vision, language, retrieval, detection, generative models, and distributed settings show KD can close much of the performance gap between large and compact models, but best outcomes require tailoring what and how knowledge is transferred and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques and domain-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multi-faceted framework for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory use, and latency while retaining task performance. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational signals) and across multiple training regimes (offline teacher→student, online/self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, and data‑free variants). Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when paired with appropriate teacher–student design, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives, but key limitations remain around data scarcity, teacher–student mismatch, transfer of undesirable behaviors, and insufficient theoretical understanding of what to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely used set of techniques for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods transfer information at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/relational structure) and operate across diverse protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free approaches). Empirical work shows KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. At the same time, KD is context-sensitive: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection (or the ability to synthesize data), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred biases, degraded rare-case behavior, and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of integrated compression pipelines rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Rejuvenating Low-Frequency Words: Making the Most of Parallel Data in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is commonly used to construct synthetic data for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models. However, there exists a discrepancy on low-frequency words between the distilled and the original data, leading to more errors on predicting low-frequency words. To alleviate the problem, we directly expose the raw data into NAT by leveraging pretraining. By analyzing directed alignments, we found that KD makes low-frequency source words aligned with targets more deterministically but fails to align sufficient low-frequency words from target to source. Accordingly, we propose reverse KD to rejuvenate more alignments for low-frequency target words. To make the most of authentic and synthetic data, we combine these complementary approaches as a new training strategy for further boosting NAT performance. We conduct experiments on five translation benchmarks over two advanced architectures. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly and universally improve translation quality by reducing translation errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach achieves 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets, respectively. Our code, data, and trained models are available at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

papers_seen.author: Johnston
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and broadly useful approach for compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods span soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free schemes, and variants such as multi‑teacher, online, and self‑distillation. KD routinely yields strong tradeoffs between efficiency and performance when it is designed with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and task constraints, and when it is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). However, KD is not a universal recipe: practical success requires task‑aware choices, careful layer or feature alignment, and explicit remedies for distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, and transferred biases. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable component within compression pipelines and offers evidence‑based best practices and caveats for its effective use.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Bailey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The literature develops multi-level transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure), multi‑teacher and online variants, data-aware and data‑free protocols, and integrations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks when teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and mapping between teacher and student are carefully managed; however, success is context-dependent and limited by optimization gaps, data scarcity, capacity mismatch, and the risk of transferring teacher artifacts or biases. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable component of broader compression workflows tailored to deployment constraints such as latency, memory, privacy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Insights, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques reduce the size and computational cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Across classification, sequence modeling, generation, and structured prediction, researchers have developed soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature guidance, adversarial and contrastive objectives, projector and embedding modules, and privacy-aware mechanisms to transfer knowledge from large teacher models to smaller students. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs among bias, variance, teacher quality, and data complexity, and shows that distillation interacts with pre-training, label smoothing, and modality differences. Applications span speech and machine translation to GANs and graph neural networks; complementary methods such as pruning and block-structured compression can further improve deployment on constrained hardware.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and often more deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal systems, and specialized domains such as healthcare and novel-view synthesis, KD yields large reductions in parameter count and inference cost while retaining most of the teacher performance when applied with task-aware design choices. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on what information is transferred (logits, features, relational structure), the availability and nature of data, teacher quality and design, and careful integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Pragmatic deployment requires attention to robustness, bias propagation, data scarcity, and domain mismatch, and benefits most from combining KD with task- and hardware-aware practices.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Carter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. KD methods vary in their transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals), training protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, self‑distillation), and data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free or synthetic-data). In practice KD is frequently combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task-aware design choices to meet latency, memory, privacy, and robustness constraints. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but outcomes are context dependent: success hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and layer mappings, and data strategies. Important open issues include theory for when particular signals transfer, reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, preserving long‑tail/low‑frequency behaviors, and preventing propagation of teacher errors and biases.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable technique for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training regimes (offline, online, multi-teacher, and data-free variants), and combinations with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, detection, and healthcare shows KD routinely enables substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and careful objective and architecture design. Best practice treats KD as the central, configurable element of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that explicitly addresses data scarcity, distribution shift, privacy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, faster, or deployment-specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A large family of distillation objectives and training protocols has been developed—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial and data-free schemes, and online or multi-teacher setups—and these are frequently combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance while lowering latency and memory, but practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Open problems include robust and private distillation under data scarcity and distribution shift, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student mapping for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teachers into smaller, faster, or specialized student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A broad and practical toolbox has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free/zero-shot protocols, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search—that is applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative settings. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance when applied carefully, but success depends on student capacity, teacher design/quality, data availability and augmentation, and task-aware choices; important open problems remain in principled theory, fairness/privacy-aware protocols, heterogeneous and federated settings, and robust distillation for generative and structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact student models. The literature establishes a rich taxonomy of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, contrastive objectives), training protocols (offline, online, self-distillation, data-free), and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical success depends on task- and data-aware choices, teacher and student design, and integration with other compression strategies; KD is powerful but not universally sufficient on its own. Ongoing directions emphasize task-adaptive objectives, data-efficient and privacy-preserving workflows, federated and heterogeneous-device scenarios, and theoretical understanding of when and why particular distilled signals help.

papers_seen.author: Summers
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models or ensembles into smaller, deployable student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while retaining much of task performance. Modern KD methods span soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data- or privacy-aware synthesis. KD is commonly combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence indicates KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and suitable data strategies are aligned, but its success is context-dependent and requires task-aware design to mitigate limits related to teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Learning Compact Metrics for MT
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in machine translation and multilingual text generation have led researchers to adopt trained metrics such as COMET or BLEURT, which treat evaluation as a regression problem and use representations from multilingual pre-trained models such as XLM-RoBERTa or mBERT. Yet studies on related tasks suggest that these models are most efficient when they are large, which is costly and impractical for evaluation. We investigate the trade-off between multilinguality and model capacity with RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model, using data from the WMT Metrics Shared Task. We present a series of experiments which show that model size is indeed a bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, then demonstrate how distillation can help addressing this bottleneck, by leveraging synthetic data generation and transferring knowledge from one teacher to multiple students trained on related languages. Our method yields up to 10.5% improvement over vanilla fine-tuning and reaches 92.6% of RemBERT's performance using only a third of its parameters.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Configurable Core of Practical Model-Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically supported approach for converting large teacher models into compact, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Treated as a configurable toolbox rather than a single recipe, KD produces favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when combined with complementary compression primitives and with intentional choices about what and how to transfer. At the same time, KD is not automatic: reliable deployment requires addressing teacher–student mismatch, data limitations, and the risk of propagating undesirable behaviors. I argue that KD should be adopted as a central, context‑sensitive component of hybrid compression pipelines whose design is driven by task constraints and by explicit mitigation strategies for known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of the Provided Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under constraints of latency, memory, compute, or privacy. Methods range from matching soft logits to imitating intermediate features, attention maps, and relational structure, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and specialized data strategies. KD has enabled strong empirical gains across modalities and tasks (classification, generation, translation, graph learning, and recommender systems) but requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of undesirable behaviors. Key practical themes include selecting appropriate distillation signals, handling teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatches, designing or synthesizing data when originals are unavailable, and integrating KD with complementary compression methods to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted framework for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher networks to smaller student networks. Methods span soft-label (logit) matching, alignment of internal representations and attention patterns, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols; KD is often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative modeling shows KD can dramatically reduce compute and memory with modest accuracy loss (and sometimes improvements), but outcomes depend on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and task-specific design. Important open issues include principled theory for different transfer objectives, robust and private distillation under data heterogeneity, and specialized protocols for structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Mcclain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation from Internal Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is typically conducted by training a small model (the student) to mimic a large and cumbersome model (the teacher). The idea is to compress the knowledge from the teacher by using its output probabilities as soft-labels to optimize the student. However, when the teacher is considerably large, there is no guarantee that the internal knowledge of the teacher will be transferred into the student; even if the student closely matches the soft-labels, its internal representations may be considerably different. This internal mismatch can undermine the generalization capabilities originally intended to be transferred from the teacher to the student. In this paper, we propose to distill the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a simplified version of it. We formulate two ways to distill such representations and various algorithms to conduct the distillation. We experiment with datasets from the GLUE benchmark and consistently show that adding knowledge distillation from internal representations is a more powerful method than only using soft-label distillation.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. Across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, and multimodal tasks) KD methods include logits/soft-target matching, representation- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial or generator-based data synthesis, and variants that operate offline, online, self-, multi-teacher, or data-free. KD is most effective when used as a configurable component within a broader compression pipeline (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, availability or synthesis of training data, and explicit mitigation of failure modes (optimization limits, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and propagation of teacher biases).

papers_seen.author: Morris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied framework for producing smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact student models. A wide range of distillation objectives (logit/soft-target matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive losses), training protocols (offline, online/self-, multi-teacher), and data strategies (full-data, limited-data, data-free, and privacy-aware synthesis) have been proposed and combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Empirical studies show KD often recovers much of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and suitable data strategies are available, but KD is context-dependent and must be integrated with task-aware design choices to manage limits related to teacher–student mismatch, optimization, data scarcity, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Hoover
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably improves accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across modalities when combined with task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and complementary compression techniques. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional mismatch create failure modes that require deliberate mitigation and integrated design.

papers_seen.author: Meza
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of KD objectives and workflows—ranging from soft-logit matching to intermediate-feature alignment, multi‑teacher and self‑distillation, data‑free and adversarial approaches, and projector or curriculum-based engineering—has been developed and applied across vision and language tasks. Distillation enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints but is not universally guaranteed: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful choice of transfer signals and training procedures. The practical consensus is to treat KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline combined with complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Garrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Practical, but Not Sufficiently Complete Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. KD techniques extend beyond logit matching to feature- and layer-level alignment, attention and projection-based mappings, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and data-constrained regimes (few-shot, data-free). KD reliably improves deployment trade-offs (latency, memory, and sometimes robustness or privacy), but it has concrete limits—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data heterogeneity, and task-specific design needs—that make KD most effective when integrated with complementary compression and training practices.

papers_seen.author: Guerra
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Sensitive Core for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. When used as a configurable core—selecting appropriate transfer targets, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining with complementary compression methods and data strategies—KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. Its success is context dependent: task properties, data availability, teacher quality, student capacity, privacy constraints, and deployment requirements all shape which distillation protocols and auxiliary methods will work best. Responsible application therefore treats KD as the central element of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a one-size-fits-all remedy.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods aim to transfer behavior and representations from larger, more expensive models into smaller, efficient ones while retaining task performance. Across modalities and tasks, research has developed many complementary mechanisms — soft-label mimicry, intermediate representation matching, teacher-student curriculum designs, self-distillation, multi-teacher and online schemes, data- or generator-based transfer, and domain- or modality-specific adaptations — to balance accuracy, latency, and resource constraints. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation can recover most teacher performance (and in some settings even surpass it) while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and improving reproducibility and privacy. Success depends on the distillation targets, the teacher-student pairing and training regime, the use of auxiliary data or synthetic examples, and task-specific modifications.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Nuanced Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger or ensemble teachers. It supports a wide range of objectives—logit-level transfer, feature- and representation-level matching, relational and adversarial objectives, and many-to-many layer mappings—and is applicable across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models) and settings (offline, online, data-free, federated, multi-teacher). When combined with careful teacher-student co-design, targeted data strategies, and complementary compression techniques, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while also serving secondary goals such as interpretability or robustness. KD is powerful but not automatic: success depends on matching objectives to tasks, mitigating teacher-induced errors or biases, and addressing optimization and data-distribution challenges.

papers_seen.author: Reyes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and communication overhead. Across vision, language, speech, retrieval, and generative settings, KD variants routinely yield substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance when designed with attention to task objectives, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives. Practical deployments treat KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and appropriate data handling—rather than as a one‑shot cure; remaining challenges include capacity mismatch, distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, bias transfer, and data- or privacy-constrained scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or specialized teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed many variants—logit transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble- and teacher-aware algorithms, data-free and few-shot protocols, and meta-learned teachers—to address practical deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, device heterogeneity) while also pursuing robustness, fairness, and task adaptation. This synthesis summarizes dominant methods, representative applications, empirical patterns, and common failure modes that guide practical use and future research.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques form a diverse set of methods for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring knowledge from larger or specialized models. Approaches span from simple soft-label supervision to richer transfers of internal representations, intermediate-layer mappings, attention-guided projections, adversarial feature alignment, and task- or device-aware compression. KD is used across domains—image classification, detection (2D and 3D), recommendation/CTR, language model compression, federated and heterogeneous-device learning, and reinforcement learning—and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or curriculum strategies. Recent work examines theoretical aspects (e.g., bias–variance tradeoffs and statistical interactions with data augmentation), practical design choices (teacher-student layer alignment, many-to-many mappings, ensemble teachers), and extensions that address privacy, fairness, and low-data regimes. Despite strong empirical success, open problems remain in understanding when particular KD variants best transfer generalization, how to measure and mitigate transferred biases, and how to optimally combine KD with other compression primitives for different constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bennett
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely applied family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks, KD variants (logit/soft-label matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data-free/zero-shot synthesis) combined with complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) enable substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, availability or synthesis of data, and integration with other compression methods. Remaining challenges include principled theory connecting distilled signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, transfer across heterogeneous architectures and non-iid data, and mitigation of propagated biases and degraded behavior on rare or long‑tail phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Jennings
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression: Effectiveness, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, empirically validated set of techniques that reliably reduces model size and inference cost while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD is not a single recipe; its practical success depends on task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, the distillation data regime, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression primitives. Treating KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline—rather than as a standalone silver bullet—produces the most robust and deployment-ready outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Santana
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Model Compression with Practical Caveats
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an adaptable, empirically validated family of techniques that enables production of compact, efficient models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller students. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when its objectives, data, and teacher-student design are matched to deployment constraints, but it is not a turnkey remedy: careful method selection and safeguards are required to avoid capacity mismatch, optimization failure modes, and transfer of undesirable behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central to making large deep models practical for deployment. Research has explored diverse teacher-student architectures, alternatives to relying on original training data, adaptations to heterogeneous devices and federated settings, methods that transfer intermediate representations (features, relations, attention), adversarial and ensemble strategies, and task- or domain-specific compression. Empirical work across NLP, vision, reinforcement learning, recommendation, graph and 3D detection demonstrates that careful design of the distillation objective, choice of teacher(s), and selection of data (real, synthetic, or none) strongly affect student performance and efficiency. Remaining challenges include handling data heterogeneity, preserving low-frequency or minority information, and designing teacher models that are optimal for transfer. This review synthesizes findings across these directions and highlights practical approaches and open problems.

papers_seen.author: Wise
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, empirically supported approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. Rather than a one-shot cure, KD is most effective when treated as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that explicitly addresses teacher–student alignment, data strategies, complementary compression techniques, and known failure modes. This position emphasizes KD's practical value, its conditional limits, and a set of operational practices that convert KD's flexibility into reliable, production-ready compression.

papers_seen.author: Carroll
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable collection of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary models (“teachers”) into smaller, more deployable models (“students”). Over the last decade KD has diversified beyond simple soft-label matching to include feature- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free protocols, and online or self-distillation schemes. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of a teacher’s performance while enabling reductions in parameters, latency, and memory, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware design, careful handling of data and teacher imperfections, and integration with complementary compression methods.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical paradigm for producing compact, efficient models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. A diverse set of distillation objectives and workflows — including soft-logit matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and adversarial or curriculum-based training — has been developed and applied across modalities (NLP, vision, speech, graphs) and tasks (classification, generation, detection, ranking, and more). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables deployment in resource- and latency-constrained settings while often preserving most teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher-student compatibility, data regimes, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, optimization mismatch, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Buchanan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Context‑Aware, and Insufficient Alone for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques that reliably improves the efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs of deep models across modalities. KD enables deployment by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students, and it supports many training protocols and transfer targets. However, KD is not a standalone solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability or synthesis of suitable data, and careful mitigation of failure modes (distribution shift, low-frequency degradation, and bias propagation). Therefore, for robust real-world deployment KD should be treated as a configurable, task‑aware core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design), teacher–student co‑design, and data strategies tailored to the application.

papers_seen.author: Hoover
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Context‑Sensitive, and Best‑Practice Driven
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically essential tool for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. When integrated with complementary compression techniques and adapted to the data and deployment constraints, KD routinely yields students that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and inference cost. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of transferred signals, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. Responsible application requires explicit mitigation of failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, distribution shift, and privacy risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and provides practical recommendations for when and how to apply KD effectively in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer behavior and/or internal structure from larger, often ensemble or multi-modal teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to intermediate-feature, attention, and relational matching—and are widely used to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under memory or latency constraints, and support domain or modality adaptation. The effectiveness of KD depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and careful design of what and how knowledge is transferred; combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and targeted training protocols improves reliability in practice.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels — soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives — and in many training protocols (offline/online, multi-teacher, self-distillation, and data-free/zero‑shot schemes). Empirical results across vision and language show that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and appropriate data or synthesis strategies are addressed. Practical application treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component of integrated compression pipelines (often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search), while explicit attention is required for limits such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, bias transfer, and degraded modeling of rare outputs.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models across computer vision, NLP, multilingual metrics, and multimodal tasks. A range of complementary techniques — layer-wise mapping, data-free and zero-shot synthesis, self-distillation, adversarial and robust distillation, online/ensemble methods, and task-adaptive architecture search — together make distillation applicable under constraints such as limited data, privacy restrictions, heterogeneous devices, and production-scale training. I argue that adopting a portfolio of distillation strategies, chosen to match data availability and deployment constraints, yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, robustness, and interpretability for modern deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation: A Versatile Framework for Model Compression, Robustness, and Privacy in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models. Beyond mere size reduction, contemporary KD techniques transfer internal representations, enable deployment under data- and privacy-constrained conditions, mitigate architectural and modality mismatches, and interact non-trivially with regularization practices. I argue that KD should be treated as a foundational toolchain in applied deep learning and NLP systems—one that must be combined with tailored alignment, privacy-preserving, and teacher-selection strategies to fully realize its benefits in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for transferring functionality from large teacher models to smaller students so that compressed models retain much of the teacher's performance while meeting constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and communication. KD covers a spectrum of techniques—from soft-target matching to internal representation transfer, multi-teacher/online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware approaches, and architecture-aware solutions such as task-adaptive compression—and integrates naturally with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, adversarial training). When implemented with care about teacher selection, data selection or synthesis, and representation alignment, KD enables practical deployment of high-performing models across modalities; when misapplied it can propagate teacher errors, amplify biases, or fail due to optimization and data-mismatch issues. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a first-order engineering primitive for model compression in deep learning and NLP, and outlines recommended practices and known limitations to guide responsible adoption.

papers_seen.author: Stephenson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesized Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically validated family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, compute, and privacy. KD methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-side strategies (including data-free and synthesized data). Reliable compression uses KD as a configurable core within hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and task-aware data and evaluation practices.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When adapted to task, data availability, and deployment constraints, KD preserves much of a teacher's performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprint, and improved adaptability across domains and modalities. However, KD is a family of techniques rather than a single algorithm: best outcomes arise from combining distillation with complementary methods (e.g., pruning, architecture search, curriculum design, data synthesis) and from explicitly addressing challenges such as imperfect teachers, domain shift, privacy, and heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practically indispensable technique for compressing and adapting large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD is highly versatile—supporting logits-, feature-, attention- and relation-level transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and privacy- or data-constrained workflows—but it is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, what signals are transferred, data availability and distribution, and careful training protocol design. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines and combining it with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, data augmentation, and curriculum strategies) leads to the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Mack
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD enables meaningful reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving much of teacher performance, but its success is conditional on task- and data-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged — soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online/co-distillation, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search — and these techniques are applied across vision, language, generative models, speech, graphs, and retrieval. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance when protocols, student capacity, and data strategies are chosen thoughtfully, but success is context-dependent and important open problems remain around theory, fairness/privacy, heterogeneous or federated settings, and robust distillation for generative and structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Marks
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. A wide set of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training paradigms (offline, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation), and data strategies (real, synthetic, or data‑free) have been developed. KD is often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count, but reliable success depends on deliberate, task‑aware choices about transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and mitigation of bias, robustness, and distributional risks.

papers_seen.author: Stevens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single trick into a broad, practical family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-aware models while retaining much of their performance. The techniques differ by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel statistics), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, data-free/zero-shot, few-shot), and which complementary strategies are used (projectors, mixup/data augmentation, pruning, or architecture-aware design). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as information transfer and as a regularizer; success depends critically on choices about teacher signals, student capacity, the availability and nature of data, and task-specific design. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation under limited or private data, preventing transfer of teacher errors, adapting to heterogeneous or federated settings, and scaling distillation to very large models and complex structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile family of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial or data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher protocols—have been shown to recover much of a teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and computational cost. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful selection of what and how to transfer; open challenges remain in robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and enabling private or data-free distillation at scale.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Releasing Graph Neural Networks with Differential Privacy Guarantees
papers_seen.abstract: With the increasing popularity of graph neural networks (GNNs) in several sensitive applications like healthcare and medicine, concerns have been raised over the privacy aspects of trained GNNs. More notably, GNNs are vulnerable to privacy attacks, such as membership inference attacks, even if only black-box access to the trained model is granted. We propose PrivGNN, a privacy-preserving framework for releasing GNN models in a centralized setting. Assuming an access to a public unlabeled graph, PrivGNN provides a framework to release GNN models trained explicitly on public data along with knowledge obtained from the private data in a privacy preserving manner. PrivGNN combines the knowledge-distillation framework with the two noise mechanisms, random subsampling, and noisy labeling, to ensure rigorous privacy guarantees. We theoretically analyze our approach in the Renyi differential privacy framework. Besides, we show the solid experimental performance of our method compared to several baselines adapted for graph-structured data. Our code is available at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context-Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. However, KD is not automatic: its benefits depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and complementary compression methods; it also requires safeguards to avoid propagating teacher errors or biases. When treated as a configurable component of compression pipelines and paired with targeted techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, and selection of transfer signals), KD is the most practical first-line strategy for many deployment scenarios in deep learning and NLP.
