papers_seen.author: Fox
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted set of techniques for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller student models so they can meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Across vision, language, speech, and other modalities, KD spans logit/soft-target matching, intermediate- representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or synthesized-data protocols. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables substantial efficiency gains, but its effectiveness is context-dependent and benefits from careful, task-aware choices about signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Key limitations include optimization challenges, teacher–student mismatch, transfer of teacher errors or biases, degradation on low-frequency or long-tail phenomena, and sensitivity to distribution shift; proposed remedies include multi-signal objectives, augmentation and synthesized data, teacher scheduling, and combining KD with other compression and design techniques. Open research directions center on theoretical understanding, robust and privacy-aware distillation under limited or mismatched data, automated teacher/student co-design, and principled mitigation of fairness and rare-token failures.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Uses, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or relational structure from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models. Across vision and language tasks KD has enabled substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving most teacher performance. Practical deployments use KD as one component in an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—and require task‑aware choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Known limitations include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, degraded performance on long‑tail or rare outputs, and sensitivity to distribution shift; these motivate multi‑teacher, selective, or data‑synthesis protocols and careful evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Strong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesized Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and richer internal information. A broad toolbox of distillation targets and protocols has emerged—soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free sample synthesis, self- and online-distillation, and multi-teacher schemes—and these are routinely combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD has been applied across vision, language, graphs, speech, generative models, and federated settings, yielding large reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance when design choices are task- and architecture-aware. Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, data scarcity or privacy constraints, and instability in optimization; practical remedies emphasize task-aware signal selection, learned teacher adaptation, layer mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-preserving protocols. This review synthesizes empirical patterns, common mechanisms, practical recommendations, and open problems for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often retaining substantial parts of teacher performance. A broad family of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals; offline, online, self-, multi-teacher, and data-free variants). Practical success depends on aligning the distillation signal to task and student capacity and on combining distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Key challenges include teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatch, limited or unavailable data, propagation of teacher biases or errors, distribution shift, and difficulties preserving low-frequency or structured behaviors. Continued progress requires principled choices about what, when, and how to transfer knowledge, better theory linking distillation choices to student generalization, and engineering pipelines that pair KD with task-aware data and model design.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact student models. The literature establishes a rich taxonomy of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, contrastive objectives), training protocols (offline, online, self-distillation, data-free), and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical success depends on task- and data-aware choices, teacher and student design, and integration with other compression strategies; KD is powerful but not universally sufficient on its own. Ongoing directions emphasize task-adaptive objectives, data-efficient and privacy-preserving workflows, federated and heterogeneous-device scenarios, and theoretical understanding of when and why particular distilled signals help.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques that transfer information from larger, often multi-source or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal and generative settings, KD has evolved beyond simple logit matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free generation, online and self-distillation protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization and architecture search. These approaches routinely enable large reductions in inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance, but reliable deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Important open directions remain in principled theory, robust distillation under heterogenous and low-data regimes, and preserving long-tail or low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques that make large, high-performing models practical for deployment by transferring behavior, representations, or decision structure to smaller models. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when combined with appropriate supervision signals, data practices, and architectural alignment, but it also has important failure modes—propagated teacher errors, sensitivity to data distribution and teacher quality, and limits when student capacity is insufficient. I argue KD should be treated as a foundational component of model-compression pipelines, applied thoughtfully and in combination with complementary methods (augmentation, pruning/quantization, privacy mechanisms, and federated protocols) to realize robust, efficient systems for real-world NLP and deep-learning applications.

Its empirical strengths make KD a first‑line approach for many deployment problems, but reliable, production‑grade compression requires explicit attention to teacher–student alignment, data selection or synthesis, capacity matching, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

The field encompasses a wide family of distillation targets and protocols (logit matching, feature- and attention-level transfer, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and federated variants) and is frequently combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, recommendation, and other modalities shows that distilled students often recover much of the teacher’s performance, though outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and task-aware choices. papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, flexible approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students. Practical success is highly context-dependent: it hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and match, and complementary compression choices. Persistent challenges include reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, robust transfer of rare behaviors, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student alignment for heterogeneous deployments.

However, KD has predictable failure modes (teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare outputs) that require explicit mitigation and evaluation in real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Christian
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Practical Findings, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models into smaller students. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when combined with deployment-aware design choices and complementary compression tools. However, realizing robust, fair, and privacy-preserving compressed models requires attention to teacher–student alignment, data regimes, and method selection.

papers_seen.author: Hale
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of teacher performance when treated as a configurable, task‑aware component of an integrated compression pipeline. Its reliability depends on teacher–student alignment, the data regime, and explicit safeguards; therefore KD should be the default first‑line strategy for compression but always combined and tuned with complementary methods for robust real‑world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Morrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context-Dependent Tool Best Used in a Compression Portfolio
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students. It reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment across modalities when paired with careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or mismatched data. KD should be treated as a core, necessary element of practical compression pipelines but not as a standalone solution: the best results come from integrating KD with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from applying context-aware design and mitigation for bias, robustness, and data constraints.

papers_seen.author: Carlson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Core of Model-Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile toolkit for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech and multimodal tasks shows KD can produce compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance and meet latency, memory and privacy constraints when used with complementary compression techniques. However, KD is not a universal cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distillation signals and training regime, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. Best practice treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline with explicit safeguards for optimization gaps, bias transfer and low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Suarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade‑offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques for transferring information from larger, more expensive teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD supports multiple transfer signals (soft labels, features, attention/relations, contrastive objectives) and modes (offline, online, multi‑teacher, data‑free), and is widely used across modalities including NLP, vision, recommender systems, GANs, and reinforcement learning. Practical deployment of KD hinges on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of bias and distributional failures; combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and deployment‑aware safeguards typically yields the best trade‑offs.

papers_seen.author: Glass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Necessary, Configurable Core of Practical Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically validated, versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD methods span output-level soft-targets, intermediate representation and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online/self-distillation protocols. When treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with targeted data, architecture, and optimization strategies, KD reliably yields favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases, optimization gaps, and distributional failures. Deployment-grade outcomes require task-aware design, complementary compression primitives, and safeguards for robustness and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, flexible set of techniques for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. The literature frames KD as a configurable core of practical compression pipelines: methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data‑free synthesis, and multi-/self-distillation workflows. KD is effective across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks when combined with task- and capacity-aware design choices and complementary compression methods (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability or synthesis of suitable data, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation under data scarcity or distribution shift, preventing propagation of teacher biases and low-frequency degradation, and automating teacher–student co‑design for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Dunn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. By transferring predictive behavior or internal representations, KD enables substantial reductions in latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance. Its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware training, KD forms an essential, configurable component of modern compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Versatile, but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large models and transferring their knowledge into smaller, faster models for deployment in resource-constrained settings and domain-specific applications. Advances in layer- and feature-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, data- and augmentation-aware practices, and federated or privacy-sensitive adaptations have expanded KD's applicability across vision, NLP, and graph domains. However, KD is not a universal remedy: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle under data heterogeneity, and depend critically on teacher quality, data choices, and optimization design. Best outcomes follow when practitioners combine KD with complementary techniques (careful layer matching, feature mimicking, data selection/augmentation, and pruning or quantization) and explicitly address heterogeneity and teacher reliability.

papers_seen.author: Thompson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful and empirically validated approach for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment, privacy-aware releases, and domain adaptation when designed with task- and data-awareness. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and match of data, and careful handling of transferred biases and low-frequency phenomena. The strongest practical systems treat KD as a central component within an integrated compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture search, and targeted data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Myers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile toolkit that often enables substantially smaller, faster models to retain a large fraction of the performance of larger teachers. Its effectiveness is well supported empirically across vision, language, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data and augmentation strategy, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and low‑frequency failures. Best practice treats KD as an integrated component of a compression pipeline—paired with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies—rather than a universal one‑size‑fits‑all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques provide flexible, broadly applicable ways to transfer performance from large teacher models to compact student models so they can run under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. A diverse set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel maps, relational signals) and procedures (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, meta-learned teachers, data-free synthesis) have been developed and integrated with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, ensembling). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, graphs, and recommendation systems shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve deployability, though success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and mitigation of transferred biases. Remaining directions include automated, task-adaptive transfer choices, robust data-free distillation, and principled controls for fairness and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that enable model compression, domain- and task-level transfer, privacy-preserving distillation, and improvements in interpretability and fairness. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can compress large models into efficient students, transfer inductive biases, support multi-task and lifelong learning, and enable data-free or zero-shot distillation when training data are unavailable. At the same time, KD faces concrete limitations due to data heterogeneity, teacher-student capacity mismatch, and the need to select or synthesize appropriate supervision; hybrid solutions that combine feature-level matching, adversarial sample synthesis, curriculum strategies, and architectural compression achieve the best practical results. Based on evidence across domains (vision, language, graphs, retrieval, reinforcement learning), we argue that KD should be used as part of an integrated compression pipeline that is task-aware, data-aware, and often combined with pruning, layer skipping, or module replacement to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Marks
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. A wide set of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training paradigms (offline, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation), and data strategies (real, synthetic, or data‑free) have been developed. KD is often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count, but reliable success depends on deliberate, task‑aware choices about transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and mitigation of bias, robustness, and distributional risks.

papers_seen.author: Carrillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile method for transferring predictive behavior from larger teacher models to smaller student models, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of the original performance. KD spans logits-based supervision, feature and relational matching, adversarial or synthetic data generation, and architectural or curriculum adaptations. Its practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how teachers and students are aligned, and complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD can enable deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings and sometimes yield students that match or exceed teacher performance, but it also carries risks—propagating teacher errors and biases, struggling under data scarcity or mismatch, and requiring task-specific engineering. I argue KD should be treated as a central component of compression pipelines, applied conditionally with targeted remedies and validated against task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost and enable deployment in constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. The literature documents a wide set of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training protocols (offline teacher–student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, multi-teacher), and data strategies (data-rich, data-free, augmentation and selective-sample curricula). Empirical work across vision, language, graph, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling shows that well-designed KD pipelines — especially those that match internal representations, align layers thoughtfully, and combine KD with pruning/quantization or student-aware teacher design — can retain much of teacher performance while substantially lowering model size and latency. However, KD has failure modes (teacher mismatch, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, privacy and bias transfer, and sensitivity to data availability) that require complementary methods such as data-free synthesis, domain-aware adaptation, privacy-preserving noise, and careful objective design. The field continues to refine when and how to apply KD so that compact models are accurate, robust, and suitable for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Harrington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Context-Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and generative settings. KD reliably improves student performance when teacher quality, the form of transferred signals, and data/augmentation strategies are chosen to match the task and deployment constraints. However, KD is not sufficient by itself: best outcomes arise when distillation is integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful data or augmentation strategies, and task- or architecture-aware adaptations. This article argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of compression pipelines rather than a standalone cure-all, and it highlights empirical evidence, mechanisms, limitations, and practical recommendations drawn from recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Valdez

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and properties of larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and privacy-sensitive settings, KD variants transfer logits, intermediate representations, relations, or synthesized data to produce students that meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often yields favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size, but its success depends on data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and careful objective and training choices.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models using targets ranging from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals. Across vision, language, multimodal, and speech tasks, KD combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation or synthetic-data generation) enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical results show distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can sometimes match or exceed teachers when distillation is carefully designed. Important open problems include teacher–student capacity mismatch, optimization and belief-matching limits, distribution shift and domain adaptation, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, and avoiding transfer of teacher biases. This synthesis summarizes mechanisms, practical variants, representative empirical patterns, and recommended directions for research and deployment.

However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful objective and pipeline design. Best practice treats KD as a core element of an integrated, task-aware compression strategy combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware mapping) and targeted remedies for failure modes such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, rare-token degradation, and bias transfer.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practically oriented family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, faster student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Modern KD goes well beyond matching soft logits: it includes intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online/self-distillation and multi-teacher regimes, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies. Practical limits—teacher–student capacity and optimization mismatch, teacher errors and bias propagation, domain shift, and scarce or private data—motivate task-aware design, layer-mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-preserving approaches.

Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and selection of distillation data (or reliable synthesis strategies), and careful protocol design to mitigate robustness, fairness, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

A principled KD practice chooses what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to generate or select data, and which complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to combine with distillation. Properly applied, KD is a practical and general component of modern model-deployment toolkits; misapplied, it can propagate teacher errors or fail when data or teacher–student alignment is poor.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Bruce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven, flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. I argue that KD should be treated as a core, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines rather than a standalone solution, and I summarize practical recommendations and open challenges that follow from this position.

papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a multifaceted framework—spanning soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational objectives, selective sample policies, and data-side interventions—KD reliably improves efficiency while preserving much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on matching distilled signals to student capacity and task structure, integrating KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation), and explicitly addressing failure modes such as transferred biases, low-frequency token degradation, and data scarcity. KD should therefore be a first-class component in compression pipelines, applied conditionally and engineered around task- and deployment-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Foundational, Context-Dependent, and Best Deployed as Part of an Integrated Compression Toolkit
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful set of methods for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD variants—from logits and feature matching to self-, multi-teacher, and data-free protocols—have been shown to reduce model size and latency while often retaining much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, generative, and detection tasks. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, what is transferred, and interactions with other training practices. To realize KD’s practical value one should design distillation around task objectives and deployment constraints and combine it with complementary compression and data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile family of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial or data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher protocols—have been shown to recover much of a teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and computational cost. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful selection of what and how to transfer; open challenges remain in robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and enabling private or data-free distillation at scale.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational, and data‑free objectives—enable substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success is conditional on task-aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and integration with complementary compression primitives; open challenges remain in capacity mismatch, distributional robustness, preservation of rare behaviors, and privacy-aware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis reviews empirical and methodological advances in knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques as applied across vision, language, generative models, retrieval, recommender systems, federated and lifelong learning. It summarizes mechanisms for transferring teacher knowledge to smaller students (soft labels, intermediate representations, curriculum and selective sample strategies), practical challenges (data availability, teacher cost, domain shift, privacy, and bias), and targeted solutions (data-free distillation, fast label generation, multi-teacher and domain-adaptive schemes, self-distillation, and distillation-aware pruning). The goal is to map what the provided literature reports about when distillation helps, when it can hurt, and which strategies are effective for different settings and tasks.
