papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, heterogeneous hardware). Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft‑label/logit matching to intermediate feature, attention, relational, adversarial, and data‑free schemes—routinely improve student performance and often recover a large fraction of teacher accuracy when designed with task‑ and capacity‑aware choices. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of integrated compression pipelines that include pruning, quantization, and architecture search and when practitioners explicitly address data regimes, teacher–student alignment, and robustness or fairness safeguards. Important open problems remain around distribution shift, low‑frequency behavior, privacy‑sensitive distillation, heterogeneous architectures, and principled theory for different transfer objectives.

papers_seen.author: Soto
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Practices, Applications, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible framework for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while preserving much of task performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation objectives range from matching output logits to imitating intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure, and contrastive signals, and are often combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability and alignment of data, and careful design of training objectives and pipelines. KD is widely applied in domains from NLP and information retrieval to healthcare, routing, and federated settings, but it has known failure modes (teacher bias transfer, low-frequency degradation, teacher–student mismatch, and distributional shift) that require task-aware remedies and integration with other compression primitives. Ongoing directions emphasize multi-signal objectives, task-adaptive architecture search, data-efficient and privacy-preserving protocols, and principled evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Stevens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single trick into a broad, practical family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or privacy-aware models while retaining much of their performance. The techniques differ by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel statistics), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, data-free/zero-shot, few-shot), and which complementary strategies are used (projectors, mixup/data augmentation, pruning, or architecture-aware design). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as information transfer and as a regularizer; success depends critically on choices about teacher signals, student capacity, the availability and nature of data, and task-specific design. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation under limited or private data, preventing transfer of teacher errors, adapting to heterogeneous or federated settings, and scaling distillation to very large models and complex structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a broadly useful means to transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students so that compressed models can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when it is adapted to the problem: what to transfer (logits, features, attention), which data to use or synthesize, how to weight multiple teachers or imperfect supervision, and how to integrate complementary compression techniques. However, KD is neither automatic nor sufficient on its own: careful, task-aware design and combination with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies are required to realize reliable, production-ready compression.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practically indispensable technique for compressing and adapting large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD is highly versatile—supporting logits-, feature-, attention- and relation-level transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and privacy- or data-constrained workflows—but it is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, what signals are transferred, data availability and distribution, and careful training protocol design. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines and combining it with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, data augmentation, and curriculum strategies) leads to the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Kerr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. When designed with task-aware objectives, appropriate teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression primitives, KD routinely yields large efficiency gains while preserving predictive quality. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on choices of what to transfer, teacher quality, student capacity, and data availability, and it requires explicit strategies to avoid propagating teacher errors or losing rare/low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile framework that reliably produces compact, deployable models by transferring behavior and representations from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD methods—ranging from soft-target matching to intermediate-feature and relational objectives—have been shown across vision, language, recommendation, and generative tasks to reduce latency and memory while retaining much of teacher performance. At the same time, KD is not a singular cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data choices, and objective design, and it can propagate biases or fail on rare or out-of-distribution phenomena. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline, combined with architecture-aware mapping, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and targeted safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Webster
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, and privacy. The literature develops a broad taxonomy of distillation signals (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention and relational maps, contrastive objectives), training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free and federated), and integrations with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows distilled students can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while greatly improving efficiency, but success is context-dependent, hinging on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of bias, robustness, and privacy risks. Best practice treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component within integrated compression pipelines rather than a standalone recipe, and open problems remain in principled choice of distilled targets, reliable distillation with limited or private data, and theory connecting distilled signals to student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Hayes

When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design) and task- and data-aware practices, KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs, but its success is context dependent and requires careful attention to teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Jones

Empirical results indicate distilled students often approach teacher performance with substantially lower cost, but important limitations persist (teacher bias transfer, low-frequency token degradation, data access constraints, and capacity mismatch), motivating hybrid pipelines that combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and careful teacher–student design.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for transferring predictive capacity from large, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). Empirical work shows KD can recover much of the teacher's performance and, when carefully engineered, support robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving releases, and practical latency- or memory-constrained deployment. papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Potency, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile toolkit for compressing and adapting large neural models for deployment, cross-task transfer, federated settings, and multi-modal scenarios. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or module replacement), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and compute with modest accuracy loss. However, gains are not automatic: careful choice of what to distill (outputs, intermediate representations, or selected samples), how to mix hard/soft signals, and how to adapt KD to distributed or data-free regimes strongly affects outcomes. I argue that KD is most effective when it is task-aware, representation-aware, and integrated with other compression methods, and that future work should prioritize principled selection of distilled knowledge, robustness to teacher imperfections, and practical protocols for heterogeneous and privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a narrow training trick into a broad, practical paradigm for compressing and adapting large deep models to resource- and data-constrained deployment settings. However, KD is not universally effective out-of-the-box: its benefits and risks depend on task characteristics, data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and deliberate choices of what and how to transfer. When practitioners treat KD as a toolkit of targeted strategies and validate choices against task constraints, it yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity to the original model.

papers_seen.author: Fisher

papers_seen.author: Stewart

Best practice is to treat KD as a family of tools (logit, intermediate-layer, feature, adversarial, data-driven, self-distillation) and to adapt the distillation design to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Rubio
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD transfers information from teacher to student via soft logits, intermediate representations, attentional or channel signals, and relational objectives; it is often combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies to meet latency, memory, privacy, and domain-adaptation constraints. While KD frequently preserves much of a teacher’s performance and can improve robustness or generalization in some settings, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and responsible handling of bias, privacy, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across vision, language, multimodal and reinforcement settings, KD variants (soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives) and complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, neural architecture search, data synthesis) enable practical deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover most teacher performance and, in some settings, exceed it, but success depends on data availability, teacher–student alignment, choice of distillation targets, and targeted engineering such as projectors, pre-training for compact architectures, and curriculum or multi-teacher schemes.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft targets/logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals, contrastive or adversarial objectives) and in varied protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co‑distillation, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free and federated regimes). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multimodal domains shows KD frequently restores a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success depends critically on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data strategy, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as teacher-error propagation, bias transfer, and degraded low‑frequency behaviour. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and careful data/objective choices—to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lawson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations so that compact models meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. A diverse toolkit has emerged — soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, self- and online-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data strategies including data-free synthesis and targeted augmentation — which is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical work shows distilled students frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and distillation data are aligned, but KD has documented limitations (teacher–student mismatch, degradation on low-frequency behaviors, bias and privacy transfer, and sensitivity under data scarcity or distribution shift). Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, selecting distilled signals, data protocols, and complementary compression techniques according to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Tyler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster, or deployment‑specialized student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal, and federated settings, KD methods—including soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial or data‑free generation, and self- or online‑distillation—enable substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success depends on aligning distillation signals to student capacity and task requirements, selecting or synthesizing suitable data, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Important limitations remain (teacher–student capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, failures on low‑frequency phenomena, and distribution shift), so KD is best used as a configurable component within an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline with explicit evaluation of robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Ortega
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used approach for producing compact models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. It offers multiple mechanisms (soft-targets, intermediate representation matching, attention- or channel-wise transfers, multi-teacher and data‑free variants) that, when combined with complementary compression techniques, can yield substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss. However, KD’s effectiveness is highly dependent on task, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints; consequently, it should be treated as an adaptable component within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Fields
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Tool — Argument for Integrated, Context‑Aware Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, broadly applicable set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, and multimodal tasks shows KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD’s effectiveness is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals, and the availability or synthesis of suitable training data. For robust, real‑world compression, KD should be treated as a configurable component within an integrated pipeline that combines representation-level transfer, data and curriculum strategies, and architecture‑aware compression (pruning, quantization, or search), together with explicit safeguards for bias, robustness, and low‑frequency behavior.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central, practical toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. A diverse set of distillation signals and training protocols—ranging from logits/soft labels to feature- and attention-level matching, contrastive and relational objectives, ensemble and online schemes, and data‑free or privacy-preserving techniques—are routinely combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and neural architecture search. Empirical evidence shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while producing substantial efficiency gains, but practical success is context dependent and requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, data availability, and mitigation of transferred failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit — from soft-label matching to representation-level, adversarial, and data-free approaches — has been developed and successfully applied across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains. Practical success depends on careful choice of distillation targets, teacher–student compatibility, data regime, and integration with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Cunningham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of a Context‑Aware Model‑Compression Pipeline
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable core of a compression workflow—selecting appropriate transfer signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, and combining KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance. Effective deployment requires explicit handling of teacher quality, data regimes, fairness/privacy risks, and rare‑token or long‑tail behaviors; KD should therefore be used as the first‑line, task‑aware component of integrated compression pipelines rather than as a standalone, one‑size‑fits‑all solution.

papers_seen.author: Snyder
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably transfers behavior from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory and compute while preserving much of task performance. KD techniques span logits/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, relational and contrastive signals, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data-free or domain-adaptive variants. Empirical evidence shows KD is a practical first-line strategy for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, but it is not a standalone cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, objective design, and careful integration with complementary compression tools. For robust, real-world deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with targeted engineering to mitigate failure modes such as capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Settings, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or specialized students to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners use a range of objectives — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, contrastive and relational losses, adversarially generated supervision, and teacher-free/self-distillation variants — often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Distillation is effective in many settings (supervised, self-supervised, online, federated, and data-free), but its success depends on choices about what information to transfer, teacher quality and alignment to the student, availability and selection (or synthesis) of data, and the complement of compression techniques used. Empirical and theoretical work identifies both why distillation helps (regularization, privileged information, smoother targets) and when it struggles (capacity mismatch, distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena), suggesting hybrid pipelines and task-aware designs as practical routes forward.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Mcdaniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD is effective across modalities when treated as a configurable toolbox—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, attention, relations), how to align teacher and student (layer mapping, projectors, curricula), and how to handle data constraints (augmentation, data-free synthesis, federated protocols). KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search, but it is context-dependent: limitations include teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and difficulties with rare/long-tail phenomena. Best practice is to use KD as a principled component of an integrated compression pipeline, paired with task-aware design choices and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Henry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of methods that transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD can materially reduce latency, memory, and energy costs while preserving much of teacher performance, and its variants (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational objectives, online/mutual schemes, and data-free synthesis) extend its applicability across tasks and deployment constraints. However, the benefits of distillation depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and the choice of which signals to transfer; practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable component integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware practices rather than as a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to representation and feature matching—and has been adapted for online, multi-teacher, self-supervised, data-free, cross-modal, and federated scenarios. Across vision, language, speech, and graph domains, careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate teacher imperfections determines the success of compression. Best results arise when distillation is combined with complementary techniques (architecture adaptation, quantization, pruning, or curriculum strategies) and when practitioners attend to data-availability, distribution shift, and task-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Versatile, but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD supports diverse transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), adapts to data-limited and privacy‑sensitive settings, and interoperates with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Its empirical strengths make KD a first‑line approach for many deployment problems, but reliable, production‑grade compression requires explicit attention to teacher–student alignment, data selection or synthesis, capacity matching, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compressing large models for deployment and domain-specific use. Across modalities and tasks, KD can preserve much of the teacher's performance in compact students, but it must be combined with task-aware engineering—such as teacher adaptation, layer-wise selection, data augmentation, and hardware-aware pruning—to address heterogeneity, domain shift, and efficiency constraints. This article argues that KD is necessary but not sufficient: best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques chosen for the target modality, deployment constraints, and learning scenario.

papers_seen.author: Marks
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. A wide set of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training paradigms (offline, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation), and data strategies (real, synthetic, or data‑free) have been developed. KD is often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count, but reliable success depends on deliberate, task‑aware choices about transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and mitigation of bias, robustness, and distributional risks.

papers_seen.author: Campbell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Flexible, but Not Panacea Approach to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students and for transferring task- or modality-specific capabilities. KD supports many transfer targets and training protocols and can be combined with pruning, quantization, pretraining, and data synthesis to meet deployment constraints. However, reliable outcomes require careful teacher–student design, attention to data and privacy constraints, and targeted solutions for failure modes such as distribution shift, optimization mismatch, and preserved low-frequency behavior.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Extensions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a core technique for producing compact, efficient models and for enabling cross-model, cross-modal, and privacy-sensitive transfer in deep learning and NLP. KD can be implemented at the logit, feature, and layer levels, and extended to ensemble teachers, data-free scenarios, federated settings, and task-adaptive architecture search. While KD often yields large efficiency gains with small accuracy loss, its effectiveness depends on data properties, teacher–student alignment, and training choices; addressing limitations such as data heterogeneity, low-frequency token degradation, and mismatched inputs requires tailored methods (e.g., feature mimicking, teacher adaptation, multi-teacher weighting, and specialized divergences). Building on empirical and methodological work across modalities, I argue that KD should be treated as a versatile, application-driven toolkit rather than a single recipe, and that future progress will come from combining representational-level distillation, teacher-aware training, and methods that reduce reliance on original training data.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and powerful technique for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. When matched to the task and deployment constraints, KD can preserve most teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs; its value increases when combined with complementary compression methods and task-aware design. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer, data and curriculum strategies, teacher–student compatibility, and mitigation of transferred biases and rare-case failures. Treating KD as a configurable, first-order element of an integrated compression pipeline—rather than a one-shot solution—yields the best tradeoffs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically validated framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational and contrastive signals), can operate in multi-teacher and data-free settings, and integrates with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data strategy (including synthetic or public data when originals are unavailable), and task-aware objective design. KD has documented failure modes — e.g., propagation of teacher errors or biases, difficulty preserving low-frequency phenomena, and distributional mismatch — which motivate targeted remedies such as multi-signal objectives, teacher scheduling, meta-learned teachers, and joint optimization with other compression tools. Treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a single recipe, KD is an essential practical tool for model deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Vang
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models. KD encompasses a range of transfer targets and training protocols and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods to meet deployment constraints. Practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis strategies, and careful choice of distilled signals and training procedures.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad and practical toolbox has been developed—output-level (soft-target) matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, contrastive and relational objectives, adversarial and data-free methods, online and multi-teacher protocols, and curriculum- or architecture-aware pipelines. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can improve generalization when objectives, layer mappings, and data choices are well matched to student capacity and task constraints. Success requires careful design around what to transfer, how to align layers and inputs, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate bias, rare-token degradation, and teacher errors; combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and neural architecture search) and using task-aware curricula or projectors typically yields better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically motivated family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels of abstraction (output logits, intermediate features, attention and relational maps), can be adapted to scarce- or privacy-constrained data regimes, and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirically, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of transfer targets, and the availability or synthesis of appropriate distillation data. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

However, effectiveness is context dependent: practitioner choices about what to transfer, how to generate or select data, and how to mitigate transferred errors, bias, or distribution shift determine real-world outcomes.

Best practice treats KD as a configurable core element within an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and task-aware data strategies—and couples it with explicit measures to mitigate bias, robustness failures, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practically driven toolbox for transferring performance from large teacher models to smaller student models across modalities and tasks. papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used framework for transferring predictive behavior from large, expensive teachers to smaller, efficient students. Across vision, language, recommendation, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD has been extended beyond logits-matching into feature and layer-level mimicry, online and self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, task-adaptive architecture search, and combinations with pruning and quantization. Empirical results show KD enables substantial latency and memory reductions while often preserving accuracy, improving calibration, and helping robustness; success depends strongly on choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, data and augmentation, and alignment strategies between heterogeneous models.

papers_seen.author: Turner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD encompasses logits-based supervision, feature- and representation-level matching, attention- and channel-wise transfers, and data-aware or data-free extensions. It is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods and when practitioners adapt objectives, data strategies, and optimization schedules to task, student capacity, and deployment constraints. KD is therefore a first-line instrument for model compression, but its reliable use requires explicit, task-aware protocols that mitigate teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity, distribution shift, and transfer of undesirable teacher traits.

papers_seen.author: Walls
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques have been adapted across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models) to produce smaller, faster, or more robust models while attempting to retain performance of larger teachers. Approaches vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational information, or structural/topological properties), how transfer is scheduled or weighted (confidence-aware, progressive replacement, or multi-teacher aggregation), and how distillation is combined with other compression methods (pruning, architecture search, or compact operator substitution). Empirical work shows strong practical benefits—improved runtime, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness—while theoretical and analytical work begins to explain when and why distillation helps (e.g., role of soft targets, label smoothing analogies, and behavior with imperfect teachers). Remaining challenges include transferring rare-word or low-frequency information in sequence tasks, preserving relational/global structure in graph and link tasks, adapting to evolving domains, and automating generator compression for GANs. This synthesis summarizes key methods, insights, and open directions from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Harvey

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile family of techniques for compressing large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial or data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher protocols—have been shown to recover much of a teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and computational cost. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful selection of what and how to transfer; open challenges remain in robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and enabling private or data-free distillation at scale.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Phelps
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, practically indispensable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. When applied as a configurable component of an end-to-end compression pipeline—aligned with appropriate distillation targets, data strategies, and complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search—KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of the teacher performance. However, its effectiveness is conditional on factors including teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and augmentation strategy, optimization practices, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and robustness failures. Careful, task-aware design and integrated pipelines are therefore required for reliable deployment and continued research into data-free distillation, bias mitigation, and teacher–student co‑design remains crucial.
