papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and widely adopted family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, persistent limits — including capacity and optimization mismatch, data scarcity, propagation of teacher biases, and failures on low-frequency behaviors or distribution shift — mean KD should be treated as a configurable core component integrated with complementary compression primitives and task-aware practices rather than a standalone remedy.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as Central but Insufficient: A Task‑Aware, Pipeline‑Centric Position for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable set of techniques that reliably reduces inference cost by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models. Empirical evidence across vision, language, multimodal, and speech tasks shows that carefully designed KD pipelines often recover most of teacher performance — and in some circumstances can even improve student generalization — but consistent success requires task‑aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. I argue KD should be treated as the default, central component of model‑compression workflows while being explicitly integrated into broader, deployment‑aware pipelines that address teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, fairness/privacy risks, and hardware constraints.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models by transferring behavior from larger teacher models. When used as a configurable, task- and deployment-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline, KD routinely reduces latency and memory while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Its practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and complementary compression primitives; persistent challenges include bias transfer, handling low-frequency phenomena, distribution shift, and automating signal selection.

papers_seen.author: Villarreal
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically powerful and practically flexible approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD should be treated as a central, configurable element of compression workflows: it routinely delivers large reductions in inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance, but it is not sufficient on its own. Reliable deployment requires task‑aware choices of distilled signals, teacher–student co‑design, data strategies (including data‑free and privacy‑aware options), and combination with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Matthews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A wide variety of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational maps), protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, data-free), and integrations with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) have been developed. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a primary practical technique for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD supports a wide variety of goals—reducing latency and memory, enabling on-device inference, preserving privacy when data are unavailable, and transferring robustness or domain knowledge—by varying what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, relational/contrastive signals) and how training is scheduled (offline, online, progressive replacement, or data-free synthesis). While KD is not a universal cure, its flexibility and empirical success make it a first-choice strategy for compression when combined with careful design choices about teacher quality, transfer signals, and data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Santiago
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger or auxiliary teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving most of a teacher's performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Its practical value is greatest when integrated with complementary compression primitives and when adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints. However, KD also has clear limits—teacher–student capacity gaps, data scarcity or mismatch, and transferred biases or robustness failures—that require targeted mitigation and careful evaluation.

papers_seen.author: Hart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the behavior and performance of larger teachers. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when integrated thoughtfully into compression pipelines and paired with complementary techniques, but its effectiveness is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student design, data strategy, and safeguards for robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Mack
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD enables meaningful reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving much of teacher performance, but its success is conditional on task- and data-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses the capabilities of large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring information beyond hard labels. A variety of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, channel statistics, relational signals, or synthesized data) and protocols (offline teacher, online co-training, self-distillation, meta-learned teachers, teacher-free schemes, and data-free variants) have been developed to address deployment constraints across vision, language, speech, retrieval, detection, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation objectives and training schedules often preserve most teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but important trade-offs remain — including transferred biases, optimization and capacity gaps, data access and privacy constraints, and difficulties under distribution shift — motivating numerous methodological refinements and open research directions.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad and practical toolbox has been developed—output-level (soft-target) matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, contrastive and relational objectives, adversarial and data-free methods, online and multi-teacher protocols, and curriculum- or architecture-aware pipelines. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can improve generalization when objectives, layer mappings, and data choices are well matched to student capacity and task constraints. Success requires careful design around what to transfer, how to align layers and inputs, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate bias, rare-token degradation, and teacher errors; combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and neural architecture search) and using task-aware curricula or projectors typically yields better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practically driven toolbox for transferring performance from large teacher models to smaller student models across modalities and tasks. Methods span soft-label supervision, feature- and layer-wise imitation, adversarial and ensemble-based transfer, data- and privacy-aware protocols, and integration with complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but gains depend strongly on what is transferred, teacher–student alignment, domain shift, and data availability.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Morrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques that are often the first and most effective instrument for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers. KD methods now operate across multiple levels of supervision (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals) and protocols (offline, online, multi‑teacher, data‑free), and they are most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and tailored to task, data, and deployment constraints. However, the value of KD is conditional: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data regime, and mitigation of bias and distribution‑shift risks determine success. Consequently, best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey cure.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Sensitive Core of Integrated Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Treated as a configurable core of compression workflows, KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory footprint while preserving much of teacher performance when its objectives, teacher–student alignment, and data strategy are chosen to match task and deployment constraints. However, KD is not a standalone cure: reliable production deployments combine KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), targeted data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or privacy-preserving data), and explicit mitigations for known failure modes such as capacity mismatch, propagated teacher biases, and low-frequency degradation.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost and enable deployment in constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. The literature documents a wide set of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training protocols (offline teacher–student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, multi-teacher), and data strategies (data-rich, data-free, augmentation and selective-sample curricula). Empirical work across vision, language, graph, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling shows that well-designed KD pipelines — especially those that match internal representations, align layers thoughtfully, and combine KD with pruning/quantization or student-aware teacher design — can retain much of teacher performance while substantially lowering model size and latency. However, KD has failure modes (teacher mismatch, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, privacy and bias transfer, and sensitivity to data availability) that require complementary methods such as data-free synthesis, domain-aware adaptation, privacy-preserving noise, and careful objective design. The field continues to refine when and how to apply KD so that compact models are accurate, robust, and suitable for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Weiss
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical, flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. The literature shows a broad family of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relations), multiple training paradigms (offline, online, co-distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free), and frequent combination with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD works both as a method for transferring predictive behavior and as an implicit regularizer, but its empirical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability (including synthesized or data‑free regimes), and careful engineering choices to mitigate optimization gaps, distributional mismatch, and transferred biases.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Young
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly validated set of techniques for producing smaller, deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into compact students. Across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains, KD methods and protocols—when combined with careful data, architecture, and deployment-aware decisions—regularly yield substantial efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance. Success is context dependent, and practical deployments pair KD with complementary compression primitives and targeted safeguards for robustness, privacy, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Singleton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Insufficient Core of Model-Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and widely adopted family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, persistent limits — including capacity and optimization mismatch, data scarcity, propagation of teacher biases, and failures on low-frequency behaviors or distribution shift — mean KD should be treated as a configurable core component integrated with complementary compression primitives and task-aware practices rather than a standalone remedy.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Practical Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer knowledge from larger or more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, faster, or more interpretable students. Over the past decade these approaches have been adapted across modalities and tasks — from image classification and object detection to sequence models and large pretrained language models — and have been combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning and low-precision quantization. Empirical and theoretical work has highlighted both the practical gains of distillation (improved student generalization, reduced latency and memory, enabling deployment) and key limitations (optimization gaps, distribution mismatch, loss of certain types of information). A range of innovations — feature- and attention-based matching, layer-wise/task-aware distillation, self-distillation, data-free distillation with generative replay, teacher adaptation, and weighted/importance-aware soft labels — have been proposed to close these gaps and extend KD to settings such as domain adaptation, privacy-preserving federated learning, cross-modal transfer, and low-resource devices.

papers_seen.author: Stephenson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesized Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically validated family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, compute, and privacy. KD methods span soft-target/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-side strategies (including data-free and synthesized data). Reliable compression uses KD as a configurable core within hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and task-aware data and evaluation practices.

papers_seen.author: Coleman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficiently Complete Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practical set of techniques that enables production of compact models that retain much of larger teachers' functionality across modalities and tasks. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component of a broader compression pipeline, KD supports deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and hardware constraints. However, distillation has concrete failure modes — propagation of teacher errors, difficulty preserving low-frequency phenomena, capacity and distribution mismatches, and privacy or robustness concerns — which require complementary methods, data strategies, and careful teacher–student design. I argue KD should be adopted as a central, configurable tool in compression workflows but not relied on alone: best practice integrates KD with representation-aware objectives, curriculum/data strategies, multi-teacher or collaborative teaching, and targeted safeguards for bias, rare-case behavior, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Contextual Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and empirically validated approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students. It operates at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/relational signals, contrastive and adversarial objectives) and is most effective when tailored to the task, student capacity, data regime, and deployment constraints. Practical deployments combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and explicit protocols to mitigate failure modes such as teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and the transfer of biases or private information. Responsible application requires task-aware teacher–student design, data strategies (including data-free or few-shot methods when necessary), and monitoring for degraded behavior on low-frequency or structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to reduce the resource footprint of large neural networks while preserving performance. The literature surveys a range of approaches — from vanilla teacher-student soft-target transfers to layer-wise, attention- and channel-wise methods, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, and combinations with pruning and adversarial training — and demonstrates successful applications across NLP, speech, vision, graph, and multimodal problems. Empirical results show effective speedups and parameter reductions with modest accuracy loss; theoretical and empirical analyses also connect KD to label-smoothing and regularization effects that can improve generalization.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Vasquez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise deployment‑suitable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners use logits/soft targets, intermediate feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, and data‑side strategies (including data‑free synthesis and augmentation). KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when its design is adapted to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints. Important limitations include capacity mismatch, teacher error or bias transfer, distribution shift, and challenges in preserving low‑frequency or long‑tail behavior; addressing these requires task‑aware objective design, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of distillation objectives—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature-, attention- and layer-wise alignment, relational/contrastive signals, adversarial and data-free sample synthesis, and meta- or multi-teacher schemes—has been developed and applied across vision, language, retrieval, graph, and federated settings. In practice, KD is most effective when combined with task- and architecture-aware design choices and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, limited or private data, and optimization stability; proposed remedies emphasize task-aware filtering of teacher signals, learned teacher adaptation, layer mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Cunningham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD variants—including logits/soft-target matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and adversarial generation, and self-distillation—are combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines typically recover most teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of transfer signals, and the availability or synthesis of data; remaining challenges include robustness, bias transfer, low-frequency/structured-output preservation, privacy-aware distillation, and automating teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted set of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. The literature develops multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), training protocols (offline multi-stage, online, self-distillation, data-free/generative, adversarial), and application-specific adaptations (NLP transformer compression, vision, speech, graph models, federated and privacy-aware settings). Empirical work shows KD frequently yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when paired with architecture-aware design and complementary compression methods, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, data availability, and distributional or fairness concerns. Practical success generally requires matching the distillation objective to the task, handling data limitations with augmentation or synthetic generators, and integrating KD into a broader compression portfolio (pruning, quantization, architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Phelps
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, practically indispensable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. When applied as a configurable component of an end-to-end compression pipeline—aligned with appropriate distillation targets, data strategies, and complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search—KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of the teacher performance. However, its effectiveness is conditional on factors including teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and augmentation strategy, optimization practices, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and robustness failures. Careful, task-aware design and integrated pipelines are therefore required for reliable deployment and continued research into data-free distillation, bias mitigation, and teacher–student co‑design remains crucial.

papers_seen.author: Frank
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practically oriented family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, faster student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, data strategies (including augmentation and data-free synthesis), and robustness or privacy safeguards.

papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Arnold

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses information from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. The literature provides a diverse toolkit—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, contrastive and relational objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or synthetic-data approaches—together with engineering practices that pair KD with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, and data/curriculum strategies. Empirical results show KD often preserves much of the teacher’s performance across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, yet important challenges remain around teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity and privacy, robustness and fairness, and reliable transfer of low-frequency or structured behaviors. Continued progress centers on designing what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to integrate KD into end-to-end compression pipelines for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Peck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Dependent Engine for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and flexible family of methods for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, speech, and recommendation tasks show KD can recover most of a teacher’s performance while delivering substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication cost. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime and selection, the choice of transfer signals, and how KD is combined with complementary compression methods. For reliable deployment, practitioners should treat KD as a task‑aware toolbox—selecting what to transfer, aligning teacher and student carefully, addressing data or privacy constraints, and integrating pruning/quantization or architecture-aware design—while explicitly mitigating limitations such as teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Cole
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely adopted toolkit for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely reduces inference cost and parameter counts while preserving much of teacher performance, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core element within integrated compression pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, architecture design, data strategies, and explicit robustness and fairness evaluations.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Snyder
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably transfers behavior from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory and compute while preserving much of task performance. KD techniques span logits/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, relational and contrastive signals, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data-free or domain-adaptive variants. Empirical evidence shows KD is a practical first-line strategy for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, but it is not a standalone cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, objective design, and careful integration with complementary compression tools. For robust, real-world deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with targeted engineering to mitigate failure modes such as capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Wheeler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used family of techniques that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and hardware constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate features, attention/relational signals) and in diverse protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free). Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of a teacher's performance and can even improve generalization in some settings, but it also has well-known failure modes—teacher bias propagation, difficulty preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and sensitivity to data availability and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, as well as careful data and objective design.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost and enable deployment in constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. The literature documents a wide set of distilled signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training protocols (offline teacher–student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, multi-teacher), and data strategies (data-rich, data-free, augmentation and selective-sample curricula). Empirical work across vision, language, graph, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling shows that well-designed KD pipelines — especially those that match internal representations, align layers thoughtfully, and combine KD with pruning/quantization or student-aware teacher design — can retain much of teacher performance while substantially lowering model size and latency. However, KD has failure modes (teacher mismatch, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, privacy and bias transfer, and sensitivity to data availability) that require complementary methods such as data-free synthesis, domain-aware adaptation, privacy-preserving noise, and careful objective design. The field continues to refine when and how to apply KD so that compact models are accurate, robust, and suitable for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for transferring information from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels — soft targets (logits), intermediate representations, attention and relational structure, and contrastive objectives — and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, pretraining, and architecture adaptation. Practical success is conditional on teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful optimization and evaluation to avoid propagating teacher artifacts, degrading rare-case behavior, or failing under distribution shift. The field shows strong empirical gains across vision, language, speech, recommendation, generative, and multimodal tasks, while open problems remain in theory, heterogeneous architectures, privacy-aware protocols, and robust transfer of low-frequency or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Wolf
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact models from larger teachers and ensembles. It frequently yields strong efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance, but its reliability depends on task‑aware design, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression methods. Responsible deployment of KD requires explicit safeguards for bias, distributional shift, and rare behaviours.

papers_seen.author: Mejia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Tool Best Used in a Compression Portfolio
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Best practice treats KD as a core component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design—and demands task-aware protocols and safeguards for robustness, rare-token behavior, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Berry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Benefits, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring behavior or internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Empirically, KD reduces inference latency, memory footprint, and compute while often preserving most of a teacher's task performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD methods vary in what they transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), how data are used (real, augmented, synthesized, or zero-shot), and whether distillation is performed online, with multiple teachers, or self-supervised. KD is most effective when configured to task and deployment constraints and combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search). It also has well-documented failure modes—capacity mismatch, propagated teacher artifacts, degraded long-tail performance, and data-availability or privacy limits—that require explicit mitigation strategies. This synthesis summarizes established techniques, practical trade-offs, and actionable design patterns for applying KD in real-world deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. The methods range from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structures, and they operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, cross-modal, and data-constrained regimes. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align layers, and how to handle limited or private data. While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, open challenges remain in teacher–student mismatch, distribution shift, robustness and fairness transfer, data-free/privacy-preserving distillation, and principled selection of distilled signals.

papers_seen.author: Hayden
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded framework for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or auxiliary teacher models into compact students. KD methods include soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online protocols, data-free or zero-shot schemes, and self-distillation. Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of teacher performance when combined with suitable data strategies, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD’s effectiveness is context dependent: success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and safeguards against transferred artifacts, distributional mismatch, and social harms. The practical consensus treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a plug-and-play solution.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Challenges

papers_seen.author: Murray

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Treated as a configurable core of compression workflows, KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory footprint while preserving much of teacher performance when its objectives, teacher–student alignment, and data strategy are chosen to match task and deployment constraints. However, KD is not a standalone cure: reliable production deployments combine KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), targeted data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or privacy-preserving data), and explicit mitigations for known failure modes such as capacity mismatch, propagated teacher biases, and low-frequency degradation.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Bennett
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely applied family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks, KD variants (logit/soft-label matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data-free/zero-shot synthesis) combined with complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) enable substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, availability or synthesis of data, and integration with other compression methods. Remaining challenges include principled theory connecting distilled signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, transfer across heterogeneous architectures and non-iid data, and mitigation of propagated biases and degraded behavior on rare or long‑tail phenomena.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broad, practically driven family of methods that transfer predictive behavior, internal representations, or structured information from large teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful data and training practices, distillation often preserves much of the teacher's performance and can add functional guarantees (robustness, low-precision accuracy, privacy-aware releases). Key limitations include dependence on teacher quality, student capacity and architectural alignment, distributional mismatch or limited data, and the risk of propagating teacher errors or biases, motivating continued work on principled objectives, data strategies, and deployment-aware pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression

Treating KD as a configurable element within an integrated compression pipeline—combined with representation alignment, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture-aware design—yields the most reliable and deployable outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick; it is a versatile, practically proven framework that enables resource-efficient deployment, privacy-preserving learning, cross-modal and cross-domain transfers, and even improvements in robustness. When combined with complementary techniques — feature mimicking, projector modules, teacher annealing, label-smoothing–style regularization, and data-free or federated protocols — distillation can address the main bottlenecks of modern deep and multilingual models: size, latency, heterogeneity of devices, limited or private data, and domain shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component in any strategy for compressing or adapting deep models for real-world NLP and vision deployments.

papers_seen.author: Collins

papers_seen.author: Arnold

papers_seen.author: Carr
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for transferring functionality from large teacher models to smaller students so that compressed models retain much of the teacher's performance while meeting constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and communication. papers_seen.author: Ryan

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Walters
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. Modern KD methods span simple soft-target matching to representation-, attention-, and relation-level transfer, and they are routinely combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware training protocols. Empirical work shows KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss when teacher quality, student capacity, data, and transfer signals are carefully aligned; open problems include theory, robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare-token behavior, privacy, and principled automation of teacher–student alignment.

papers_seen.author: Richard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation is Central but Insufficient: A Position on Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, latency, and memory, but reliable deployment requires integrating KD into a broader, task- and hardware-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Vance
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component: The Case for Integrated, Task‑Aware Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and widely applied method for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller students. KD variants (logits, feature- and layer-level matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data-free and federated protocols) have enabled practical deployment across vision, language, retrieval, generative modeling, and healthcare. However, KD faces concrete limitations—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity or privacy constraints, degraded performance on low-frequency phenomena, and potential fairness or robustness regressions—that reduce its effectiveness when used alone. The strongest practical outcomes come from integrating KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful selection or synthesis of distilled supervision, and task- and data-aware training schedules.

papers_seen.author: Lynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Aware Component for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically effective family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal settings when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student design are selected for the deployment context. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all cure: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as propagated bias, poor low-frequency behavior, and distribution shift. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware distillation, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Lyons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression methods form a broadly applicable toolkit for producing smaller, faster, or more interpretable models from large teacher networks. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners transfer information via softened outputs, intermediate representation matching, attention/relational signals, and synthetic data, and they commonly combine KD with pruning, quantization, and automated architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most teacher performance while substantially reducing latency and memory, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and task-specific adaptations.
