papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational, and data‑free objectives—enable substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success is conditional on task-aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and integration with complementary compression primitives; open challenges remain in capacity mismatch, distributional robustness, preservation of rare behaviors, and privacy-aware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers. Its methods and protocols span soft-logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, ensemble and multi-teacher schemes, online and data-free variants, and task-specific adaptations. I argue KD should be treated as the central, configurable element of integrated compression pipelines whose design is driven by task constraints, data regimes, and deployment requirements.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Component of Task‑Aware Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable technique for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller student models, producing compact systems suitable for resource‑constrained deployment. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or hardware‑optimal compression. Reliable production compression pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable core element that must be combined with teacher–student co‑design, data strategies (including data‑free synthesis), and complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation to meet practical constraints and mitigate failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Versatile, but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD supports diverse transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), adapts to data-limited and privacy‑sensitive settings, and interoperates with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Its empirical strengths make KD a first‑line approach for many deployment problems, but reliable, production‑grade compression requires explicit attention to teacher–student alignment, data selection or synthesis, capacity matching, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Principled Toolbox for Practical and Responsible Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood not as a single algorithm but as a flexible, task-aware toolbox that can produce compact, deployable models when combined with complementary design choices. Properly applied—selecting what to transfer (logits, features, attention), how to map layers, and which auxiliary techniques to use (pretraining, curriculum, adversarial or privacy safeguards)—KD can deliver students that approach or sometimes match teacher performance while enabling latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained deployment. At the same time, KD has clear failure modes (data heterogeneity, low-frequency phenomena, imperfect teachers, and optimization challenges) that demand targeted mitigations rather than blind application.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, latency, and communication while attempting to preserve task performance. The literature characterizes a wide taxonomy of distillation targets and protocols, documents strong empirical gains when KD is carefully configured, and emphasizes that KD is most reliable when integrated into hybrid compression pipelines that address teacher–student alignment, data regime, and deployment constraints. Known limitations include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and bias, difficulties under data scarcity or privacy constraints, and instability under distribution shift; current best practice is task- and deployment-aware application of KD combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Spence
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Task‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques that should be treated as an essential, task-aware component of model-compression pipelines rather than a one-size-fits-all solution. Properly designed KD—choosing what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student architectures, selecting or synthesizing suitable data, and integrating complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search—regularly yields compact models that preserve most teacher performance for deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. However, KD has predictable failure modes (teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare outputs) that require explicit mitigation and evaluation in real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Santiago
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable, but Insufficient Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly effective and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Treated as a configurable toolkit—selecting what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to combine distillation with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—KD yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and mitigation of bias, distribution shift, and low-frequency or rare-case behaviors. Best practice treats KD as the central component of an integrated compression pipeline tailored to task, data regime, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely applicable approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component of a broader compression pipeline, KD can deliver substantial gains in latency, memory, and often accuracy while enabling deployment in resource- and privacy-constrained settings. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, signal selection, and complementary compression methods. Responsible application requires explicit mitigation of failure modes such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and bias transfer, and integration with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, or data‑free methods when appropriate.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Effectiveness, Limitations, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible method for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more interpretable models across vision, language, speech, and recommendation systems. KD works both as a stand-alone compression technique and as a complementary tool that combines well with pruning, quantization, multi-teacher strategies, and privacy-aware or federated settings. While highly effective in practice, KD has limits—especially around data availability, heterogeneity, and theoretical understanding—that recent work addresses with data-free methods, meta-learning teachers, and principled analyses.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Patterns, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practically essential family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information beyond hard labels. Research across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and reinforcement-learning settings has produced a toolkit of transfer targets and training protocols that, when combined with complementary compression primitives, routinely yield large reductions in latency and memory with modest performance loss. KD’s success is highly context-dependent: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and careful objective and curriculum design. Remaining challenges include robustness under distribution shift, preservation of low-frequency behaviors, bias transfer, and privacy-aware or data-free regimes; best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all remedy.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD techniques encompass output-level supervision (soft logits), representation- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, progressive module replacement, and online or multi-teacher protocols. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost, but success is context-sensitive: it depends on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and distribution of data (including data-free or synthesized alternatives), and careful loss and layer-mapping choices. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable toolbox to be combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and domain-, fairness-, or privacy-aware interventions. Remaining scientific and engineering challenges include principled selection of distillation targets, reliable distillation under limited or mismatched data, mitigation of transferred biases and rare-token degradation, theoretical understanding of when and why different KD objectives help, and automated, hardware-aware co-design for heterogeneous deployment.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Integrated Framework for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the functionality of larger teachers. KD works across modalities, supports deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and also acts as a regularizer; however, it has concrete failure modes that require complementary methods and careful teacher–student design. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of any compression pipeline, used in combination with representation-aware objectives, curriculum and data strategies, and targeted safeguards for bias, low-frequency behavior, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD encompasses many techniques — from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational structure — and is effective across vision, language, speech, and graph tasks when designed around task constraints and student capacity. However, KD is not a stand‑alone solution: its practical success depends on data availability, teacher quality, student architecture, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases, robustness deficits, and low-frequency behavior. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, data strategies (including augmentation and data-free synthesis), and robustness or privacy safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted, practical family of techniques for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models across vision, speech, retrieval, and NLP. The literature shows a broad toolkit of transfer signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational maps, contrastive or adversarial objectives) and protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free variants). Empirical work demonstrates that KD yields substantial efficiency gains when aligned to student capacity and combined with complementary compression primitives, while persistent challenges remain around teacher error propagation, distribution shift, low‑frequency/rare-output preservation, and principled theoretical understanding.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD encompasses matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning internal representations and features, transferring relational or contrastive structure, and using curriculum or search to adapt students and their architectures. Applied across vision, language, retrieval, generation, and federated settings, KD enables latency and memory reductions, on-device deployment, ensemble compression, and privacy-aware releases. Effectiveness depends on what is distilled, teacher–student compatibility, data and optimization choices, and problem-specific designs; as a result, KD functions best as a toolbox of choices (targets, mappings, curricula, privacy/robustness safeguards) rather than a single recipe. Remaining challenges include theoretical understanding of which teacher signals matter across tasks, robustness under data heterogeneity, privacy-preserving distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods aim to transfer behavior and representations from larger, more expensive models into smaller, efficient ones while retaining task performance. Across modalities and tasks, research has developed many complementary mechanisms — soft-label mimicry, intermediate representation matching, teacher-student curriculum designs, self-distillation, multi-teacher and online schemes, data- or generator-based transfer, and domain- or modality-specific adaptations — to balance accuracy, latency, and resource constraints. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation can recover most teacher performance (and in some settings even surpass it) while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and improving reproducibility and privacy. Success depends on the distillation targets, the teacher-student pairing and training regime, the use of auxiliary data or synthetic examples, and task-specific modifications.

papers_seen.author: Wells
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD techniques—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or privacy-preserving protocols, and online/co-distillation schemes—enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute with modest accuracy loss when applied with task-aware design. Effective use of KD typically combines careful selection of what to transfer, attention to teacher–student capacity and data regimes, and integration with complementary compression mechanisms such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Remaining challenges include teacher imperfection and bias transfer, data scarcity and domain shift, capacity and optimization mismatch, and reliably distilling structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Quinn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential but Not Sufficient — A Case for Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated toolkit that transfers information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. KD methods span soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention and relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-aware or data-free schemes. While KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher capability and enables deployment under resource and privacy constraints, its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the distillation signals chosen, and the data regime. Consequently, KD is best treated as a central, configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and careful data and evaluation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Gallegos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Configurable Core of Hybrid Model‑Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential and highly practical class of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers. Its many variants—soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, contrastive and relational objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, self-distillation, and data-free generation—make KD applicable across vision, language, reinforcement learning, and multimodal tasks. However, KD is not a universal solution: its reliability depends on careful matching of distilled signals to student capacity, data strategy, and targeted mitigations for bias, rare-case behavior, and distribution shift. The most dependable deployments treat KD as a configurable core within hybrid compression pipelines that combine representation-aware distillation objectives with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum/data strategies, and privacy- or fairness-aware safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Gillespie
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller student models. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target (logit) matching into a diverse toolbox that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher training, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows that KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while delivering latency, memory, and deployment benefits, but its success is context dependent: it requires careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, data strategy (including synthetic or privacy-preserving data), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, optimization mismatch, and degradation on rare or low-frequency phenomena. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core element within hybrid compression pipelines rather than as a standalone cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Bates
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically oriented set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory use, latency, and communication while often retaining much of task performance. Over the past decade KD has diversified from simple logit/soft-target matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, data‑ and privacy‑aware protocols, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success is highly context dependent: it depends on teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and choice of distillation data (or synthetic alternatives), and explicit handling of transferred biases, low‑frequency phenomena, and distribution shift. Practical deployments treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines, applying task‑aware objective design, layer mapping, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Reliable Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework for transferring behavior from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost and enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. KD encompasses many targets and protocols and—when designed with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data, and complementary compression methods—regularly yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. However, KD is not a universal remedy: careful protocol design, combination with pruning/quantization/architecture search, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and long‑tail behaviors are required for dependable real‑world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Wallace
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically proven family of methods for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD spans outputs-only approaches (soft targets) to rich objectives that match intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure, or contrastive signals. It operates across many data regimes (full-data, limited-data, data-free, synthetic-data), and is frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to achieve deployment constraints on latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity. The effectiveness of KD is strongly context dependent: success requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of distilled signals and layer mappings, and data strategies (including augmentation, curriculum, and synthetic generation). Common failure modes include propagation of teacher errors or biases, difficulty preserving low-frequency or long-tail behaviors, and optimization barriers that prevent perfect mimicry, motivating targeted remedies such as multi-signal objectives, multi-teacher ensembles, teacher scheduling, meta-learned teachers, and joint optimization with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Frank
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practically oriented family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, faster student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Modern KD goes well beyond matching soft logits: it includes intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online/self-distillation and multi-teacher regimes, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with complementary primitives such as pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies. Practical limits—teacher–student capacity and optimization mismatch, teacher errors and bias propagation, domain shift, and scarce or private data—motivate task-aware design, layer-mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-preserving approaches.

papers_seen.author: Landry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Tool That Must Be Integrated for Reliable Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical family of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and generative domains. Empirical evidence shows KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its effectiveness is strongly context dependent: it hinges on what signals are transferred, teacher and student capacity and alignment, availability and composition of data, and mitigation of robustness, fairness, and low‑frequency behavior issues. Therefore, KD should be treated as a first‑line, configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation‑aware distillation with data strategies, projector or layer‑mapping modules, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to produce robust, deployable compact models.

papers_seen.author: Guerrero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically validated and flexible approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment across modalities when integrated thoughtfully with complementary compression methods. Its success is context dependent — determined by teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and loss of rare behaviors — so practitioners should treat KD as a configurable element of a broader compression pipeline rather than a one-shot solution.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Federated Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Distributed learning frameworks often rely on exchanging model parameters across workers, instead of revealing their raw data. A prime example is federated learning that exchanges the gradients or weights of each neural network model. Under limited communication resources, however, such a method becomes extremely costly particularly for modern deep neural networks having a huge number of model parameters. In this regard, federated distillation (FD) is a compelling distributed learning solution that only exchanges the model outputs whose dimensions are commonly much smaller than the model sizes (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset). The goal of this chapter is to provide a deep understanding of FD while demonstrating its communication efficiency and applicability to a variety of tasks. To this end, towards demystifying the operational principle of FD, the first part of this chapter provides a novel asymptotic analysis for two foundational algorithms of FD, namely knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD), by exploiting the theory of neural tangent kernel (NTK). Next, the second part elaborates on a baseline implementation of FD for a classification task, and illustrates its performance in terms of accuracy and communication efficiency compared to FL. Lastly, to demonstrate the applicability of FD to various distributed learning tasks and environments, the third part presents two selected applications, namely FD over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels and FD for reinforcement learning.

papers_seen.author: Brooks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: an Essential, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD methods extend beyond simple logit matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, multi-teacher and online protocols, and data- or privacy-aware variants. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and applied with task-aware design, KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs. However, KD is context-dependent: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of bias, low-frequency/fine-grained behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Durham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically indispensable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. Empirical work shows KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count. Its effectiveness depends on deliberate choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student design and capacity alignment, data availability and selection, and integration with complementary compression techniques. Treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a standalone recipe, KD delivers the most reliable and deployable gains.

papers_seen.author: Hawkins
papers_seen.title: A Fast Knowledge Distillation Framework for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: While Knowledge Distillation (KD) has been recognized as a useful tool in many visual tasks, such as supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning, the main drawback of a vanilla KD framework is its mechanism, which consumes the majority of the computational overhead on forwarding through the giant teacher networks, making the entire learning procedure inefficient and costly. ReLabel, a recently proposed solution, suggests creating a label map for the entire image. During training, it receives the cropped region-level label by RoI aligning on a pre-generated entire label map, allowing for efficient supervision generation without having to pass through the teachers many times. However, as the KD teachers are from conventional multi-crop training, there are various mismatches between the global label-map and region-level label in this technique, resulting in performance deterioration. In this study, we present a Fast Knowledge Distillation (FKD) framework that replicates the distillation training phase and generates soft labels using the multi-crop KD approach, while training faster than ReLabel since no post-processes such as RoI align and softmax operations are used. When conducting multi-crop in the same image for data loading, our FKD is even more efficient than the traditional image classification framework. On ImageNet-1K, we obtain 79.8% with ResNet-50, outperforming ReLabel by ~1.0% while being faster. On the self-supervised learning task, we also show that FKD has an efficiency advantage. Our project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/FKD/index.html, source code and models are available at: https://github.com/szq0214/FKD.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques constitute a flexible toolkit for transferring behavior and internal structure from large, high‑capacity teacher models into smaller, faster, or deployment‑specific student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relations, and structured objectives) and across protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co‑distillation, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free, and federated schemes). Empirical practice shows KD often retains a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in compute, memory, and latency when combined with complementary compression methods and careful data and architecture choices. However, KD’s effectiveness is context dependent: it is sensitive to teacher quality and mismatch, student capacity, data availability and distribution, and the risk of propagating teacher artifacts (biases, low‑frequency errors). Remaining needs include principled theory linking distilled signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under heterogeneous or non‑i.i.d. data, and robust privacy/fairness guarantees for compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Nolan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reduces large, high-performing models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision and language modalities, KD variants (logit matching, feature/attention matching, data-free/adversarial synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation) enable deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device heterogeneity constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students often retain much of teacher performance, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Remaining challenges include robust transfer under data heterogeneity, avoidance of bias propagation, and principled design choices for heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: Bailey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The literature develops multi-level transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure), multi‑teacher and online variants, data-aware and data‑free protocols, and integrations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks when teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and mapping between teacher and student are carefully managed; however, success is context-dependent and limited by optimization gaps, data scarcity, capacity mismatch, and the risk of transferring teacher artifacts or biases. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable component of broader compression workflows tailored to deployment constraints such as latency, memory, privacy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Pena
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Order, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: I argue that knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first-order technique for compressing and adapting deep models for practical deployment in vision and language systems. KD's flexibility—supporting logits, intermediate features, relational signals, online/multi-teacher regimes, and data-free variants—lets practitioners address latency, memory, on-device inference, privacy, and domain adaptation constraints. However, KD is not a plug-and-play cure: its success depends on teacher quality, the choice of transfer signals, data availability (or synthetic data methods), and explicit measures to mitigate bias, low-frequency degradation, and distribution shift. Accordingly, KD should be used as a configurable toolkit combined with task-aware design, auxiliary compression methods, and deployment-aware safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Nguyen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger teacher models to smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Across vision, language, speech, and graph tasks, KD uses a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and protocols (offline multi‑teacher, online/self‑distillation, data‑free or generator‑based synthesis, and federated/zero‑shot transfer). KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search or NAS) and when adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints. However, practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability and alignment of data, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases, low‑frequency failures, and distribution shift. However, its empirical success is context dependent: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and domain match, and objective design, and open challenges remain around robustness, fairness, low-frequency behavior, and automated, privacy-preserving deployment pipelines.

papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware toolbox for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into compact student models. KD methods include output-level (soft logits) supervision, intermediate representation and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and online or multi‑teacher training. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which data to use or synthesize, KD routinely yields large reductions in parameter count and latency while preserving most of teacher performance. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it is limited by teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution shift, and risks such as propagated teacher biases and degraded rare-token or out‑of‑distribution behavior. Addressing these limits requires task-specific protocols, privacy‑ and robustness‑aware designs, and more principled, automated approaches to objective selection and layer alignment.

Practical success requires matching distillation objectives to task and student capacity, choosing appropriate data strategies, and integrating KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Important open issues include optimization and capacity gaps, teacher-bias transfer, limited- or no-data scenarios, domain shift, privacy guarantees, and automated teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Payne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, empirically validated approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task- and deployment-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline—and combined with complementary techniques and explicit safeguards—KD routinely delivers strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, KD is not automatic: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and mitigation of robustness and fairness risks.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for transferring predictive behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, efficient students. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods extend beyond logits-matching to include intermediate-feature and attention-level transfer, data-free and privacy-aware variants, multi-teacher and online protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Empirical work shows KD can yield compact models that retain much teacher performance, but success depends on careful selection of what and how to transfer, data availability, and the match between teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models. A rich set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention/relational structure, contrastive and adversarial objectives) and protocols (offline, online, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free, privacy‑aware) has been developed and applied across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative modeling. Practical effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and integration with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Ongoing challenges include aligning heterogeneous architectures, distilling under data or privacy constraints, mitigating transferred biases and degraded rare-event behavior, and designing principled layer-to-layer mappings and data‑efficient protocols.

papers_seen.author: Mendoza
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Effects, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used, flexible framework for producing smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD encompasses a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals) and protocols (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free, and curriculum-driven). Empirical work demonstrates KD often preserves much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute, but its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure-all. Key open directions include principled selection of signals to transfer, robust privacy-preserving distillation, automation of deployment-aware pipelines, and reliable compression of large transformer and generative models.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Integrated Framework for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the functionality of larger teachers. KD works across modalities, supports deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and also acts as a regularizer; however, it has concrete failure modes that require complementary methods and careful teacher–student design. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of any compression pipeline, used in combination with representation-aware objectives, curriculum and data strategies, and targeted safeguards for bias, low-frequency behavior, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models using targets ranging from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals. Across vision, language, multimodal, and speech tasks, KD combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation or synthetic-data generation) enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical results show distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can sometimes match or exceed teachers when distillation is carefully designed. Important open problems include teacher–student capacity mismatch, optimization and belief-matching limits, distribution shift and domain adaptation, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, and avoiding transfer of teacher biases. This synthesis summarizes mechanisms, practical variants, representative empirical patterns, and recommended directions for research and deployment.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies transfer information from larger or differently structured models to smaller, more efficient ones. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants—matching teacher logits, intermediate representations, attention, or relational structure—enable large reductions in latency, memory, and communication while often preserving most of the teacher's performance. Practical deployment benefits from combining KD with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from careful choices about what and how to transfer, which data to use, and how to design teacher-student pairings. Key challenges remain around teacher error propagation, low-frequency/rare behavior preservation, data and domain mismatch, privacy constraints, and heterogeneous deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit — from soft-label matching to representation-level, adversarial, and data-free approaches — has been developed and successfully applied across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains. Practical success depends on careful choice of distillation targets, teacher–student compatibility, data regime, and integration with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Dougherty
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically effective approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD works at multiple levels (soft targets, intermediate representations, relational/contrastive signals, and data‑synthesis protocols) and is most reliable when adapted to task constraints, teacher and student capacity, and available data. I argue that KD should be treated as the central, configurable core of any compression pipeline but not as a standalone cure: to be robust and production‑ready it must be combined with complementary compression primitives, careful layer and signal design, and specific remedies for documented failure modes such as teacher–student mismatch, transferred biases, and degradation on low‑frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Suarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade‑offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques for transferring information from larger, more expensive teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD supports multiple transfer signals (soft labels, features, attention/relations, contrastive objectives) and modes (offline, online, multi‑teacher, data‑free), and is widely used across modalities including NLP, vision, recommender systems, GANs, and reinforcement learning. Practical deployment of KD hinges on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of bias and distributional failures; combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and deployment‑aware safeguards typically yields the best trade‑offs.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Versatile, but Context‑Dependent Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely applicable family of techniques for producing compact student models from larger teachers. When designed as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline, KD routinely yields strong tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity; however, reliable deployment requires task‑aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and explicit mitigations for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Shepherd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically supported toolkit for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants (logit/soft-target matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, multi- and online-teacher schemes, data- and privacy-aware workflows) consistently enable favorable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, and model size. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability and match of data, and distribution shift shape outcomes. For robust, production-ready compression, KD should be configured and combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design), data strategies, and task-aware safeguards against bias and low-frequency failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Practical, and Careful Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach for compressing large neural models into compact, efficient students while preserving much of their performance. Across logits-based soft-label transfer, intermediate feature and attention matching, curriculum and sample-selection methods, adversarial and data-free variants, and module-replacement and pruning hybrids, KD enables deployment in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings, supports domain and modality transfer, and is complementary to quantization and architecture search. However, reliable application requires attention to teacher quality, layer mapping, sample selection, and interactions with regularization and pretraining; when designed for the target task and environment, KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance and unlock real-world deployment scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Bauer
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically proven approach for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models so they meet latency, memory, compute, and deployment constraints. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness. While KD can recover much of teacher performance across modalities, reliable deployment requires deliberate choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Oconnell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. When designed as part of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline — integrating pretraining, multi-signal transfer (logits, features, relational signals), data strategies, and compatible architecture choices — KD can preserve most teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its effectiveness is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the distilled signals and data, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases or rare-case failures. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the practical core of modern model-compression toolkits, outlines concrete mechanisms by which it helps, surveys domain- and task-specific variants that address common failure modes, and summarizes actionable design principles for robust, responsible deployment.

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. It supports multiple information-transfer mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and can be adapted to constrained settings (limited data, privacy, heterogeneous devices). KD is most effective when used as part of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or pretraining—and when practitioners mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer, rare-token degradation, or teacher–student mismatch. With careful design choices (what to transfer, how to align layers, which data to use), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving task performance across modalities.

KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when its design is adapted to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints. Important limitations include capacity mismatch, teacher error or bias transfer, distribution shift, and challenges in preserving low‑frequency or long‑tail behavior; addressing these requires task‑aware objective design, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness and privacy.

Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of a teacher's performance and can even improve generalization in some settings, but it also has well-known failure modes—teacher bias propagation, difficulty preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors, teacher–student capacity mismatch, and sensitivity to data availability and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, as well as careful data and objective design.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Revisiting Knowledge Distillation via Label Smoothing Regularization
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to distill the knowledge of a cumbersome teacher model into a lightweight student model. Its success is generally attributed to the privileged information on similarities among categories provided by the teacher model, and in this sense, only strong teacher models are deployed to teach weaker students in practice. In this work, we challenge this common belief by following experimental observations: 1) beyond the acknowledgment that the teacher can improve the student, the student can also enhance the teacher significantly by reversing the KD procedure; 2) a poorly-trained teacher with much lower accuracy than the student can still improve the latter significantly. To explain these observations, we provide a theoretical analysis of the relationships between KD and label smoothing regularization. We prove that 1) KD is a type of learned label smoothing regularization and 2) label smoothing regularization provides a virtual teacher model for KD. From these results, we argue that the success of KD is not fully due to the similarity information between categories from teachers, but also to the regularization of soft targets, which is equally or even more important.   Based on these analyses, we further propose a novel Teacher-free Knowledge Distillation (Tf-KD) framework, where a student model learns from itself or manuallydesigned regularization distribution. The Tf-KD achieves comparable performance with normal KD from a superior teacher, which is well applied when a stronger teacher model is unavailable. Meanwhile, Tf-KD is generic and can be directly deployed for training deep neural networks. Without any extra computation cost, Tf-KD achieves up to 0.65\% improvement on ImageNet over well-established baseline models, which is superior to label smoothing regularization.

We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.
