papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and often more deployable models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal systems, and specialized domains such as healthcare and novel-view synthesis, KD yields large reductions in parameter count and inference cost while retaining most of the teacher performance when applied with task-aware design choices. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on what information is transferred (logits, features, relational structure), the availability and nature of data, teacher quality and design, and careful integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Pragmatic deployment requires attention to robustness, bias propagation, data scarcity, and domain mismatch, and benefits most from combining KD with task- and hardware-aware practices.

papers_seen.author: Wolf
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large, high‑performance models into smaller, deployable students. When designed as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with task‑aware objectives, data strategies, and complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD regularly delivers favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs. However, realizing robust, fair, and reliable compressed models requires careful attention to teacher–student alignment, the nature and availability of distillation data, and targeted remedies for known failure modes such as capacity mismatch, bias transfer, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Strategy for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible technique for compressing large models and transferring capabilities across domains, modalities, and architectures. When combined with task-aware objectives, careful layer/feature matching, and appropriate data or privacy strategies, KD yields compact models that retain much of the original performance while enabling lower latency, smaller memory footprints, and new deployment patterns. KD’s strengths span supervised, self-supervised, online, and privacy-constrained settings, but realizing them requires attention to teacher quality, what knowledge is transferred, and how student capacity and data constraints are handled.

papers_seen.author: Alvarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while often preserving much of task performance. KD is a flexible family of techniques that operate at output, representation, relational, or decision-boundary levels and is commonly combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful design of objectives and training pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Butler
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When applied thoughtfully — choosing appropriate distillation targets, aligning teacher and student capacity, selecting or synthesizing data, and combining KD with complementary compression methods — KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute. However, KD is context dependent: it has known failure modes (teacher–student capacity gaps, propagated biases, loss of rare or long‑tail behaviors, and domain shift) that require targeted remedies and integration with other compression primitives and data strategies. I argue KD should be treated as the configurable core of any compression pipeline, not a stand‑alone panacea, and I outline practical design principles and open problems to guide robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Strategy for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. Across computer vision, generative modeling, cross-modal systems, and NLP, distillation can be combined with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, adversarial training, and feature alignment) to meet deployment constraints and domain requirements. Success depends on teacher design, the availability and nature of data used for transfer, careful alignment of representations, and training objectives that address optimization challenges.

papers_seen.author: Johnston
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Context‑Aware, and Best Deployed in Hybrid Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal structure across vision and language tasks, but it is not a universal cure: its value depends on choices about what is distilled, how teachers and students are aligned, and how data, privacy, and bias concerns are handled. I argue KD should be a first‑line, configurable component of compression pipelines, augmented by teacher‑aware design, complementary compression primitives, and principled mitigations for its known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multifaceted Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Responsible NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large models into efficient students while also serving as a lever for regularization, robustness, privacy, fairness, interpretability, and continual/multi-task learning. When applied thoughtfully—combining soft-label distillation with feature- and representation-level matching, layer mapping, attention or projector modules, and task-aware curricula—KD can produce lightweight models that approach or sometimes exceed teacher performance on constrained devices and specialized tasks. However, KD is not automatic: optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and mismatches in the information transferred (e.g., for low-frequency tokens or internal features) limit its effectiveness unless complemented by targeted methodological choices. I argue that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe: choose distillation targets (outputs, features, internal representations), mapping strategies (many-to-many layer mapping, attention, projectors), and auxiliary safeguards (privacy-preserving noise, fairness interventions, adversarial distillation) to align compression goals with safety and utility requirements.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers predictive ability from large, expensive teacher models to smaller, efficient student models. Across modalities and architectures, KD variants extend beyond matching teacher output probabilities to include internal representation matching, contrastive objectives, adversarial learning, selective sample supervision, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. These methods enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, reduce inference latency, support domain adaptation and federated settings, and in some cases improve student generalization beyond the teacher. Practical challenges include input/representation mismatches between teacher and student, propagation of teacher biases (e.g., low-frequency lexical errors), and the need for careful selection of what is distilled and how. Empirically, tailored distillation objectives and training procedures—such as internal-representation matching, progressive module replacement, ensemble distillation, and contrastive or relational objectives—have produced strong compression results across vision, language, graph-structured data, and generative scene models.

papers_seen.author: Hayes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Versatile, and Context-Sensitive
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a core technique for compressing and adapting large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD offers a flexible set of targets and workflows—soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational and contrastive signals, online and self-distillation, and data-free protocols—that enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and alignment between teacher and student; it also risks transferring undesirable behaviors. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-aware objectives, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet production constraints and preserve downstream performance.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a narrow training trick into a broad, practical paradigm for compressing and adapting large deep models to resource- and data-constrained deployment settings. A rich family of KD formulations — from logit matching and feature imitation to adversarial, data-free, and online schemes — together with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and teacher ensembles) enables substantial reductions in memory and latency while largely preserving model quality. However, KD is not universally effective out-of-the-box: its benefits and risks depend on task characteristics, data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and deliberate choices of what and how to transfer. When practitioners treat KD as a toolkit of targeted strategies and validate choices against task constraints, it yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, robustness, and fidelity to the original model.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and versatile toolkit for producing compact models from larger teachers. When designed and validated against task and deployment constraints, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute; however, its success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data strategy, and complementary compression and safeguarding measures.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of methods for transferring knowledge from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, efficient student models so that students achieve improved accuracy, latency, or resource use while retaining much of teacher behavior. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, internal features, relational structure, or contrastive/global representations), how supervision is scheduled (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and how distillation is combined with other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows substantial gains across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and generative models, but limitations remain around data availability, teacher-student mismatch, low-frequency information transfer, privacy constraints, and robustness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Long
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A diverse set of techniques has emerged — from soft-label/logit transfer to feature- and layer-level matching, adversarial or ensemble-driven schemes, data-free generation, and task-adaptive architecture search — yielding practical gains across NLP, vision, speech, and recommendation systems. Successes are widespread, but effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful alignment of objectives; combining KD with complementary compression methods and task-aware design is generally required for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile framework that enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component—combining logits, intermediate-feature matching, contrastive objectives, data augmentation, and privacy-aware techniques—distillation supports deployment across modalities and constrained devices. However, KD is not automatic: it propagates some teacher errors, can lose low-frequency or structured information, and requires careful design choices (teacher selection, objective weighting, data strategy). A principled practice that matches the distillation objective to the task, augments or tailors distillation data, and applies privacy- or domain-aware protocols yields the best trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Woods
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, Practical Guidance, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teachers into compact students. KD methods operate at multiple levels—from soft-label (logit) matching to feature-, attention-, and relation-level transfers—and have been adapted to many training and deployment protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co‑distillation, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free, and federated schemes). Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, retrieval, and recommendation shows that KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and distillation data are properly matched. In practice, KD is most effective when used as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, pretraining, data augmentation, and careful layer alignment. Remaining challenges include handling teacher biases and errors, preserving low-frequency or minority behaviors, operating under data absence or strict privacy constraints, and automating teacher–student design for heterogeneous deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for producing compact, deployable neural models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational or contrastive signals) and across diverse protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data-free/privacy-aware schemes). When combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables large reductions in latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of teacher performance. Its empirical success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability and synthesis strategies, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, distribution shift, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Hoffman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Versatile, but Context‑Dependent Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely applicable family of techniques for producing compact student models from larger teachers. When designed as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline, KD routinely yields strong tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity; however, reliable deployment requires task‑aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and explicit mitigations for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit — from soft-label matching to representation-level, adversarial, and data-free approaches — has been developed and successfully applied across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains. Practical success depends on careful choice of distillation targets, teacher–student compatibility, data regime, and integration with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of methods for transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Across vision and natural language tasks, distillation targets range from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals; KD is frequently combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with domain- or task-specific procedures to improve efficacy. KD delivers strong empirical gains in many settings but is bounded by teacher quality, availability and match of data, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the risk of transferring teacher biases; effective application therefore requires task-aware choices of signals, data strategies, and often hybrid compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Ponce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models across vision, language, speech, and other modalities. KD methods operate over multiple signals and protocols and are most effective when treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that also addresses data, architecture, and robustness constraints.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teacher models. KD methods span output-level supervision, intermediate representation matching, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-aware or data-free protocols. While KD routinely yields favorable trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness, its success is strongly context dependent: choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data availability and synthesis, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy determine practical outcomes. As a result, KD should be treated as a configurable, first‑line element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone panacea.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression: Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster models while retaining much of their performance. KD has been shown to work across modalities and tasks by transferring logits, intermediate representations, attention patterns, or relational structure. It can also be combined with data augmentation, adversarial schemes, online or teacher-free training, and architecture-aware adaptations to meet deployment constraints. KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on choices about which teacher signals to transfer, alignment of inputs and architectures, student capacity, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. When used as part of a task-aware compression pipeline that addresses these issues, KD delivers substantial practical benefits for latency- and resource-constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques that transfer information from larger, often multi-source or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal and generative settings, KD has evolved beyond simple logit matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free generation, online and self-distillation protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization and architecture search. These approaches routinely enable large reductions in inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance, but reliable deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Important open directions remain in principled theory, robust distillation under heterogenous and low-data regimes, and preserving long-tail or low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Montoya
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and often more deployable models by transferring information from larger or specialized models. It supports a broad range of objectives beyond raw compression—improving robustness, enabling domain adaptation, supporting privacy-aware or federated workflows, and permitting deployment on constrained hardware. KD methods range from simple soft-label matching to richer transfers of intermediate representations, attention patterns, and relational or contrastive structure. While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, alignment between teacher and student, data availability and distribution, and the choice of signals and losses. When applied with attention to these constraints and combined sensibly with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), KD is a practical foundational technique for real-world model compression in vision, language, and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Hubbard
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, a diverse set of transfer targets and training protocols has emerged — from matching soft logits to imitating intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and even using synthesized or privacy-aware pseudo-data. Best results typically come from combining multiple distilled signals, aligning teacher and student architectures (or adding projector layers), and integrating KD with complementary compression primitives and data strategies. Despite broad empirical success, persistent challenges include handling distribution shift and low-frequency behavior, aligning heterogeneous architectures, safeguarding privacy and fairness, and automating principled teacher selection. This synthesis condenses prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical guidance, and open research directions documented in the supplied literature.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques transfer information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Approaches vary by what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel statistics, or decision-boundary information), by whether original training data are available, and by whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work across vision, multimodal, speech, and natural language tasks shows that careful choices of transfer targets, loss formulations, teacher ensembles, and training schedules can yield compact models that approach — and in some cases match or exceed — teacher performance while enabling deployment under resource, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. Remaining challenges include optimization difficulties that prevent perfect belief matching, distribution-shift and heterogeneity issues in federated or data-free settings, and trade-offs among accuracy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Freeman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Directions (Synthesis)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, ensemble, or otherwise specialized teacher models into smaller, faster, or deployment-ready student models. KD techniques operate at different supervision granularities (soft-labels, intermediate representations, relational or attention maps, adversarial objectives, and many-to-many layer mappings) and are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or data synthesis to meet latency, memory, privacy, or heterogeneity constraints. Across modalities—NLP, vision, speech, graph learning, generation, and reinforcement learning—KD has enabled large reductions in model size and runtime with modest performance loss and has been adapted for settings without access to original training data, for federated or continual learning, and for transferring inductive biases. Important practical challenges remain (teacher selection and adaptation, data availability and distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, bias transfer, and privacy), and current best practices emphasize carefully matched teacher-student design, auxiliary training signals, and integration with other compression tools to achieve reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, pragmatic set of techniques for transferring behavior from larger teacher models into smaller student models so that compact models can preserve much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD is effective across modalities and tasks when its objectives, training protocols, and data strategies are chosen to match the task, teacher–student capacities, and deployment constraints; however, KD has clear failure modes and limits that require integrated mitigation. I argue that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of end-to-end compression pipelines rather than a standalone, one-size-fits-all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, latency, and communication while attempting to preserve task performance. KD methods include matching output distributions, aligning intermediate representations and attention, relational or contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture/behavior-aware design. Empirical evidence across modalities shows KD often recovers a substantial fraction of teacher performance and enables real-world deployment, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the data used for distillation, and strategies for mitigating transferred errors, distribution shift, privacy risks, and degraded performance on low-frequency or minority behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. A diverse toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational structure, and decision-boundary or synthetic-data signals), training protocols (single/multi-teacher, online/self-distillation, task- and layer-aware schedules), and architecture-aware adaptations (projectors, layer mapping, and combinations with pruning/quantization/NAS) has been developed. Empirically, properly designed distillation pipelines recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks, and can be combined with complementary compression methods to meet device and domain requirements. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps, teacher–student capacity mismatch, distribution shift and data scarcity (including privacy- and data-free regimes), and trade-offs among accuracy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Sanders
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Conditional, and Best-Practice‑Driven for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings. KD provides a flexible family of mechanisms (soft-targets, feature and attention matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data-free or federated protocols) that, when combined with complementary compression primitives and task-aware design, yield strong empirical trade-offs between efficiency and performance. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred biases. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone recipe.

papers_seen.author: Higgins
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster models while preserving or even improving task performance. Beyond simple size reduction, KD enables domain adaptation, multimodal capability lifting, robustness transfer, privacy-aware compression, and practical deployment on constrained hardware. The technique is complementary to pruning and quantization and can be adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, few-shot samples, and heterogeneous teacher ensembles. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, sample selection, layer-mapping strategies, and interactions with regularization techniques such as label smoothing.

papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and broadly effective set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. KD reduces latency, memory, and communication costs while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance; its toolbox includes soft-target (logit) supervision, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocols ranging from offline to online, multi-teacher, and data-free distillation. However, KD’s success is conditional on task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to obtain or synthesize distillation data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design). Responsible, robust deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline rather than as a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: The Core, Conditional, and Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task‑aware component of compression pipelines and combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis, or multi-teacher ensembles), KD routinely delivers large reductions in latency and memory while preserving most teacher performance. Its practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy; KD is therefore best used as a first-line, integrated tool rather than a standalone cure.

papers_seen.author: Blair
papers_seen.title: Distilling Policy Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The transfer of knowledge from one policy to another is an important tool in Deep Reinforcement Learning. This process, referred to as distillation, has been used to great success, for example, by enhancing the optimisation of agents, leading to stronger performance faster, on harder domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Despite the widespread use and conceptual simplicity of distillation, many different formulations are used in practice, and the subtle variations between them can often drastically change the performance and the resulting objective that is being optimised. In this work, we rigorously explore the entire landscape of policy distillation, comparing the motivations and strengths of each variant through theoretical and empirical analysis. Our results point to three distillation techniques, that are preferred depending on specifics of the task. Specifically a newly proposed expected entropy regularised distillation allows for quicker learning in a wide range of situations, while still guaranteeing convergence.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Durham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context‑Dependent Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practically indispensable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. Empirical work shows KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count. Its effectiveness depends on deliberate choices about which signals to transfer, teacher–student design and capacity alignment, data availability and selection, and integration with complementary compression techniques. Treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a standalone recipe, KD delivers the most reliable and deployable gains.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is now a central, broadly applicable approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and functional behavior of larger teachers. The literature describes a rich taxonomy of KD objectives and protocols — from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structures — together with specialized strategies for online, multi-teacher, data-free, federated, and privacy-sensitive settings. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often improves student generalization and acts as a regularizer, but success depends on task-aware choices: which signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous architectures, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of teacher errors or low-frequency behaviors. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable component combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and augmentation strategies, and targeted safeguards for robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Andrews
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, efficient students by transferring information from teachers via outputs, internal representations, or relational signals. KD is broadly applicable across modalities and settings and is most effective when combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods. Despite strong empirical successes, important practical and theoretical challenges remain—teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity or scarcity, transferred biases, robustness under distribution shift, and privacy constraints—motivating targeted algorithmic and systems-level remedies and further study.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for transferring predictive capacity from large, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). A wide range of KD objectives and protocols have been developed — from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, adversarially chosen samples, and data-free or zero-shot synthesis — and these are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of the teacher's performance and, when carefully engineered, support robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving releases, and practical latency- or memory-constrained deployment. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization choices, leaving open practical challenges around heterogeneous architectures, distribution shift, and preserving fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Benson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Foundational, Context-Dependent Path for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a single compression trick into a flexible framework for producing compact, deployable models and for transferring behavior across domains, modalities, and privacy-constrained settings. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacities, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods—KD enables significant reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. At the same time, distillation has clear failure modes (optimization gaps, distributional mismatch, and social harms) that require targeted mitigation and careful evaluation. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, application-driven toolkit for model compression and adaptation, not a one-size-fits-all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Core of Practical Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for producing compact models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. KD offers many targets and protocols—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data‑free or privacy-aware variants—that routinely improve efficiency while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD’s success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability or synthesis of distillation data, and careful objective design; it therefore functions best as a configurable component inside an integrated compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, teacher adaptation, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Richard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation is Central but Insufficient: A Position on Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, latency, and memory, but reliable deployment requires integrating KD into a broader, task- and hardware-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Versatile, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central practical technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and generative tasks. When designed with attention to what is transferred (logits, features, attention, or generated data), data strategy, and teacher–student alignment, KD routinely yields substantial inference and memory gains while preserving much of teacher performance. At the same time, KD is bounded by data availability, teacher quality, capacity mismatch, and potential transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors, so it is best used as part of an integrated compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Rosales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teachers into compact students. KD variants—ranging from logits and feature matching to relational, contrastive, and data-free protocols—have been demonstrated across vision, speech, and NLP to deliver favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. At the same time, KD’s success depends on teacher quality, signal choice, data regime, and careful training design, and it is most reliable when integrated with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware engineering. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a central, configurable element of any compression pipeline, but not as a standalone solution: use KD deliberately, combine it with other methods, and adopt practices that mitigate its failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Versatile, but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD supports diverse transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), adapts to data-limited and privacy‑sensitive settings, and interoperates with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Its empirical strengths make KD a first‑line approach for many deployment problems, but reliable, production‑grade compression requires explicit attention to teacher–student alignment, data selection or synthesis, capacity matching, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Cain
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a flexible set of methods for transferring information from larger or more expressive teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD spans output-level (soft-target) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and protocol variants such as offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free, and privacy-aware workflows. In practice KD is frequently combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and must be tailored to teacher/student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints; while empirical results across modalities often show students can recover much of teacher performance, important challenges remain in handling capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias and robustness, and formal theoretical guarantees.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthetic Overview
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical set of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. The approach has diversified beyond simple logits-matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, multiple training protocols (offline, online, self-, multi-teacher, and data-free), and task-aware adaptations such as layer mapping, projector modules, and synthetic-data strategies. Empirical work across vision, language, recommendation, graph, and multimodal tasks demonstrates that KD can deliver substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and latency while often retaining most of a teacher’s performance; success in practice requires careful matching of distillation signals, attention to teacher–student alignment, and integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Elliott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, Challenges, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation comprises a broad set of techniques that transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, and privacy. Over the past decade researchers have extended simple logit-matching to feature-, relation-, and layer-wise objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and integrations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work demonstrates that distilled students frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, recommendation, and other modalities, but success depends on student capacity, alignment of targets and layers, the nature and availability of distillation data, and mitigation of transferred biases or teacher errors. Ongoing priorities are principled objectives for what to transfer, robust and private distillation under heterogeneous and federated data, and automated teacher–student design for practical deployments.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Compression, Robustness, and Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique that compresses large models into smaller, faster ones while transferring performance and often additional properties such as robustness or cross-domain adaptability. Evidence across vision, language, graph, and sequential domains shows KD enables deployable models for latency- and resource-constrained settings, supports continual and federated learning, and can be combined with pruning, architecture search, and adversarial strategies. However, distillation is not a universal panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, interact nontrivially with regularization strategies, and requires careful alignment of inputs, representations, and objectives. Best practice is to treat KD as a family of tools (logit, intermediate-layer, feature, adversarial, data-driven, self-distillation) and to adapt the distillation design to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Hubbard
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, a diverse set of transfer targets and training protocols has emerged — from matching soft logits to imitating intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and even using synthesized or privacy-aware pseudo-data. Best results typically come from combining multiple distilled signals, aligning teacher and student architectures (or adding projector layers), and integrating KD with complementary compression primitives and data strategies. Despite broad empirical success, persistent challenges include handling distribution shift and low-frequency behavior, aligning heterogeneous architectures, safeguarding privacy and fairness, and automating principled teacher selection. This synthesis condenses prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical guidance, and open research directions documented in the supplied literature.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more deployable student models. KD operates via many targets and protocols—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals, adversarial or data‑free generation, and online or multi‑teacher training—and is typically combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet practical latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task‑aware design, but its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and careful engineering to avoid failure modes such as teacher error transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare or low‑frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Marks
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. A wide set of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive structure), training paradigms (offline, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, self‑distillation), and data strategies (real, synthetic, or data‑free) have been developed. KD is often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count, but reliable success depends on deliberate, task‑aware choices about transfer signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and mitigation of bias, robustness, and distributional risks.

papers_seen.author: Jennings
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression: Effectiveness, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, empirically validated set of techniques that reliably reduces model size and inference cost while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD is not a single recipe; its practical success depends on task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, the distillation data regime, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression primitives. Treating KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline—rather than as a standalone silver bullet—produces the most robust and deployment-ready outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Configurable Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and empirically validated family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) to smaller student models. KD variants — from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate‑feature and relational objectives, multi‑teacher and online regimes, and data‑free or privacy-aware methods — routinely yield strong accuracy–efficiency trade‑offs when combined with task‑aware design and complementary compression primitives. However, KD’s practical success is conditional on careful choices about teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the signals to transfer, and data strategies; thus KD should be used as a configurable core within integrated compression pipelines rather than as a plug‑and‑play cure.

papers_seen.author: Peck
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context‑Dependent Engine for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and flexible family of methods for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, speech, and recommendation tasks show KD can recover most of a teacher’s performance while delivering substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication cost. However, KD is not a one-size-fits-all solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime and selection, the choice of transfer signals, and how KD is combined with complementary compression methods. For reliable deployment, practitioners should treat KD as a task‑aware toolbox—selecting what to transfer, aligning teacher and student carefully, addressing data or privacy constraints, and integrating pruning/quantization or architecture-aware design—while explicitly mitigating limitations such as teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and privacy risks.

papers_seen.author: Snyder
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably transfers behavior from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory and compute while preserving much of task performance. KD techniques span logits/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, relational and contrastive signals, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data-free or domain-adaptive variants. Empirical evidence shows KD is a practical first-line strategy for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, but it is not a standalone cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, objective design, and careful integration with complementary compression tools. For robust, real-world deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with targeted engineering to mitigate failure modes such as capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Burgess
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods include output-level supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, online and multi-teacher protocols, and progressive or task-aware procedures. Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, generative and multimodal tasks shows that when KD is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task- and data-aware engineering, it often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing resource cost. Practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Important open challenges remain in principled selection of distillation targets, reliable transfer under data scarcity and distribution shift, avoiding propagation of teacher biases and rare-token degradation, and automated, hardware-aware co-design.

Empirical evidence shows KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when its design is matched to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints; however, its success is conditional and benefits from integration with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a logits-matching trick into a broad, practical framework for shrinking and adapting large models while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, language, recommendation, and domain-adaptation settings, KD is most effective when combined with complementary strategies (pretraining, pruning, quantization, curriculum or online training, and task-aware losses). KD is best treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, augmentation, or synthetic-data strategies—rather than as a standalone panacea.

papers_seen.author: Hensley
papers_seen.title: Apprentice: Using Knowledge Distillation Techniques To Improve Low-Precision Network Accuracy
papers_seen.abstract: Deep learning networks have achieved state-of-the-art accuracies on computer vision workloads like image classification and object detection. The performant systems, however, typically involve big models with numerous parameters. Once trained, a challenging aspect for such top performing models is deployment on resource constrained inference systems - the models (often deep networks or wide networks or both) are compute and memory intensive. Low-precision numerics and model compression using knowledge distillation are popular techniques to lower both the compute requirements and memory footprint of these deployed models. In this paper, we study the combination of these two techniques and show that the performance of low-precision networks can be significantly improved by using knowledge distillation techniques. Our approach, Apprentice, achieves state-of-the-art accuracies using ternary precision and 4-bit precision for variants of ResNet architecture on ImageNet dataset. We present three schemes using which one can apply knowledge distillation techniques to various stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Not Panacea Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted technique for compressing large models into smaller ones and transferring capabilities across tasks and modalities. When thoughtfully designed—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations), preparing or augmenting data, and matching teacher-student capacity—KD yields substantial gains in inference efficiency with modest performance loss and can enable deployment under tight latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, optimization dynamics, and architecture alignment; complementary tools (pretraining, projector modules, online schemes, and privacy-aware protocols) and careful engineering are often required to realize consistent, robust results. Open directions include principled data-free distillation, better theoretical characterizations of what is transferred, and joint co-design of architectures and distillation objectives for specific deployment targets.
