papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while enabling adaptation across tasks, domains, and modalities. When combined with representation-level objectives, careful teacher engineering, pre-training of compact architectures, and input-side interventions (e.g., augmentation or data synthesis), KD routinely yields large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss and can enable deployment under tight compute, latency, or privacy constraints. At the same time, KD is not a single recipe: success depends on optimization choices, teacher–student alignment, and dataset properties, which motivates tailored distillation objectives, data strategies, and evaluation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Santiago
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable, but Insufficient Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly effective and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Treated as a configurable toolkit—selecting what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to combine distillation with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies—KD yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and mitigation of bias, distribution shift, and low-frequency or rare-case behaviors. Best practice treats KD as the central component of an integrated compression pipeline tailored to task, data regime, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Aguilar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Campbell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Flexible, but Not Panacea Approach to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students and for transferring task- or modality-specific capabilities. KD supports many transfer targets and training protocols and can be combined with pruning, quantization, pretraining, and data synthesis to meet deployment constraints. However, reliable outcomes require careful teacher–student design, attention to data and privacy constraints, and targeted solutions for failure modes such as distribution shift, optimization mismatch, and preserved low-frequency behavior.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Understanding and Improving Lexical Choice in Non-Autoregressive Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is essential for training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models by reducing the complexity of the raw data with an autoregressive teacher model. In this study, we empirically show that as a side effect of this training, the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words are propagated to the NAT model from the teacher model. To alleviate this problem, we propose to expose the raw data to NAT models to restore the useful information of low-frequency words, which are missed in the distilled data. To this end, we introduce an extra Kullback-Leibler divergence term derived by comparing the lexical choice of NAT model and that embedded in the raw data. Experimental results across language pairs and model architectures demonstrate the effectiveness and universality of the proposed approach. Extensive analyses confirm our claim that our approach improves performance by reducing the lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Encouragingly, our approach pushes the SOTA NAT performance on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets up to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. The source code will be released.

papers_seen.author: Simon
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Insufficient Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks. KD variants transfer outputs, internal representations, attention patterns, or relational structures and are frequently combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies to meet deployment constraints. While KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and supports domain adaptation, privacy-aware training, and robustness improvements, its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful objective and architecture design; therefore KD should be treated as a central element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a practical, flexible approach to compressing large neural models into resource-efficient students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Across modalities and tasks — from language and retrieval to vision, generation, and graph learning — distillation techniques enable trade-offs between accuracy, compute, and memory that make deployment feasible on constrained hardware. However, the effectiveness of distillation depends strongly on the distillation objective, the information transferred (probabilities, internal representations, or structured signals), availability of original data, and care to avoid transferring undesirable teacher properties. When combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, architecture search, low-precision training, or curriculum strategies), distillation can yield compact models that approach or sometimes even exceed teacher performance while meeting practical latency and size constraints.

papers_seen.author: Shaw
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often retaining substantial parts of teacher performance. A broad family of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals; offline, online, self-, multi-teacher, and data-free variants). Practical success depends on aligning the distillation signal to task and student capacity and on combining distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Key challenges include teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatch, limited or unavailable data, propagation of teacher biases or errors, distribution shift, and difficulties preserving low-frequency or structured behaviors. Continued progress requires principled choices about what, when, and how to transfer knowledge, better theory linking distillation choices to student generalization, and engineering pipelines that pair KD with task-aware data and model design.

papers_seen.author: Lyons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD reliably reduces model size and latency while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance when its objectives, data strategy, and architecture-aware choices are selected for the deployment context. However, KD is not a universal solution: its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis methods, and mitigation of bias and distribution-shift risks. The most consistent practical outcomes come from treating KD as a configurable component within integrated compression pipelines that combine representation-aware distillation signals, augmentation or data-free techniques, and complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Lucas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. The literature converges on a toolbox of distillation signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and layer-mapping, relational and contrastive objectives), a variety of training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data-free/zero-shot), and common integrations with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance, but outcomes are strongly context-dependent: they depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, choice of transfer signals and data regime, and explicit measures to avoid transferring teacher errors, biases, or fragile behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Greene
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Practical, and Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often recovers much of a teacher’s performance while reducing latency, memory, and deployment cost, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, choice of distilled signals, and data availability. Best results arise when KD is treated as a configurable toolkit integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful layer- and task-alignment, and safeguards for bias, privacy, and distributional shift.

papers_seen.author: Guerrero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically validated and flexible approach for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment across modalities when integrated thoughtfully with complementary compression methods. Its success is context dependent — determined by teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and loss of rare behaviors — so practitioners should treat KD as a configurable element of a broader compression pipeline rather than a one-shot solution.

papers_seen.author: Bennett
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely applied family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks, KD variants (logit/soft-label matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data-free/zero-shot synthesis) combined with complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) enable substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, availability or synthesis of data, and integration with other compression methods. Remaining challenges include principled theory connecting distilled signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, transfer across heterogeneous architectures and non-iid data, and mitigation of propagated biases and degraded behavior on rare or long‑tail phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Towards Understanding Ensemble, Knowledge Distillation and Self-Distillation in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We formally study how ensemble of deep learning models can improve test accuracy, and how the superior performance of ensemble can be distilled into a single model using knowledge distillation. We consider the challenging case where the ensemble is simply an average of the outputs of a few independently trained neural networks with the SAME architecture, trained using the SAME algorithm on the SAME data set, and they only differ by the random seeds used in the initialization.   We show that ensemble/knowledge distillation in Deep Learning works very differently from traditional learning theory (such as boosting or NTKs, neural tangent kernels). To properly understand them, we develop a theory showing that when data has a structure we refer to as ``multi-view'', then ensemble of independently trained neural networks can provably improve test accuracy, and such superior test accuracy can also be provably distilled into a single model by training a single model to match the output of the ensemble instead of the true label. Our result sheds light on how ensemble works in deep learning in a way that is completely different from traditional theorems, and how the ``dark knowledge'' is hidden in the outputs of the ensemble and can be used in distillation. In the end, we prove that self-distillation can also be viewed as implicitly combining ensemble and knowledge distillation to improve test accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Compression of Deep Learning Models for Text: A Survey
papers_seen.abstract: In recent years, the fields of natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR) have made tremendous progress thanksto deep learning models like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs)networks, and Transformer [120] based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], GenerativePre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98] and GShard [63]. But these models are humongous in size. On the other hand,real world applications demand small model size, low response times and low computational power wattage. In this survey, wediscuss six different types of methods (Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, andSub-quadratic Transformer based methods) for compression of such models to enable their deployment in real industry NLP projects.Given the critical need of building applications with efficient and small models, and the large amount of recently published work inthis area, we believe that this survey organizes the plethora of work done by the 'deep learning for NLP' community in the past fewyears and presents it as a coherent story.

papers_seen.author: Combs
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an adaptable, empirically validated approach for producing compact student models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with appropriate data strategies and complementary techniques, KD routinely delivers substantial reductions in inference cost and model size while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is context-dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, choice of distilled signals, and careful handling of data- and fairness-related failure modes. Responsible, deployment-ready use therefore requires task-aware design, explicit mitigation of transfer limits, and continued research into robust, privacy-preserving, and automated distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Cordova
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD routinely reduces inference cost and memory while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its reliability is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, architecture alignment, and complementary compression primitives critically shape outcomes. A pragmatic recommendation is to treat KD as the central component of compression pipelines while explicitly adapting objectives, data protocols, and auxiliary methods to the deployment constraints and known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression strategies have become central to deploying large neural networks in resource-constrained settings. Across vision, multimodal, and language domains, researchers have developed approaches that transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller students via logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or adversarial objectives. Work spans supervised and unsupervised settings, data-free or black-box scenarios, continual and federated use-cases, and concerns such as privacy and adversarial robustness. Practical recipes combine distillation with pruning, structured sparsity, progressive module replacement, and many-to-many layer mapping to balance accuracy, latency, and memory. Open challenges remain in data- and domain-limited regimes, robust and private compression, and principled selection of which teacher knowledge to transfer for a given downstream task.

papers_seen.author: Robertson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. The literature shows that appropriately chosen distillation signals, teacher–student design, and data strategies allow compact models to recover much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and deployment cost. Practical pipelines commonly combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and adapt to constraints such as privacy, heterogeneous devices, and limited or unlabeled data. Despite widespread empirical success, important limitations persist—teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, degraded rare-output behavior, and theoretical gaps linking distillation signals to student generalization—motivating ongoing work in adaptive teacher selection, data-free distillation, and task-aware compression design.

papers_seen.author: Contreras
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal settings. KD yields substantial gains in inference efficiency and can transfer task-relevant structure from teachers to students, but its success depends on careful, task-aware choices of what to transfer, teacher selection, data and optimization strategies, and complementary compression techniques. Responsible deployment requires attention to robustness, fairness, privacy, and teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Ramsey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly effective and widely adopted framework for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD is best understood as a configurable core technique: it provides many transferable signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, contrastive objectives, and synthesized data), and—when combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search and coupled with task‑aware data strategies—can enable large reductions in size and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. However, KD is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data regime, and explicit measures for robustness, privacy, and fairness strongly shape outcomes. Practitioners should therefore treat KD as an essential but non‑turnkey component of integrated compression pipelines, selecting targets, mapping strategies, and safeguards to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Brooks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: an Essential, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD methods extend beyond simple logit matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, multi-teacher and online protocols, and data- or privacy-aware variants. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and applied with task-aware design, KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs. However, KD is context-dependent: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of bias, low-frequency/fine-grained behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Bender
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. A rich set of methods—ranging from logits/soft-target supervision to intermediate-feature matching, contrastive and relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants—has been developed and is routinely combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture/parameter adaptations). Empirical and conceptual work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, signal choice, data availability or synthesis strategy, and careful integration with other compression tools. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a one-size-fits-all solution.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential but Insufficient — A Practical Position for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a central, practically proven strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and deployable students across vision and language tasks. While distilled students often recover much of teacher performance, distillation alone is not a complete solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and careful selection of what to transfer. In practice, distillation should be treated as a configurable core of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that integrates complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation), explicit fairness and robustness interventions, and data strategies ranging from augmentation to data-free synthesis.

papers_seen.author: Bailey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving much of the original performance. KD operates at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/relational signals) and across multiple training regimes (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free/synthetic data). Empirical work across vision, speech, and language shows KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs when combined with appropriate architecture alignment, data strategies, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical application treats KD as a configurable, context‑sensitive element of an integrated compression pipeline; its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and complexity, and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Frost
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical and flexible pathway to compress large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their performance. Across NLP and other modalities, researchers have developed logit-level, representation-level, layer-wise, multi-teacher, data-free, privacy-aware, and task-aware distillation variants and combined KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows that careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data and low-frequency phenomena materially affects student quality and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Clay
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Core of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, broadly applicable mechanism for transferring behavior from large teacher models into smaller student models and is essential for practical model compression in deep learning and NLP. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or hardware‑optimal deployment: it must be designed in a task‑aware way, combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and paired with data and curriculum strategies to mitigate failure modes such as teacher bias, poor low‑frequency behavior, capacity mismatch, and distribution shift. Treating KD as a configurable core inside an integrated compression pipeline yields the most reliable production outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a logits-matching trick into a broad, practical framework for shrinking and adapting large models while retaining much of their performance. Modern KD techniques include soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, multi- and ensemble-teacher schemes, online and distributed formulations, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants. Across vision, language, recommendation, and domain-adaptation settings, KD is most effective when combined with complementary strategies (pretraining, pruning, quantization, curriculum or online training, and task-aware losses). Despite strong empirical successes, practitioners must attend to teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and domain mismatch; many current research directions focus on robust, privacy-preserving, and data-limited distillation for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Lamb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Conditional Core of Model-Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically proven approach for producing smaller, faster, or deployment-specialized models in deep learning and NLP. When treated as a configurable core technique—choosing what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods and data strategies—KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and explicit mitigation of failure modes (bias propagation, low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift). Robust deployment requires task-aware design, multi-signal objectives, and integration with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or data synthesis strategies.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile, and widely applicable framework for compressing large models into smaller, efficient students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD has matured into a toolbox that includes logit- and feature-level transfer, relational and contrastive objectives, data-free and adversarial generation, online and multi-teacher schemes, and task-aware layer alignment. Its effectiveness in reducing parameters, latency, and memory—often with modest performance loss—makes KD a core first-line method for deployment. At the same time, KD has clear failure modes (teacher–student mismatch, domain shift, bias transfer, limited or private data) that require task-aware protocols, complementary compression techniques, and targeted research into robustness, privacy, and automated teacher/student design.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD encompasses logit/soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online and data-free variants, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Its practical strengths include enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, improving generalization and some robustness properties, and serving as a core component of compression pipelines when used with task-aware design choices. At the same time, KD exhibits clear failure modes—teacher–student mismatch, bias transfer, poor preservation of low-frequency behaviors, and sensitivity to data availability and domain shift—that motivate complementary methods and targeted research into robust, privacy-preserving, and automated distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Mccormick
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for producing compact student models from larger teachers. When designed with attention to which signals to transfer, student capacity and architecture, and distillation-data strategies, and when combined with complementary compression primitives, KD routinely yields favorable tradeoffs between efficiency and performance across modalities. However, KD is not a universal cure: its reliability depends on mitigating failure modes such as transferred biases, degraded rare‑token behavior, teacher–student mismatch, and distributional shift. Treating KD as a configurable, task‑aware element of integrated compression pipelines — rather than a turnkey replacement for other techniques — produces the most reproducible deployments and points to principled research directions for robust, privacy‑aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Ramsey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly effective and widely adopted framework for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD is best understood as a configurable core technique: it provides many transferable signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, contrastive objectives, and synthesized data), and—when combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search and coupled with task‑aware data strategies—can enable large reductions in size and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. However, KD is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data regime, and explicit measures for robustness, privacy, and fairness strongly shape outcomes. Practitioners should therefore treat KD as an essential but non‑turnkey component of integrated compression pipelines, selecting targets, mapping strategies, and safeguards to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: The Centrality and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster ones while preserving much of their performance. Beyond reducing parameter counts and inference latency, distillation enables transferring inductive biases, protecting privacy in federated settings, enabling few- and zero-shot compression, and supporting task-adaptive and automated compression workflows. However, distillation is not a panacea: dataset heterogeneity, teacher–student mismatch, and redundant teacher representations can limit gains. Best practice combines representation-level and layer-aware techniques, multi-teacher or teacher-free strategies where appropriate, and task-aware selection of distilled information to maximize compressed-model utility.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Empirical work across vision, language, recommendation, and multimodal tasks shows KD can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing parameters, latency, and memory. Success is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of transferred signals, and the availability or synthesis of appropriate data. Best practice treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies rather than as a one-shot cure.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Compressing GANs using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been used in several machine learning tasks such as domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation. State-of-the-art GANs often use tens of millions of parameters, making them expensive to deploy for applications in low SWAP (size, weight, and power) hardware, such as mobile devices, and for applications with real time capabilities. There has been no work found to reduce the number of parameters used in GANs. Therefore, we propose a method to compress GANs using knowledge distillation techniques, in which a smaller "student" GAN learns to mimic a larger "teacher" GAN. We show that the distillation methods used on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets can compress teacher GANs at ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, while retaining the quality of the generated image. From our experiments, we observe a qualitative limit for GAN's compression. Moreover, we observe that, with a fixed parameter budget, compressed GANs outperform GANs trained using standard training methods. We conjecture that this is partially owing to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs which allows efficient training using alternating gradient descent. Thus, training an over-parameterized GAN followed by our proposed compression scheme provides a high quality generative model with a small number of parameters.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. A diverse toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, many-to-many layer mappings, projector-based feature transforms, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or adversarial sample synthesis — enables large reductions in parameters and inference cost while often preserving much of teacher performance. Successful application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, how to handle data availability and privacy, and how to combine KD with complementary compression methods such as pruning and quantization. Remaining research challenges include principled theory for objective selection, reliable transfer under data heterogeneity and privacy constraints, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student matching for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques reduce the size and computational cost of large deep models while retaining much of their performance. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs among bias, variance, teacher quality, and data complexity, and shows that distillation interacts with pre-training, label smoothing, and modality differences. Applications span speech and machine translation to GANs and graph neural networks; complementary methods such as pruning and block-structured compression can further improve deployment on constrained hardware.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Practical Deep Learning and NLP: Evidence, Methods, and Remaining Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for transferring capabilities from large teacher models into smaller student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while often preserving much of teacher performance. A large body of work develops variants that match logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, or relational structure, supports multi-teacher and teacher‑free regimes, and combines distillation with data augmentation, adversarial synthesis, or architectural adaptations. Despite robust practical gains, important open problems remain in data‑scarce or privacy‑constrained distillation, transferring fine-grained or low-frequency behaviors, principled layer mapping for heterogeneous architectures, and fairness- and robustness-aware compression.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques provide a practical path to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. Across vision and language, researchers have explored teacher-student training, intermediate-layer alignment, data- and label-space manipulations, data-free or few-shot settings, and architecture-aware compression. These techniques can preserve much of a teacher's performance while yielding smaller, faster models, and they can be combined with pruning, architecture search, or ensemble compression. KD also intersects with concerns about fairness, generalization, and privacy, and its effectiveness depends on design choices such as the form of distilled targets, data augmentation, and the match between teacher, student, and task.

papers_seen.author: Hickman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, deployable student models. Across modalities and tasks, a diverse toolkit — including logits/soft-target matching, feature- and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online and data-free protocols, and hybrid pipelines that combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design — has been shown to deliver large efficiency gains with modest performance loss when applied with task-aware engineering. Important remaining challenges include theoretical understanding of what is transferred, robust and private distillation under data scarcity or distribution shift, and reliably preserving fine-grained or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Path to Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and adaptable strategy for compressing deep models across modalities and tasks. It can preserve much of a teacher's performance while reducing memory, computation, and inference latency; it also enables task-adaptive and privacy-conscious deployments. Remaining challenges—data availability, matching student capacity to teacher signals, and choosing the right transfer targets—can be mitigated by a suite of complementary KD techniques.

papers_seen.author: Holmes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to produce smaller, faster models while preserving much of the performance of large teachers. Approaches vary from matching final logits to transferring internal representations, attention maps, or layer-wise information, and they are applied across modalities including NLP, vision, speech, and reinforcement learning. Practical extensions address multi-teacher setups, data-free scenarios, domain adaptation, quantization, and architecture-aware compression; remaining challenges include handling heterogeneous architectures, data heterogeneity, fairness, and reliably preserving inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Core of Practical Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for producing compact models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. KD offers many targets and protocols—soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation, and data‑free or privacy-aware variants—that routinely improve efficiency while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD’s success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, availability or synthesis of distillation data, and careful objective design; it therefore functions best as a configurable component inside an integrated compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, teacher adaptation, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Zamora
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger or differently structured models to smaller or more efficient ones, reducing computational cost and enabling deployment in resource-constrained settings. Approaches vary in what is transferred (logits/soft labels, intermediate representations, feature maps, attention or decision-boundary information), how the transfer is staged (offline teacher-student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, ensemble distillation, data-free or privacy-preserving setups), and how training data or augmentation is used. Empirical results across computer vision, speech/lipreading, retrieval, translation, reading comprehension, CTR prediction, federated learning, GANs, NAS, and Transformer compression show that appropriate combination of distillation objective, data strategy, and model design can yield large gains in efficiency with modest or no loss in accuracy. Practical factors that shape success include teacher strength and mismatch to the student, the complexity of distilled data, the role of pre-training for compact models, targeted selection or augmentation of distillation samples, and orthogonal compression techniques such as structured pruning.
